18441.q: Which Köppen-Geiger climate zone does most of the Swiss Plateau belong to?
18441.e: Cfb means warm temperate, humid all year, with warm summers. Higher parts of the Alps belong to colder climate types.
18441.m: The Swiss Plateau has a humid temperate climate.

18442.q: What is the figure called that tells you how much the global temperature rises in the long term if the CO2 content doubles?
18442.e: The 2021 international assessment report puts the most likely equilibrium climate sensitivity at about 3 °C. The likely range is 2.5 to 4 °C.
18442.m: Climate sensitivity describes the warming when CO2 content doubles.

18443.q: What is the intergovernmental body founded in 1988 that sums up the state of climate research called?
18443.e: The IPCC was founded in 1988 by UNEP and the WMO. It produces assessment reports but does not do research itself.
18443.m: The IPCC sums up the knowledge of climate research.

18444.q: Which temperature target does the 2015 Paris Agreement set?
18444.e: Warming is to be kept well below 2 °C compared with pre-industrial levels. Efforts are to be made to limit it to 1.5 °C.
18444.m: Paris aims to limit warming to 1.5 °C if possible.

18445.q: Roughly what was the CO2 concentration of the atmosphere before industrialisation?
18445.e: Ice cores show pre-industrial values of about 280 ppm. Today they are over 420 ppm (as of 2025).
18445.m: The CO2 content has risen by about half since industrialisation.

18446.q: Why is Switzerland warming faster than the global average?
a: Land areas warm faster than oceans
Switzerland is closer to the sun
The Gulf Stream ends in Switzerland
18446.e: Oceans store a lot of heat and warm more slowly than land. Switzerland has already become about 2.9 °C warmer since pre-industrial times, about twice as much as the global average (as of 2025).
18446.m: Landlocked countries such as Switzerland warm faster than the global average.

18447.q: Which two main causes contribute to sea level rise?
a: Thermal expansion and melting ice on land
18447.e: Warmer water expands, and melting glaciers and ice sheets bring extra water into the sea. Melting sea ice hardly raises sea level, as it is already floating.
18447.m: Thermal expansion and melting land ice raise the sea level.

18448.q: Which greenhouse gas has a global warming potential about 28 times higher than CO2 over 100 years?
18448.e: Methane is much stronger per molecule but stays in the atmosphere for only about a decade. Important sources are livestock farming, rice growing and fossil fuels.
18448.m: Methane is a short-lived but very powerful greenhouse gas.

18449.q: According to the GLAMOS monitoring network, how did Swiss glaciers change in the record years 2022 and 2023?
a: Together they lost about 10 per cent of their volume
They grew by about 10 per cent
18449.e: According to GLAMOS, about 6 per cent of the ice volume melted in 2022 and about 4 per cent in 2023. 2022 was the largest loss and 2023 the second largest since measurements began.
18449.m: Swiss glaciers are melting faster and faster because of warming.

18450.q: Which enzyme binds CO2 from the air in photosynthesis and is considered the most common protein on Earth?
18450.e: In the Calvin cycle, RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto a sugar with five carbon atoms. This is how carbon from the atmosphere gets into biomass.
18450.m: The enzyme RuBisCO brings carbon from the air into plants.

18451.q: Which store contains far more carbon than the atmosphere and takes up a large part of human CO2?
18451.e: The ocean contains about 50 times as much carbon as the atmosphere. It has taken up about a quarter of human CO2 emissions.
18451.m: The ocean is a huge carbon store.

18452.q: What is the result of seawater taking up CO2?
18452.e: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which lowers the pH. This makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build their limestone shells.
18452.m: More CO2 in the sea lowers the pH of the water.

18453.q: In which rock is most of the Earth's carbon stored in the long term?
18453.e: Limestone and dolomite contain huge amounts of carbon as carbonate. It is only released over geological time spans.
18453.m: Most carbon is locked up in limestone.

18454.q: How many grams of CO2 are produced when 12 g of carbon is burnt completely?
18454.e: C plus O2 gives CO2. The molar mass of CO2 is 12 plus 2 times 16, which equals 44 g/mol.
18454.m: Burning one kilogram of carbon gives about 3.7 kg of CO2.

18455.q: Why is thawing permafrost a problem for the carbon cycle?
a: Stored organic carbon is released as CO2 and methane
Permafrost binds more CO2 when it thaws
18455.e: Frozen soils store a great deal of organic material. When they thaw, microorganisms break it down and release greenhouse gases.
18455.m: Thawing permafrost can strengthen warming even more.

18457.q: What are tropical storms in the western North Pacific called?
18457.e: In the Atlantic and northeastern Pacific they are called hurricanes, in the Indian Ocean cyclones. Physically it is the same phenomenon.
18457.m: Typhoon, hurricane and cyclone describe the same weather phenomenon.

18458.q: From which sea surface temperature can tropical storms typically form?
18458.e: Through evaporation, warm water supplies the energy in the form of latent heat. Below about 26.5 °C there is usually not enough energy.
18458.m: Tropical storms get their energy from warm seawater.

18459.q: Why do tropical storms not form at the equator itself?
a: The Coriolis force is zero there
The water is too cold there
The air is too dry there
18459.e: A vortex needs the Coriolis force to spin. This disappears at the equator, so storms only form from about 5° latitude.
18459.m: Without the Coriolis force, no storm can spin.

18460.q: Which scale is used to classify tornadoes by the damage they cause?
18460.e: The Enhanced Fujita scale goes from EF0 to EF5 and estimates the wind speed from the damage. The Saffir-Simpson scale is used for hurricanes.
18460.m: Tornadoes are classified on the Fujita scale.

18461.q: Which weather situation brought an extreme heatwave to Europe and Switzerland in summer 2003?
18461.e: A stable high blocked the westerly winds for weeks. On 11 August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono in the Grisons, still the Swiss record today (as of 2026).
18461.m: Blocking high-pressure situations can cause long heatwaves.

18462.q: According to the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, roughly how much more water vapour can air hold per 1 °C of warming?
18462.e: Warmer air can hold more water vapour, about 7 per cent per degree. That is why heavy rainfall becomes more intense as the climate warms.
18462.m: Warmer air can store more water and bring heavier rain.

a: A strong downdraught from a thundercloud
A rotating whirl of air at ground level
18463.e: In a downburst, cold air plunges down from a thundercloud and spreads out at ground level. The damage is usually in straight lines, unlike with tornadoes.
18463.m: A downburst is a violent downdraught from a thunderstorm.

18464.q: Which three pillars make up integrated risk management for natural hazards in Switzerland?
18464.e: The cycle consists of prevention (e.g. protective structures), response (emergency action) and recovery (rebuilding). Experience is meant to feed into new precautions.
18464.m: Integrated risk management combines prevention, response and recovery.

18465.q: On Swiss hazard maps, which colour marks areas of considerable danger where building is generally not allowed?
18465.e: Red means considerable danger, blue medium, yellow low and yellow and white residual danger. In red zones there is generally a building ban.
18465.m: On hazard maps, red means no new buildings.

18466.q: How is risk usually defined in natural hazard management?
a: Probability of occurrence times extent of damage
Height above sea level times slope gradient
18466.e: A frequent small event can carry a similar risk to a rare large one. The formula helps to compare protective measures.
18466.m: Risk comes from probability and extent of damage.

18467.q: Which federal institute in Davos issues Switzerland's avalanche bulletin?
a: WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF
18467.e: The SLF in Davos is part of the Swiss Federal Research Institute WSL. In winter it publishes the avalanche bulletin with five danger levels.
18467.m: The SLF in Davos warns of avalanches with the avalanche bulletin.

18468.q: What function does protection forest, which makes up about half of the Swiss forest, fulfil?
a: It protects against avalanches, rockfall and landslides
It is only used for timber production
It increases the risk of earthquakes
18468.e: Trees hold snow, slow down stones and stabilise the ground. According to the Federal Office for the Environment, about half of the Swiss forest area protects against natural hazards.
18468.m: Protection forest is a natural defence against avalanches, rockfall and landslides.

18469.q: Which event buried large parts of the village of Blatten in Valais in May 2025?
a: The collapse of the Birch Glacier
18469.e: On 28 May 2025, the Birch Glacier, loaded with rock debris, collapsed and buried Blatten in the Lötschental. The village had been evacuated beforehand.
18469.m: Early monitoring and evacuation save lives when natural hazards strike.

18470.q: What is the probability that a 100-year flood occurs at least once in 30 years?
18470.e: The probability of no event is 0.99 to the power of 30, so about 0.74. One minus 0.74 gives about 26 per cent.
18470.m: Even rare events are quite likely over a longer period.

18471.q: Which renewable energy source supplies most of the electricity in Switzerland?
18471.e: In 2025, hydropower supplied about 58 per cent of the electricity produced in Switzerland. Storage lakes in the Alps are particularly important.
18471.m: Hydropower is Switzerland's most important source of electricity.

18472.q: How does a pumped storage power station work?
a: It pumps water uphill using surplus electricity and generates electricity when needed
It uses geothermal heat from deep down
18472.e: When there is surplus electricity, water is pumped into an upper reservoir. When demand is high, it flows back through turbines, as at Nant de Drance in Valais.
18472.m: Pumped storage plants store energy as the potential energy of water.

18473.q: Roughly how much energy does 1 m³ of water (1000 kg) have at a drop of 500 m (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
18473.e: Potential energy is m times g times h. 1000 kg times 9.81 m/s² times 500 m gives 4,905,000 J, so about 4.9 MJ.
18473.m: Potential energy depends on mass, gravitational acceleration and height.

18474.q: What is the figure called that tells you what percentage of solar energy a solar cell turns into electricity?
18474.e: Standard silicon modules reach about 20 to 23 per cent efficiency. The rest is reflected or turned into heat.
18474.m: Efficiency shows how much energy is converted into a usable form.

18475.q: Why can a wind turbine never use all the energy of the wind?
a: The air must still be able to flow on behind the rotor
The rotor blades are too short
18475.e: If the wind were stopped completely, no more air could flow in. According to Betz's law, at most about 59 per cent can be used.
18475.m: No wind turbine can use more than about 59 per cent of the wind's energy.

18476.q: How does the power of the wind change when the wind speed doubles?
a: It becomes eight times as large
18476.e: Wind power is proportional to the cube of the speed. 2 to the power of 3 gives 8.
18476.m: Double the wind brings eight times the power.

18477.q: On average, by how much does the temperature in the Earth's crust rise per 100 m of depth (geothermal gradient)?
18477.e: The average geothermal gradient is about 3 °C per 100 m. At a depth of 4 to 5 km the rock is therefore over 100 °C hot and can be used for electricity from deep geothermal energy.
18477.m: The deeper you drill, the warmer the rock gets.

18478.q: Which basic decision on energy did Swiss voters approve in May 2017?
a: Energy Strategy 2050 with a ban on new nuclear power stations
Immediate shutdown of all nuclear power stations
18478.e: The revised Energy Act was approved on 21 May 2017 with about 58 per cent voting yes. It promotes renewable energy and bans new general licences for nuclear power stations.
18478.m: Energy Strategy 2050 relies on efficiency and renewable energy.

18479.q: What colour is the background of the Swiss flag?
18479.e: The background of the Swiss flag is red. The Swiss cross is shown on it.
18479.m: The Swiss flag has a red background.

18480.q: What shape is the Swiss flag?
18480.e: The Swiss flag is as tall as it is wide. That makes it a square.

18481.q: What does it mean when the Swiss flag is only raised halfway?
18481.e: A flag flown halfway up is said to be at half-mast. This shows that people are mourning someone who has died.
18481.m: A flag at half-mast shows mourning.

18482.q: What is the custom called in which a large flag is skilfully thrown and swung through the air?
18482.e: In flag throwing, a flag is swung and tossed up high. You often see it at festivals in Switzerland.
18482.m: Flag throwing is an old Swiss custom.

18483.q: When do especially many people in Switzerland hang up Swiss flags?
18483.e: On National Day many people decorate houses, balconies and gardens with Swiss flags. That is how they celebrate their country.
18483.m: On National Day there are Swiss flags everywhere.

18484.q: How many arms does the Swiss cross have?
18484.e: The Swiss cross has one arm pointing up, one down and one each to the left and right. All the arms are the same length.
18484.m: The Swiss cross has four arms of equal length.

18485.q: Which aid organisation has a symbol that looks like the Swiss flag with the colours swapped?
18485.e: The symbol of the Red Cross is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped. This honours Switzerland, where the organisation was founded.
18485.m: The Red Cross has the colours of the Swiss flag swapped.

18486.q: Where is the cross on the Swiss flag?
18486.e: The cross is exactly in the middle of the flag. There is the same amount of space all around it.
18486.m: The Swiss cross is in the middle of the flag.

18487.q: What does a Swiss cross on a product often show?
18487.e: Companies may only put the Swiss cross on products that largely come from Switzerland. That is how you can recognise Swiss products.
18487.m: A Swiss cross on a product means it comes from Switzerland.

18488.q: Which canton is the youngest canton in Switzerland?
18488.e: The canton of Jura was founded in 1979. Before that, its area belonged to the canton of Bern.
18488.m: Jura is the youngest canton in Switzerland.

18489.q: Which canton is Switzerland named after?
18489.e: The name “Switzerland” comes from the canton of Schwyz. The red flag with the cross also originally comes from there.
18489.m: Switzerland is named after the canton of Schwyz.

18490.q: Which is the largest canton in Switzerland?
18490.e: The Grisons has the largest area of all the cantons. It is very mountainous and has many valleys.
18490.m: The Grisons is the largest canton.

18491.q: Which is the smallest canton in Switzerland?
18491.e: Basel-Stadt has the smallest area of all the cantons. It consists only of the city of Basel and the two municipalities of Riehen and Bettingen.

18492.q: What can you see on the coat of arms of the canton of Valais?
18492.e: The coat of arms of Valais is red and white and shows 13 stars. They stand for the 13 old districts of the canton, called Zenden.
18492.m: There are 13 stars on the coat of arms of Valais.

18493.q: Which animal's head is on the coat of arms of the canton of Uri?
18493.e: The coat of arms of Uri shows a black bull's head on a yellow background. It has a red ring in its nose.
18493.m: There is a bull's head on the coat of arms of Uri.

18494.q: Which person is shown on the coat of arms of the canton of Glarus?
18494.e: The coat of arms of Glarus shows Saint Fridolin as a traveller. He is the patron saint of Glarus.
18494.m: Saint Fridolin is on the coat of arms of Glarus.

18495.q: Which animal is leaping on the coat of arms of the canton of Schaffhausen?
18495.e: A black ram, a male sheep, leaps on the coat of arms of Schaffhausen. It suits the name, because “Schaf” is German for sheep.
18495.m: A ram leaps on the coat of arms of Schaffhausen.

18496.q: How many lions are there on the coat of arms of the canton of Thurgau?
18496.e: The coat of arms of Thurgau shows two golden lions. The background is divided diagonally into white and green.
18496.m: There are two lions on the coat of arms of Thurgau.

18497.q: Which town in Ticino is on Lake Maggiore?
18497.e: Locarno lies on the shore of Lake Maggiore. It is often warm and sunny there.

18498.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of the Grisons?
18498.e: Chur is the capital of the Grisons. It is considered one of the oldest towns in Switzerland.
18498.m: Chur is the capital of the Grisons.

18499.q: In which city is there a famous old monastery library, the Abbey Library?
18499.e: The Abbey Library is in St Gallen. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and has very old books.
18499.m: The Abbey Library is in St Gallen.

18500.q: Which town in the canton of Bern speaks German and French?
18500.e: In French, Biel is called Bienne. It is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

18501.q: In which city does the Swiss parliament meet?
18501.e: Switzerland's parliament and government work in Bern. That is why Bern is called the federal city.
18501.m: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland.

18502.q: Which animals live in the Bear Park in Bern?
18502.e: Bears live in the Bear Park in Bern. The bear is the heraldic animal of the city of Bern.
18502.m: Bears live in the Bear Park in Bern.

18503.q: What is the famous clock tower in Bern's old town called?
18503.e: The Zytglogge is an old tower with an astronomical clock. Shortly before every full hour, figures move on it.
18503.m: The Zytglogge is the clock tower of Bern.

18504.q: What is the building in Bern where the parliament meets called?
18504.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace. The Federal Council also has its offices there.
18504.m: The parliament meets in the Federal Palace.

18505.q: What is the big market in Bern in November with lots of onions called?
18505.e: At the Zibelemärit, farmers sell onions as plaits and figures. It takes place every year on the fourth Monday in November.
18505.m: There are lots of onions at the Zibelemärit.

18506.q: Which is the largest city in Switzerland?
18506.e: Zurich has the most inhabitants. At the end of 2024 there were almost 450,000 people.
18506.m: Zurich is the largest city in Switzerland.

18507.q: On which lake is the city of Zurich?
18507.e: The city of Zurich lies at the lower end of Lake Zurich. In summer many people swim there.

18508.q: Which river flows out of Lake Zurich through the city of Zurich?
18508.e: The Limmat flows out of Lake Zurich right through the old town. Later it flows into a bigger river.

18509.q: What is the spring festival in Zurich called at which the Böögg is burned?
18509.e: At Sechseläuten a snowman made of cotton wool, the Böögg, is burned. The faster its head explodes, the nicer the summer is supposed to be.
18509.m: The Böögg is burned at Sechseläuten.

18510.q: What is the big church with two towers in Zurich's old town called?
18510.e: The Grossmünster is a landmark of Zurich. Its two towers can be seen from far away.

18511.q: Which two countries does the city of Basel border?
18511.e: Basel lies where three countries meet. Switzerland, Germany and France come together there.
18511.m: Basel lies where three countries meet.

18512.q: At what time does the Morgestraich begin at the Basel carnival?
18512.e: On the Monday after Ash Wednesday, all the lights go out at 4 o'clock in the morning. Then drummers and piccolo players march through the city.
18512.m: The Morgestraich begins at four in the morning.

18513.q: What can you see on the coat of arms of Basel-Stadt?
18513.e: The coat of arms of Basel-Stadt shows a black Basel crosier on a white background. It looks like a bishop's staff.
18513.m: The Basel crosier is the symbol of Basel.

18514.q: What do the people of Basel affectionately call their zoo?
18514.e: Basel Zoo is the oldest zoo in Switzerland. In Basel people simply call it “Zolli”.
18514.m: Basel Zoo is called the Zolli.

18515.q: What are the well-known spiced biscuits from Basel called?
18515.e: Basler Läckerli are small, hard gingerbread biscuits with honey and spices. They are known all over Switzerland.
18515.m: Läckerli are gingerbread biscuits from Basel.

18516.q: What is the famous fountain in the harbour of Geneva called?
18516.e: The Jet d'eau shoots water about 140 metres into the air. It is the landmark of Geneva.
18516.m: The Jet d'eau is the landmark of Geneva.

18517.q: Which language do most people in Geneva speak?
18517.e: Geneva is in French-speaking Switzerland. People there mainly speak French.

18518.q: Which big organisation has an important office in Geneva?
18518.e: The United Nations, the UN for short, has its European headquarters in Geneva. People from all over the world meet there.
18518.m: The UN has an office in Geneva.

18519.q: What can you admire in the English Garden in Geneva?
18519.e: The Flower Clock stands in the English Garden. Its face is made of thousands of flowers.
18519.m: Geneva has a clock made of flowers.

18520.q: Which festival is celebrated in Geneva in December with pots made of chocolate?
18520.e: At the Escalade, Geneva remembers an attack in 1602 that was fought off. Children smash a pot made of chocolate.
18520.m: At the Escalade you smash a chocolate pot.

18521.q: What is the famous old wooden bridge in Lucerne called?
18521.e: The Chapel Bridge is a covered wooden bridge over the Reuss. Old paintings hang under its roof.
18521.m: The Chapel Bridge is the landmark of Lucerne.

18522.q: Which animal is shown on the famous monument in the rock in Lucerne?
18522.e: The Lion Monument shows a dying lion carved into the rock. It remembers Swiss soldiers who died in Paris in 1792.
18522.m: There is a stone lion in Lucerne.

18523.q: What is the tower that stands in the water next to the Chapel Bridge called?
18523.e: The Water Tower stands in the river next to the Chapel Bridge. It is octagonal and very old.
18523.m: The Water Tower stands next to the Chapel Bridge.

18524.q: Which mountain is right next to Lucerne?
18524.e: Pilatus is Lucerne's local mountain. The steepest cogwheel railway in the world goes up it.

18525.q: Which animal with large curved horns lives in the Alps?
18525.e: The ibex climbs very skilfully on steep rocks. The males have long, curved horns.
18525.m: The ibex climbs in the Alps.

18526.q: Which Alpine animal whistles loudly when there is danger?
18526.e: Marmots warn each other with a loud whistle. Then they all quickly disappear into their burrow.
18526.m: The marmot whistles when there is danger.

18527.q: Which well-known Alpine flower has white, woolly flowers?
18527.e: Edelweiss grows high up in the mountains. Its flowers are covered with fine white hairs.

18528.q: What do you call a large mass of ice that slowly flows down the valley in the mountains?
18528.e: A glacier forms from snow that turns into ice over many years. The largest glacier in the Alps is the Great Aletsch Glacier.
18528.m: A glacier is a river of ice.

18529.q: In which canton is the Matterhorn?
18529.e: The Matterhorn is in the canton of Valais. It is one of the best-known mountains in the world.

18530.q: Which village lies at the foot of the Matterhorn?
18530.e: Zermatt lies right below the Matterhorn. No ordinary petrol cars drive in the village.
18530.m: Zermatt lies at the foot of the Matterhorn.

18531.q: Roughly how high is the Matterhorn?
18531.e: The Matterhorn is 4,478 metres high. That is about 4,500 metres.
18531.m: The Matterhorn is almost 4,500 metres high.

18532.q: Which neighbouring country does Switzerland share the Matterhorn with?
18532.e: The border with Italy runs over the summit of the Matterhorn. In Italian the mountain is called Monte Cervino.
18532.m: The Matterhorn is on the border with Italy.

18533.e: The Matterhorn has four steep sides and a point. That is why it looks like a pyramid.
18533.m: The Matterhorn looks like a pyramid.

18534.q: What is the famous waterfall near Schaffhausen called?
18534.e: The Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen are one of the most powerful waterfalls in Europe. They are 23 metres high and 150 metres wide.
18534.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

18535.q: Roughly how long is the Rhine?
18535.e: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometres long. It is one of the longest rivers in Europe.
18535.m: The Rhine is about 1,200 kilometres long.

18536.q: Which river forms part of the border between Switzerland and Germany?
18536.e: Between Schaffhausen and Basel the Rhine often flows exactly along the border. Switzerland is on one side and Germany on the other.
18536.m: The Rhine is a border river with Germany.

18537.q: Which is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland?
18537.e: The Aare is almost 300 kilometres long. From its source to its mouth it flows only through Switzerland.
18537.m: The Aare is the longest river entirely in Switzerland.

18538.q: In which canton does the Aare rise?
18538.e: The Aare rises from glaciers in the Bernese Alps. That is near the Grimsel Pass.
18538.m: The Aare rises in the canton of Bern.

18539.q: Which river does the Aare flow into?
18539.e: At Koblenz in the canton of Aargau, the Aare flows into a bigger river. There it often carries more water than that river.
18539.m: The Aare flows into the Rhine.

18540.q: Which two lakes does the Aare flow through in the Bernese Oberland?
18540.e: The Aare first flows through Lake Brienz and then through Lake Thun. Interlaken lies between the lakes.
18540.m: The Aare flows through Lake Brienz and Lake Thun.

18541.q: Which town in the canton of Aargau gets its name from the Aare?
18541.e: Aarau lies on the Aare and is the capital of the canton of Aargau. The name Aargau also comes from the river.
18541.m: Aarau gets its name from the Aare.

18542.q: Which is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share in?
18542.e: Lake Geneva covers about 580 square kilometres. It has the shape of a crescent moon.
18542.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake on which Switzerland lies.

18543.q: What is Lake Geneva called in French?
18543.e: In French-speaking Switzerland, Lake Geneva is called “Lac Léman”. The name is very old.
18543.m: In French, Lake Geneva is called Lac Léman.

18544.q: Which country does Switzerland share Lake Geneva with?
18544.e: The north shore belongs to Switzerland, and a large part of the south shore to France. The border runs through the middle of the lake.
18544.m: Lake Geneva is also in France.

18545.q: Which river flows into Lake Geneva and out again?
18545.e: The Rhône comes from Valais into Lake Geneva. At the other end it flows on into France.
18545.m: The Rhône flows through Lake Geneva.

18546.q: Which castle stands right on the shore of Lake Geneva near Montreux?
18546.e: Chillon Castle stands on a rock in the water. It is one of the best-known castles in Switzerland.
18546.m: Chillon Castle stands on Lake Geneva.

18547.q: Which three countries border Lake Constance?
18547.e: Three countries meet at Lake Constance. Their shores all lie on the same lake.
18547.m: Three countries lie on Lake Constance.

18548.q: Which flower island is in Lake Constance?
18548.e: The island of Mainau is known for its many flowers and gardens. It belongs to Germany.
18548.m: Mainau is the flower island in Lake Constance.

18549.q: Which Swiss canton lies on Lake Constance?
18549.e: Thurgau has a long shore on Lake Constance. Places like Romanshorn and Kreuzlingen are there.

18550.q: Which big river flows into Lake Constance?
18550.e: The Rhine flows into Lake Constance in Austria, not far from Bregenz. It flows out again at Stein am Rhein.
18550.m: The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.

18551.q: What is the Bodensee called in English?
18551.e: In English the Bodensee is called “Lake Constance”. The name comes from the town of Konstanz on the lake.
18551.m: In English the Bodensee is called Lake Constance.

18552.q: How many centimes make one franc?
18552.e: One franc has 100 centimes. So two 50-centime coins together make one franc.

18553.q: Which is the largest Swiss banknote?
18553.e: The largest banknote in Switzerland is worth 1,000 francs (as of 2025). It is purple.
18553.m: The largest banknote is the 1,000-franc note.

18554.e: Every Swiss banknote has its own colour. The 50-franc note is green.

18555.q: You have 2 francs and 50 centimes. How many centimes is that?
18555.m: Two francs and fifty centimes are 250 centimes.

18556.q: Which national language do the most people in Switzerland speak?
18556.e: About 6 out of 10 people in Switzerland mainly speak German. In everyday life they mostly speak Swiss German.
18556.m: German is the most common language in Switzerland.

18557.q: Which national language is spoken almost only in the canton of the Grisons?
18557.e: Romansh is spoken almost only in the canton of the Grisons. It is the smallest national language.
18557.m: Romansh is spoken in the Grisons.

18558.q: What does the Italian word “Grazie” mean in English?
18558.e: You say “Grazie” to thank someone in Italian. In French you say “Merci”.

18559.q: What is the very long wooden musical instrument that is blown in the mountains called?
18559.e: The alphorn is often more than three metres long. In the past people used it to call across long distances in the mountains.
18559.m: The alphorn is a Swiss instrument.

18560.q: What is the Swiss sport called in which two men or women wrestle in sawdust?
18560.e: In Schwingen two people grab each other by short fabric trousers. Whoever puts the other on their back wins.
18560.m: In Schwingen people wrestle in sawdust.

18561.q: Which cheese dish is eaten together from one pot?
18561.e: For fondue, cheese melts in a pot. Everyone dips bread into it on long forks.
18561.m: Fondue is eaten together from one pot.

18562.q: Who visits children in Switzerland on 6 December?
18562.e: On 6 December Samichlaus, the Swiss Saint Nicholas, comes. He brings nuts, mandarins and gingerbread.

18563.q: What happens at the Alpabzug in autumn?
a: The cows come down from the alpine pasture to the valley
People ski down to the valley
People plant trees on the alpine pasture
People build huts on the alpine pasture
18563.e: In summer the cows are up on the alpine pasture. In autumn they are brought down to the valley, decorated with flowers and bells.
18563.m: At the Alpabzug the cows come down to the valley.

18564.q: What do people often light on hills and mountains on the evening of National Day?
18564.e: In the evening big fires burn on many hills. They are called bonfires on the heights.

18565.q: What do children often carry through the streets on the evening of 1 August?
18565.e: Lampions are colourful paper lanterns. They are often painted with Swiss crosses.

18566.e: In the Federal Charter of 1291 three valley communities promised to help each other. This is seen as the beginning of the Swiss Confederation.

18567.q: The Rütli meadow is an important place for 1 August. Which lake is it on?
18567.e: The Rütli meadow is in the canton of Uri, high above Lake Lucerne. Many people visit it on National Day.
18567.m: The Rütli is on Lake Lucerne.

18568.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Ticino?
18568.e: Lugano is the largest town in Ticino, but the capital is Bellinzona with its three castles.
18568.m: The capital of Ticino is Bellinzona, not Lugano.

18569.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Valais?
18569.e: The capital of Valais is called Sion in French and Sitten in German.
18569.m: Sion, Sitten in German, is the capital of Valais.

18570.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Jura?
18570.e: The youngest canton in Switzerland has Delémont as its capital.
18570.m: Delémont is the capital of the canton of Jura.

18571.q: Where are the government and parliament of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden based?
18571.e: Herisau is the seat of the government and cantonal parliament of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. Appenzell is the capital of the neighbouring canton of Innerrhoden.
18571.m: Herisau is the seat of government of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

18572.q: Which place is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden?
18572.e: Stans is the capital of Nidwalden, and Sarnen that of Obwalden.
18572.m: Stans is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden.

18573.q: Which region lies between the Jura and the Alps and is the most densely populated?
18573.e: On the Swiss Plateau, between Lake Geneva and Lake Constance, are most of the big cities, and most people live there.
18573.m: Most people in Switzerland live on the Swiss Plateau.

18574.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland's area belongs to the Alps?
18574.e: The Alps and Pre-Alps together cover about three fifths of Switzerland, the Swiss Plateau almost a third and the Jura about a tenth.
18574.m: About three fifths of Switzerland lies in the Alps.

18575.q: What is the French-speaking part of Switzerland called?
18575.e: French-speaking western Switzerland is called Romandie.
18575.m: The French-speaking west of Switzerland is called Romandie.

18576.q: In which canton is Romansh used as an official language?
18576.e: The Grisons has three languages: German, Italian and Romansh.
18576.m: Romansh is an official language in the canton of the Grisons.

18577.q: In which canton is Italian the only official language?
18577.e: Ticino is the only canton where Italian is the only official language.
18577.m: In Ticino, Italian is the only official language.

18578.q: What is the region with the cantons of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden and Zug called?
18578.e: Central Switzerland lies around Lake Lucerne. The founding cantons of the Confederation are also here.
18578.m: Lucerne, Uri and Schwyz belong to Central Switzerland.

18579.q: With which neighbouring country does Switzerland have the longest border?
18579.e: At more than 700 kilometres, the border with Italy is Switzerland's longest national border.
18579.m: Switzerland's longest border is the one with Italy.

18580.q: With which neighbouring country does Switzerland have the shortest border?
18580.e: The border with Liechtenstein is only about 41 kilometres long and mostly follows the Rhine.
18580.m: Switzerland's shortest national border is the one with Liechtenstein.

18581.q: Which currency do people pay with in Liechtenstein?
18581.e: Liechtenstein has no currency of its own and has used the Swiss franc since 1924.
18581.m: In Liechtenstein people also pay with Swiss francs.

18582.q: Which neighbouring country does the canton of Geneva border?
18582.e: The canton of Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France and is linked to Vaud only by a narrow strip.
18582.m: The canton of Geneva is almost entirely surrounded by France.

18583.q: Which mountain massif does the highest peak in Switzerland belong to?
18583.e: The highest Swiss peak is the main summit of the Monte Rosa massif in Valais.
18583.m: The highest peak in Switzerland belongs to the Monte Rosa massif.

18584.q: Which mountain range lies in the north-west of Switzerland along the border with France?
18584.e: The Jura is a limestone mountain range that stretches from Geneva to Schaffhausen.
18584.m: The Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland.

18585.q: Which Alpine pass links the canton of Uri with Ticino?
18585.e: The Gotthard Pass leads from Andermatt in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino.
18585.m: The Gotthard Pass links Uri with Ticino.

18586.q: Which is the longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland?
18586.e: The Aare is 288 kilometres long and flows from the Bernese Alps to where it joins the Rhine at Koblenz in Aargau.
18586.m: The Aare is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland.

18587.q: Which river from the Engadine carries its water via the Danube to the Black Sea?
18587.e: The Inn rises in the Engadine, flows through Austria and joins the Danube at Passau.
18587.m: The Inn carries water from the Engadine all the way to the Black Sea.

18588.q: Which sea does the water of the Ticino reach?
18588.e: The Ticino flows through Lake Maggiore into the Po, which flows into the Adriatic.
18588.m: The Ticino drains via the Po into the Adriatic.

18590.q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely within Switzerland?
18590.e: Lake Neuchâtel covers about 215 square kilometres and lies entirely on Swiss soil.
18590.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely in Switzerland.

18591.q: Which is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share in?
18591.e: Lake Geneva covers about 580 square kilometres. Almost 60 per cent of it belongs to Switzerland, and the rest, with most of the south shore, to France.
18591.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake with a Swiss share.

18592.q: Apart from Switzerland, which countries lie on Lake Constance?
18592.e: Switzerland, Germany and Austria meet at Lake Constance.
18592.m: Three countries border each other at Lake Constance.

18593.q: Which lake lies partly in Switzerland and partly in Italy?
18593.e: The northern part of Lake Maggiore, with Locarno, belongs to Switzerland, and the larger part to Italy.
18593.m: Lake Maggiore lies in Switzerland and Italy.

18594.q: Which town lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz?
18594.e: The name Interlaken means “between the lakes”.
18594.m: Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.

18595.q: For how many years is the Federal Council elected?
18595.e: The Federal Council is elected for a four-year term after each general election of the National Council.
18595.m: The Federal Council's term of office is four years.

18596.q: How long does the office of President of the Swiss Confederation last?
18596.e: Each year one member of the Federal Council becomes President of the Confederation and chairs the meetings.
18596.m: The presidency of the Confederation changes every year.

18597.q: What is the sharing of Federal Council seats that applied from 1959 to 2003 called?
18597.e: The magic formula shared the seven seats among the four largest parties in the ratio 2 to 2 to 2 to 1.
18597.m: The magic formula shared the Federal Council seats among the large parties.

18598.q: What does the number of National Council seats a canton has depend on?
a: on the age of the canton
18598.e: The 200 seats are shared among the cantons according to their population.
18598.m: Large cantons have more seats in the National Council than small ones.

18599.q: What is the minimum number of National Council seats each canton has?
18599.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees every canton at least one seat in the National Council, even if it has few inhabitants.
18599.m: Every canton has at least one seat in the National Council.

18600.q: Which canton has the most members of the National Council?
18600.e: As the canton with the largest population, Zurich has had 36 seats since the 2023 elections.
18600.m: Zurich has the most seats in the National Council.

18601.q: In which building does the National Council meet?
a: in the Federal Palace in Bern
in the Town Hall in Zurich
in the Palais des Nations in Geneva
in the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
18601.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the parliament building of the Federal Palace in Bern.
18601.m: Parliament meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.

18602.q: How many ordinary sessions does parliament hold each year?
18602.e: There are the spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions, which usually last three weeks each.
18602.m: Parliament meets for four ordinary sessions every year.

18603.q: How many members of the Council of States does the canton of Basel-Stadt have?
18603.e: The former half-cantons, such as Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, each have one member in the Council of States.
18603.m: Basel-Stadt has one seat in the Council of States.

18604.q: Who decides how the members of the Council of States are elected?
18604.e: Elections to the Council of States are regulated by each canton. Most cantons use a majority voting system.
18604.m: Each canton decides for itself how its members of the Council of States are elected.

18605.q: What else is the Council of States called?
18605.e: With 46 members, the Council of States is the smaller of the two chambers of parliament and represents the cantons.
18605.m: The Council of States is the small chamber and represents the cantons.

18606.q: What is needed for parliament to pass a new federal law?
a: The Council of States decides alone.
18606.e: The National Council and the Council of States have equal rights. A law is only passed if both chambers agree on the same text.
18606.m: A federal law needs the approval of the National Council and the Council of States.

18607.q: Since which year have women in Switzerland been allowed to vote and stand for election at federal level?
18607.e: On 7 February 1971 the men voted in favour of women's right to vote and stand for election at federal level.
18607.m: Since 1971 women have had the right to vote at federal level.

18608.q: Which canton was the last to introduce women's right to vote at cantonal level?
18608.e: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court forced Appenzell Innerrhoden to give women the right to vote in the canton.
18608.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce women's right to vote, in 1990.

18609.q: On which three political levels is Switzerland built?
18609.e: In Swiss federalism, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities each have their own tasks.
18609.m: Switzerland is made up of the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.

18610.q: What does a popular initiative need in order to be approved?
a: A majority of the people and of the cantons
Only a majority of the people
Only a majority of the cantons
The approval of the Federal Council
18610.e: Because a popular initiative changes the constitution, both the majority of voters and the majority of the cantons must agree.
18610.m: A popular initiative needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

18611.q: What must the people always vote on?
a: on changes to the Federal Constitution
on the election of the Federal Council
18611.e: Changes to the constitution are subject to a mandatory referendum. People only vote on laws if a referendum is called.
18611.m: Every change to the Federal Constitution is put to the people.

18612.q: On how many dates per year are federal votes usually held?
18612.e: The Federal Council usually sets four voting Sundays each year.
18612.m: There are usually four federal voting Sundays each year.

18613.q: Which canton was the first to introduce a voting age of 16 in 2007?
18613.e: In 2007 the Landsgemeinde in Glarus decided that young people from the age of 16 may have a say in the canton.
18613.m: In 2007 Glarus became the first canton with a voting age of 16.

18614.q: How many cantonal votes are there in total in a vote?
18614.e: Twenty cantons have a full cantonal vote and six cantons have half a vote. 20 plus 6 times 0.5 makes 23.
18614.m: There are 23 cantonal votes in total.

18615.q: In which year will the next general election of the National Council take place (as of 2026)?
18615.e: The National Council is elected every four years. After the 2023 election, the next one follows in autumn 2027.
18615.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

18616.q: Which system is used to elect the National Council in most cantons?
18616.e: With proportional representation, parties get seats in proportion to their votes. Only cantons with one seat use majority voting.
18616.m: The National Council is mostly elected by proportional representation.

18617.q: What is it called when you write names of candidates from other lists onto an election list?
18617.e: With panachage you mix candidates from different parties on one list.
18617.m: Mixing names from different lists is called panachage.

18618.q: Which party won the largest share of the vote in the 2023 National Council elections?
18618.e: In 2023 the SVP won about 28 per cent of the vote and remained the party with the most voters.
18618.m: The SVP was the strongest party in 2023.

18619.q: In which year did Switzerland get its first Federal Constitution?
18619.e: With the Federal Constitution of 1848, Switzerland changed from a confederation of states into a federal state.
18619.m: Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848.

18620.q: Since when has today's Federal Constitution been in force?
18620.e: The people and the cantons approved the new constitution in 1999. It came into force on 1 January 2000.
18620.m: Today's Federal Constitution has been in force since 2000.

18621.q: What is the most important law in Switzerland, which also contains the fundamental rights, called?
18621.e: The Federal Constitution stands above all other laws. It sets out the fundamental rights and how the state is organised.
18621.m: The Federal Constitution is the most important law in Switzerland.

18622.q: How many national languages does the Federal Constitution name?
18622.e: Article 4 names German, French, Italian and Romansh as national languages.

18623.q: What is Bern officially called as the seat of the Federal Council and parliament?
18623.e: Officially, Switzerland has no capital. Bern is the federal city.
18623.m: Bern is officially the federal city of Switzerland.

18624.q: At which congress was Switzerland's neutrality recognised by the great powers in 1815?
18624.e: At the Congress of Vienna after the Napoleonic Wars, the European powers recognised Switzerland's permanent neutrality.
18624.m: Switzerland's neutrality was recognised at the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

18625.q: Which organisation is neutral Switzerland NOT a member of?
18625.e: As a neutral state, Switzerland does not belong to any military alliance.
18625.m: Neutral Switzerland does not belong to any military alliance.

18626.q: What are neutral Switzerland's mediation work and protecting power mandates called?
18626.e: Through its good offices, Switzerland mediates between states or represents countries that have no relations with each other.
18626.m: Through its good offices, Switzerland helps to mediate in conflicts.

18627.q: After which defeat in 1515 did the Confederation withdraw from the wars of the great powers?
18627.e: After the defeat at Marignano in northern Italy, the Confederates gave up playing power politics. This is seen as the beginning of neutrality.
18627.m: After Marignano in 1515, Switzerland began to stay out of foreign wars.

18628.q: Which three communities made the Federal Charter in 1291?
18628.e: The Federal Charter of early August 1291 is seen as the founding document of the Confederation.
18628.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made the Federal Charter in 1291.

18629.q: In which year did the Battle of Morgarten take place?
18629.e: At Morgarten in 1315, the men of Schwyz defeated a Habsburg army.
18629.m: The Battle of Morgarten was in 1315.

18630.q: According to legend, which hero sacrificed himself in the Battle of Sempach in 1386?
18630.e: According to legend, Winkelried grabbed the enemy's lances and so opened a gap for the Confederates.
18630.m: Arnold Winkelried is the legendary hero of the Battle of Sempach.

18631.q: What was the unitary state that the French set up in Switzerland in 1798 called?
18631.e: After the French invasion, the Helvetic Republic replaced the Old Swiss Confederacy from 1798 to 1803.
18631.m: The Helvetic Republic was created in 1798 under French influence.

18632.q: What is Switzerland's last civil war of 1847 called?
18632.e: In the Sonderbund War the liberal cantons defeated seven Catholic conservative cantons.
18632.m: The Sonderbund War of 1847 was Switzerland's last civil war.

18633.q: According to legend, in which place did William Tell shoot the apple off his son's head?
18633.e: On the village square of Altdorf in the canton of Uri, a monument recalls the apple shot.
18633.m: William Tell's apple shot took place in Altdorf.

18634.q: Which man from Geneva founded the Red Cross and received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901?
18634.e: Henry Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859 and then proposed founding the Red Cross.
18634.m: Henry Dunant is the founder of the Red Cross.

18635.q: Which writer wrote the stories about “Heidi”?
18635.e: Johanna Spyri from Hirzel published the Heidi books in 1880 and 1881.
18635.m: Johanna Spyri is the author of “Heidi”.

18636.q: Which physicist developed the special theory of relativity in Bern in 1905?
18636.e: Einstein was working at the patent office in Bern at the time and published several groundbreaking papers in 1905.
18636.m: Albert Einstein developed the theory of relativity in Bern.

18637.q: Which world-famous architect comes from La Chaux-de-Fonds?
18637.e: Le Corbusier's real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret. Several of his buildings are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
18637.m: Le Corbusier was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds.

18638.q: How many Grand Slam singles titles did Roger Federer win?
18638.e: Between 2003 and 2018 Federer won twenty Grand Slam singles tournaments, eight of them at Wimbledon.
18638.m: Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slam titles.

18639.q: Which educator from Zurich wanted children to learn with “head, heart and hand”?
18639.e: Around 1800 Pestalozzi worked for the education of poor children and shaped state schooling.
18639.m: Pestalozzi wanted children to learn with head, heart and hand.

18640.q: In which town does the food company Nestlé have its headquarters?
18640.e: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva.

18641.e: Gottlieb Duttweiler first sold goods from lorries. Later he turned Migros into cooperatives.

18642.q: What does the abbreviation SBB stand for?
18642.e: Swiss Federal Railways was formed in 1902 from several private railway companies.
18642.m: SBB stands for Swiss Federal Railways.

18643.q: In which city do the pharmaceutical companies Roche and Novartis have their headquarters?
18643.e: Basel is the centre of the Swiss pharmaceutical and chemical industry.

18644.q: Which industry is especially important in the Jura arc from Geneva to Schaffhausen?
18644.e: Places such as La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle and Biel are known worldwide for making watches.
18644.m: Many Swiss watches are made in the Jura arc.

18645.q: What did an engineer from French-speaking Switzerland invent after finding burrs in his dog's fur?
18645.e: George de Mestral saw how the tiny hooks of the burrs held on to the fur. Using this as a model, he made the hook-and-loop fastener, known as Velcro, and patented it in 1951.
18645.m: The hook-and-loop fastener was invented in Switzerland.

18646.q: Which kitchen tool from Switzerland is called “Rex”?
18646.e: The “Rex” peeler was invented in Switzerland in 1947. With its moving blade you can peel potatoes and carrots thinly.
18646.m: The “Rex” peeler is a Swiss invention.

18647.q: Which sweet was invented in 1875 in Vevey on Lake Geneva?
18647.e: Daniel Peter was the first to mix condensed milk into chocolate. This created milk chocolate, for which Switzerland is famous.
18647.m: Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland.

18648.q: What is the see-through film called that a Swiss chemist invented in 1908?
18648.e: Jacques Brandenberger wanted to make a tablecloth that stains would not stick to. In doing so he invented the see-through film cellophane.

18649.q: Which world-famous tool did Karl Elsener from Ibach in Schwyz have made for the army from 1891?
18649.e: Karl Elsener supplied the Swiss army with soldiers' knives. In 1897 he developed the officer's knife, which is known all over the world today.
18649.m: The Swiss Army knife comes from Ibach in Schwyz.

18650.q: According to the Federal Constitution, what applies to tasks that are not expressly assigned to the Confederation?
a: They remain a matter for the cantons
They automatically pass to the Confederation
They are regulated by the EU
18650.e: Article 3 of the Federal Constitution states that the cantons are sovereign as long as the Federal Constitution does not limit their sovereignty.
18650.m: Whatever the Constitution does not assign to the Confederation remains a matter for the cantons.

18651.q: Which principle states that a task should be carried out by the lowest level of government able to do it?
18651.e: Since the NFA reform, the principle of subsidiarity has been expressly laid down in Article 5a of the Federal Constitution. The Confederation only takes on tasks that the cantons cannot solve themselves.
18651.m: The higher level only steps in when the lower one cannot manage a task.

18652.q: Which reform came into force in 2008 and reorganised tasks and money flows between the Confederation and the cantons?
a: Total revision of the Federal Constitution
18652.e: The NFA was approved by the people in 2004 and came into force on 1 January 2008. It separated tasks and created equalisation of resources and burdens.
18652.m: Fiscal equalisation partly balances out the differences between financially strong and weak cantons.

18653.q: What is a contractual agreement between two or more cantons called?
18653.e: Under Article 48 of the Federal Constitution, cantons can conclude agreements with each other, called concordats. One example is the HarmoS concordat on schools.
18653.m: With concordats, cantons carry out shared tasks without the Confederation.

18654.q: Which body must guarantee a new cantonal constitution before it is recognised by the Confederation?
18654.e: Under Articles 51 and 172 of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly guarantees cantonal constitutions if they do not contradict federal law.
18654.m: Cantonal constitutions must not contradict federal law.

18655.q: How many cantonal votes are there in total when the majority of the cantons is determined?
18655.e: 20 cantons each have one whole cantonal vote and 6 cantons each have half a vote. That gives 20 + 3 = 23 cantonal votes.
18655.m: Six cantons count for only half a vote in the majority of the cantons.

18656.q: Which canton became part of the Swiss Confederation in 1979 as the youngest canton?
18656.e: The canton of Jura split off from the canton of Bern and, after the federal vote of 1978, became a canton of its own on 1 January 1979.
18656.m: Jura is the youngest of the 26 cantons.

18657.q: In which year were women given the right to vote and stand for election at federal level?
18657.e: On 7 February 1971 the male voters approved women’s suffrage at federal level. A first attempt had failed in 1959.
18657.m: Since 1971 Swiss women have been able to vote and stand for election nationally.

18658.q: Which canton had to introduce women’s suffrage at cantonal level in 1990 because of a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court?
18658.e: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court ruled that excluding women breached the equality before the law guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton without women’s suffrage.
18658.m: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court enforced equal rights in the last canton too.

18659.q: Which canton was the first to introduce a voting age of 16 at cantonal level, in 2007?
18659.e: In 2007 the Glarus Landsgemeinde decided to give the right to vote from the age of 16. At federal level the age is still 18.
18659.m: In 2007 Glarus led the way with voting from the age of 16.

18660.q: What is the open-air assembly called at which people in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden vote on issues?
18660.e: At the Landsgemeinde, voters vote openly by raising their hands. Today it exists only in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
18660.m: The Landsgemeinde is regarded as one of the oldest forms of direct democracy in Switzerland.

18661.q: What does the “double majority” mean in a federal vote?
a: A majority of the people and of the cantons
A majority in both chambers of parliament
A majority of the Federal Council and parliament
18661.e: The popular majority is the majority of valid votes in the whole country, and the cantonal majority is the majority of the cantons. In this way populous cantons cannot simply outvote the small ones.
18661.m: With the double majority, both the people and a majority of the cantons must agree.

18662.q: Since which year has the voting age at federal level been 18?
18662.e: Lowering the voting age from 20 to 18 was approved by the people and the cantons on 3 March 1991.
18662.m: Anyone aged 18 may vote nationally in Switzerland.

18663.q: How many regular voting dates are planned each year at federal level?
18663.e: Each year the Federal Council sets four provisional voting dates, usually in February or March, May or June, September and November.
18663.m: Swiss voters can go to the polls four times a year.

18664.q: Which French philosopher described the separation of state powers in “The Spirit of the Laws” in 1748?
18664.e: Montesquieu called for the separation of legislative, executive and judicial power in order to prevent abuse of power.
18664.m: The separation of powers goes back to Montesquieu.

18665.q: Which power does the Federal Council represent in the system of separation of powers?
18665.e: The Federal Council is the supreme governing and executive authority of the Confederation (Article 174 of the Federal Constitution) and therefore the executive.
18665.m: The Federal Council implements the laws and runs the administration.

18666.q: According to Article 190 of the Federal Constitution, what may the Federal Supreme Court not do with federal laws?
a: Refuse to apply them, even if they are unconstitutional
Apply them to an individual case
18666.e: Article 190 of the Federal Constitution obliges the Federal Supreme Court to apply federal laws. That is why there is no full constitutional review of federal laws in Switzerland.
18666.m: In Switzerland, parliament has the last word over the Federal Supreme Court on federal laws.

18667.q: Which rule forbids a member of the Federal Council from also being a member of the National Council?
18667.e: Article 144 of the Federal Constitution regulates incompatibilities. Members of the National Council, Council of States, Federal Council and Federal Supreme Court may not belong to another of these bodies at the same time.
18667.m: The separation of powers between people prevents holding several offices.

18668.q: Which body elects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court?
18668.e: The National Council and the Council of States elect the federal judges together as the United Federal Assembly, each time for six years.
18668.m: Federal judges are elected by parliament.

18669.q: Where does the Federal Supreme Court have its main seat?
18669.e: The Federal Supreme Court has its seat in Lausanne. Two social law divisions are located in Lucerne.
18669.m: Switzerland’s highest judicial authority is based in Lausanne.

18670.q: What is meant by the “vertical separation of powers” in Switzerland?
a: The division of power between the Confederation, cantons and municipalities
The separation of parliament and government
The election of judges by the people
The division of parliament into two chambers
18670.e: Besides the horizontal separation into legislative, executive and judiciary, power is also divided between the three levels of government.
18670.m: Federalism also divides state power between the levels of government.

18671.q: How many valid signatures does a federal popular initiative need?
18671.e: Under Article 139 of the Federal Constitution, 100,000 signatures from voters are needed. The number was doubled in 1977.
18671.m: A popular initiative needs a hundred thousand signatures.

18672.q: Within what period must the signatures for a federal popular initiative be collected?
18672.e: The collection period begins with publication in the Federal Gazette and lasts 18 months.
18672.m: Initiative committees have a year and a half to collect signatures.

18673.q: Since which year has the popular initiative for a partial revision of the Federal Constitution existed at federal level?
18673.e: The initiative for a partial revision was introduced in 1891. The initiative for a total revision had existed since 1848.
18673.m: Since 1891 the people have been able to propose individual articles of the Constitution.

18674.q: Which reason obliges the Federal Assembly to declare a popular initiative invalid?
a: A breach of mandatory provisions of international law
A contradiction with a federal law
18674.e: Article 139 of the Federal Constitution lists as grounds for invalidity a breach of the unity of form, the unity of subject matter or mandatory provisions of international law.
18674.m: An initiative must not breach mandatory international law.

18675.q: What does the principle of “unity of subject matter” govern in popular initiatives?
a: There must be a factual connection between the parts of an initiative
An initiative may only concern one canton
All signatures must come from the same municipality
An initiative may only contain a single sentence
18675.e: Voters should be able to express their will without distortion. That is why several unrelated issues may not be bundled into one proposal.
18675.m: An initiative should only combine questions that belong together in substance.

18676.q: What is an “indirect counter-proposal” to a popular initiative?
a: A change in the law that partly meets the initiative’s demand
A competing constitutional amendment on the same ballot paper
A withdrawal by the Federal Council
18676.e: With an indirect counter-proposal, parliament changes a law instead of the Constitution. The committee often withdraws the initiative afterwards.
18676.m: An indirect counter-proposal works at the level of the law.

18677.q: What is the purpose of the tie-break question, asked since 1987 when there is an initiative and a direct counter-proposal?
a: It decides which proposal applies if both are accepted
It decides whether the initiative is valid
It replaces the majority of the cantons
It sets the date of entry into force
18677.e: Since 1987 voting yes to both has been allowed. If both proposals are accepted, the tie-break question decides which one comes into force.
18677.m: With the tie-break question, the people choose between two accepted proposals.

18678.q: Which popular initiative on old-age pensions was accepted by the people and the cantons on 3 March 2024?
a: Pensions initiative with a higher retirement age
Initiative for an unconditional basic income
18678.e: The initiative “For a better life in old age” was accepted with about 58 per cent voting yes. The pensions initiative was rejected on the same day.
18678.m: In March 2024 the people and the cantons said yes to an extra monthly AHV pension payment.

18679.q: Within what period must an optional referendum be achieved?
18679.e: The period begins with the official publication of the act and lasts 100 days.
18679.m: There is only a short time to collect signatures against a new federal law.

18680.q: How many cantons together can call a cantonal referendum?
18680.e: Eight cantons can demand an optional referendum. This right was used successfully for the first time in 2003 against the tax package.
18680.m: Cantons can also force a popular vote on a federal law.

18681.q: Which proposal is always subject to the mandatory referendum?
a: Every amendment to the Federal Constitution
Every ordinance of the Federal Council
18681.e: Under Article 140 of the Federal Constitution, constitutional amendments must always be put to the people and the cantons. A double majority is required.
18681.m: The Federal Constitution does not change without the approval of the people and the cantons.

18682.q: Which majority is required in an optional referendum against a federal law?
a: Popular majority and majority of the cantons
Only the majority of the cantons
18682.e: In referendums on laws, only the majority of valid votes in the whole country counts. The majority of the cantons plays no role.
18682.m: On laws, the majority of voters alone decides.

18683.q: Which proposal did the people and the cantons narrowly reject in a mandatory referendum on 6 December 1992?
18683.e: Joining the EEA was rejected with 50.3 per cent voting no, with a turnout of about 78 per cent.
18683.m: The 1992 EEA decision still shapes Switzerland’s European policy today.

18684.q: Since which year has Switzerland had the optional referendum on laws at federal level?
18684.e: The optional referendum was introduced with the total revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874.
18684.m: The 1874 Constitution gave the people the right to challenge laws.

18685.q: What applies to a federal law declared urgent that has no constitutional basis?
a: It must be put to the people and the cantons within one year
It can never be put to a vote
It applies only to the cantons
It requires the approval of the Federal Supreme Court
18685.e: Urgent federal laws come into force immediately. If there is no constitutional basis, they are subject to the mandatory referendum and lapse after one year if not accepted.
18685.m: Even in urgent cases the people keep the last word.

18686.q: Who is regarded as the main author of the Swiss Civil Code?
18686.e: The lawyer Eugen Huber drew up the Civil Code, which was passed in 1907 and came into force in 1912.
18686.m: The Civil Code bears the mark of Eugen Huber.

18687.q: In which year did the Swiss Criminal Code come into force?
18687.e: The Criminal Code was passed by parliament in 1937, approved by the people on 3 July 1938 and came into force on 1 January 1942. With it, the death penalty was also abolished in civilian criminal law.
18687.m: Since 1942 a single criminal law has applied throughout Switzerland.

18688.q: What does Article 2 of the Civil Code require of everyone when exercising their rights and duties?
18688.e: Article 2 of the Civil Code requires acting in good faith. The obvious abuse of a right is not protected by law.
18688.m: Anyone who abuses a right is not protected by the law.

18689.q: Where is the Federal Administrative Court?
18689.e: The Federal Administrative Court has had its seat in St Gallen since 2012. It rules on appeals against decisions of the federal administration.
18689.m: Disputes with the federal administration often end up first in St Gallen.

18690.q: Since when has a uniform Code of Criminal Procedure and Code of Civil Procedure applied throughout Switzerland?
18690.e: Before that, each canton had its own rules of procedure. Since 1 January 2011 the federal Criminal and Civil Procedure Codes have applied.
18690.m: Since 2011 court cases follow the same rules in all cantons.

18691.q: What does Article 1 of the Civil Code allow the court to do if the law contains no provision?
a: Decide according to the rule it would make as legislator
Send the case back to parliament
18691.e: If there is no legal rule, the court decides according to customary law and otherwise as it would decide as legislator.
18691.m: The court fills gaps in the law by acting like the legislator.

18692.q: Which legal family does Swiss law belong to?
18692.e: Swiss law is based mainly on written codes such as the Civil Code, the Code of Obligations and the Criminal Code. This is typical of the continental European legal tradition.
18692.m: In Switzerland, written laws are at the centre of the administration of justice.

18693.q: Which industry accounts for the largest share of Swiss goods exports?
18693.e: In 2025 chemical and pharmaceutical products made up about half of Swiss goods exports. Basel is the centre of this industry.
18693.m: The pharmaceutical industry is Switzerland’s most important export sector.

18694.q: Which economic sector employs the vast majority of working people in Switzerland?
18694.e: About three quarters of working people work in the service sector, for example in trade, banking, health and education.
18694.m: Switzerland is now a service society.

18695.q: Which 1937 agreement in the metal and engineering industry is regarded as the foundation of social partnership?
18695.e: In the Peace Agreement, employers and trade unions committed themselves to resolving conflicts through negotiation instead of strikes.
18695.m: Swiss social partners usually resolve conflicts at the negotiating table.

18696.q: What is the standard rate of VAT in Switzerland (as of 2026)?
18696.e: Since 1 January 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent, previously 7.7 per cent. The increase helps to fund the AHV.
18696.m: Swiss VAT is low compared with the rest of Europe.

18697.q: Which mechanism obliges the Confederation not to spend more than it takes in over an economic cycle?
18697.e: The debt brake was approved in 2001 with about 85 per cent voting yes and has applied since 2003. Deficits are allowed in bad years, but surpluses must be made in good years.
18697.m: The debt brake is meant to stop federal debt from growing permanently.

18698.q: Which authority in Switzerland watches over cartels and company mergers?
18698.e: COMCO enforces the Cartel Act. It can impose sanctions for unlawful agreements that restrict competition.
18698.m: The Competition Commission protects free competition.

18699.q: What share of Swiss companies are SMEs with fewer than 250 employees?
18699.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, more than 99 per cent of companies are SMEs. They provide about two thirds of jobs.
18699.m: Small and medium-sized enterprises are the backbone of the Swiss economy.

18700.q: Since which year has the three-pillar principle of old-age provision been laid down in the Federal Constitution?
18700.e: In 1972 the people and the cantons approved the constitutional article on the three-pillar principle: state, occupational and private provision.
18700.m: Switzerland’s old-age provision rests on three pillars.

18701.q: By which method is the AHV mainly funded?
18701.e: The contributions of today’s working people directly pay the current pensions. The Confederation also makes contributions.
18701.m: With the AHV, working people fund the pensions of retired people.

18702.q: What is the minimum conversion rate in the compulsory part of occupational pension provision (as of 2026)?
18702.e: The rate is 6.8 per cent. The occupational pensions reform, which planned a reduction to 6.0 per cent, was rejected in September 2024.
18702.m: The conversion rate determines how much pension comes from the capital saved in the pension fund.

18703.q: In which year was the AHV introduced?
18703.e: The people clearly approved the AHV Act in 1947, and the first pensions were paid out on 1 January 1948.
18703.m: The AHV is Switzerland’s most important social insurance.

18704.q: What is the total AHV contribution rate on employees’ earned income (without disability and loss of earnings insurance, as of 2026)?
18704.e: The AHV contribution is 8.7 per cent and is paid half by the employer and half by the employee, so 4.35 per cent each.
18704.m: Employers and employees each pay half of the AHV contributions.

18705.q: What is the lowest regular deductible in compulsory health insurance for adults (as of 2026)?
18705.e: Adults can choose a deductible of between 300 and 2,500 francs. A higher deductible lowers the premium but increases the cost risk. In 2026 the Federal Council proposed raising the minimum deductible.
18705.m: With a high deductible you pay lower premiums but cover more costs yourself.

18706.q: Which pillar of old-age provision includes the restricted, tax-advantaged saving of Pillar 3a?
18706.e: The third pillar is voluntary private provision. Payments into Pillar 3a can be deducted from taxable income up to a maximum amount.
18706.m: Anyone who pays voluntarily into Pillar 3a saves tax.

18707.q: In which year did Switzerland join the UN as a full member?
18707.e: After a popular initiative was accepted in March 2002, Switzerland became the 190th member of the UN in September 2002. In 1986 membership had still been clearly rejected.
18707.m: Switzerland has been a UN member since 2002.

18708.q: In which years was Switzerland a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for the first time?
18708.e: In 2022 the UN General Assembly elected Switzerland to the Security Council for the 2023 to 2024 term.
18708.m: Switzerland sat on the UN Security Council in 2023 and 2024.

18709.q: What is meant by a Swiss protecting power mandate?
a: Switzerland represents the interests of one state in another state with which it has no diplomatic relations
Switzerland protects a country with its own troops
Switzerland guards a foreign embassy in Bern
Switzerland takes over the administration of a foreign territory
18709.e: A well-known example is the mandate for the USA in Iran since 1980. Such mandates are part of Switzerland’s good offices.
18709.m: As a protecting power, Switzerland keeps channels open between hostile states.

18710.q: In which year did Switzerland join the Council of Europe?
18710.e: Switzerland has been a member of the Council of Europe since 1963 and ratified the European Convention on Human Rights in 1974.
18710.m: Switzerland has belonged to the Council of Europe since 1963.

18711.q: Which negotiations did the Federal Council break off in May 2021?
a: The negotiations on the institutional framework agreement with the EU
The negotiations on joining the UN
The negotiations on the free trade agreement with China
18711.e: After years of talks, the Federal Council ended the negotiations on the institutional agreement on 26 May 2021 because important differences remained.
18711.m: Relations with the EU remain a central issue of Swiss foreign policy.

18712.q: Which department of the federal administration is responsible for foreign policy?
18712.e: The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs conducts foreign policy. The SDC for development cooperation also belongs to it.
18712.m: The FDFA is responsible for relations with other countries.

18713.q: In which year did the Swiss people approve association with Schengen and Dublin?
18713.e: The agreement was accepted on 5 June 2005. Operational participation began at the end of 2008.
18713.m: Switzerland is part of the Schengen area, even though it is not an EU member.

18714.q: In which city does the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) have its seat?
18714.e: The BIS was founded in 1930 and has its seat in Basel. It is regarded as the bank of central banks.
18714.m: The world’s central banks work together in Basel.

18715.q: Which UN specialised agency has its headquarters in Bern?
18715.e: The Universal Postal Union was founded in Bern in 1874 and still has its seat there. It regulates international postal services.
18715.m: The federal city of Bern is the seat of the Universal Postal Union.

18716.q: In which year was the International Committee of the Red Cross founded in Geneva?
18716.e: Henry Dunant and other people from Geneva founded the committee in 1863. A year later the first Geneva Convention was created.
18716.m: The Red Cross has its origins in Geneva.

18717.q: Which research organisation runs the world’s largest particle accelerator near Geneva?
18717.e: CERN was founded in 1954 and runs the Large Hadron Collider, with a circumference of about 27 kilometres, on the border with France.
18717.m: At CERN near Geneva, scientists study the structure of matter.

18718.q: Which organisation based in Geneva regulates world trade and settles trade disputes?
18718.e: The World Trade Organization was founded in 1995 as the successor to GATT and has its seat in Geneva.
18718.m: The rules of world trade are negotiated in Geneva.

18719.q: Which organisation had its seat in Geneva from 1920 to 1946?
18719.e: The League of Nations was founded after the First World War. Its building, the Palais des Nations, is now used by the UN.
18719.m: Since the League of Nations, Geneva has been a centre of international diplomacy.

18720.q: In which city does the International Olympic Committee have its seat?
18720.e: The IOC moved its seat to Lausanne in 1915 under Pierre de Coubertin. That is why the city calls itself the Olympic capital.
18720.m: Many international sports federations have their seat in Switzerland.

18721.q: At which congress or in which treaty of 1815 did the great powers recognise Switzerland’s permanent neutrality?
a: Congress of Vienna and Second Peace of Paris
18721.e: The great powers recognised neutrality in Paris on 20 November 1815, following the Congress of Vienna.
18721.m: Switzerland’s neutrality has been recognised under international law since 1815.

18722.q: Which international convention of 1907 governs the law of neutrality in land warfare?
18722.e: The Fifth Hague Convention of 1907 sets out the rights and duties of neutral states in land warfare, for example the ban on providing troops to warring parties.
18722.m: The law of neutrality essentially dates from 1907.

18723.q: How does neutrality policy differ from the law of neutrality?
a: It covers voluntary measures with which a state makes its neutrality credible
It is laid down as binding in the Hague Convention
It applies only to cantons in peacetime
It forbids any participation in economic sanctions
18723.e: The law of neutrality contains obligations under international law in times of war. The Federal Council decides neutrality policy flexibly depending on the situation.
18723.m: Neutrality policy is room for manoeuvre; the law of neutrality is an obligation.

a: Switzerland defends its neutrality with its own army
Switzerland supplies weapons to all warring parties
Switzerland is a member of a military alliance
Switzerland does without any military at all
18724.e: A neutral state must be able to protect its own territory. That is why Switzerland maintains a militia army.
18724.m: Neutrality requires the ability to defend one’s own territory.

18725.q: Which form of neutrality did Switzerland practise after joining the League of Nations, from 1920 to 1938?
18725.e: Switzerland took part in the League of Nations’ economic sanctions, but not in military ones. In 1938 it returned to integral neutrality.
18725.m: Between the world wars, Switzerland took part in economic sanctions.

18726.q: Which NATO initiative did Switzerland join in 1996 without becoming a member?
18726.e: The Partnership for Peace allows cooperation in training and peacebuilding without any obligation to provide assistance.
18726.m: Switzerland works with NATO but is not a member.

18727.q: Which decision by the Federal Council in February 2022 sparked a broad debate about neutrality?
a: Adopting the EU sanctions against Russia
18727.e: After the Russian attack on Ukraine, Switzerland adopted the EU’s sanctions. The Federal Council considered this compatible with the law of neutrality.
18727.m: Economic sanctions are in principle compatible with the law of neutrality.

18728.q: How were the seven Federal Council seats distributed under the “magic formula” from 1959 to 2003?
18728.e: In 1959 the major parties agreed on this distribution. In 2003 the SVP gained a second seat at the expense of the CVP.
18728.m: The magic formula stands for consensus in the Swiss government.

18729.q: Which two parties merged in 2021 to form “The Centre”?
18729.e: The CVP and the BDP merged on 1 January 2021 to form the party “The Centre”.
18729.m: The Centre was created in 2021 from the merger of two parties.

18730.q: Which party emerged in 1971 from the Party of Farmers, Traders and Citizens (BGB)?
