19038.m: Particles can also behave like waves.

19039.q: Which physicist, professor at ETH Zurich from 1928, formulated the exclusion principle for electrons?
19039.e: The Pauli exclusion principle states that two electrons in an atom cannot have all the same quantum numbers. Wolfgang Pauli received the Nobel Prize for this in 1945.
19039.m: Two electrons in an atom can never be in exactly the same state.

19040.q: At how many degrees does water boil at sea level?
19040.e: At sea level, pure water starts to boil at 100 degrees Celsius. High up in the mountains it boils at a little less than 100 degrees.
19040.m: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees.

19041.q: What colour is clean water in a glass?
19041.e: Clean water is clear and see-through. You can look through a glass of water.
19041.m: Clean water is clear and see-through.

19042.q: What does clean drinking water smell of?
19042.e: Pure water has no smell and no taste. If water smells strange, you should not drink it.

19043.q: Where does most of the drinking water in Switzerland come from?
19043.e: In Switzerland, about 80 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
19043.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.

19044.q: What happens to a puddle on a hot day?
19044.e: The sun warms the water, and it slowly goes into the air as invisible vapour. That is how the puddle disappears.
19044.m: Puddles dry up in the sun.

19045.q: What is water like at room temperature?
19045.e: At room temperature water is liquid. You can pour it and drink it.
19045.m: At room temperature water is liquid.

19046.q: Where on Earth is there the most water?
19046.e: Almost all the water on Earth is salt water in the seas. Fresh water in rivers and lakes is only a small part.
19046.m: Most of the Earth’s water is in the seas.

19047.q: What do we call water that falls from the clouds?
19047.e: When the droplets in a cloud get too heavy, they fall down. That is rain.
19047.m: Rain is water that falls from clouds.

19048.e: Air is see-through and has no colour. But you can feel it, for example as wind.
19048.m: Air is invisible, but you can feel it.

19049.q: What is inside a blown-up balloon?
19049.e: When you blow up a balloon, you blow air into it. The air pushes the skin of the balloon outwards.
19049.m: A blown-up balloon is filled with air.

19050.q: Which part of the air do we need to breathe?
19050.e: Our body needs the oxygen in the air. We breathe it in with every breath.
19050.m: We need oxygen from the air to breathe.

19051.q: What is air mostly made of?
19051.e: About four fifths of air is nitrogen. The rest is mainly other gases.
19051.m: Air is mostly made of nitrogen.

19052.q: What happens if you push an empty glass upside down into water?
19052.e: There is air in the “empty” glass. It takes up space and does not let all the water in.
19052.m: Air takes up space, even though you cannot see it.

19053.q: Where does the air get thinner?
19053.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is. That is why mountaineers find it harder to breathe on high peaks.
19053.m: The air is thinner high up in the mountains.

19054.q: What does a fire need to burn?
19054.e: A fire needs something that can burn, oxygen from the air and enough heat. If one of these is missing, it goes out.
19054.m: Fire needs fuel, air and heat.

19055.q: What happens to a candle if you put a glass over it?
19055.e: Under the glass, the oxygen runs out. Without enough oxygen, the flame goes out.
19055.m: Without fresh air a flame goes out.

19056.q: What is left when wood has burnt completely?
19056.e: When wood burns, most of it turns into gas and smoke. Grey ash is left behind.
19056.m: Ash is left over from burnt wood.

19057.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland if there is a fire?
19057.e: In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118. 117 is the police and 144 is the ambulance.
19057.m: In Switzerland the fire brigade’s number is 118.

19058.q: What does a fire give off?
19058.e: A flame shines and is hot. That is why people like sitting round a campfire.
19058.m: Fire gives off light and warmth.

19059.q: What happens when wet wood burns?
19059.e: Wet wood burns badly and makes lots of smoke. Dry wood burns better.
19059.m: Wet wood makes lots of smoke when it burns.

19060.q: Who is allowed to light a fire?
a: Only adults, or children with them
Little brothers and sisters on their own
19060.e: Fire is dangerous and can spread quickly. Children only light fires together with adults.
19060.m: Children only light fires with adults.

19061.e: When water gets very cold, it becomes solid. We call this solid water ice.

19062.q: Does an ice cube float in water or sink?
19062.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why it floats on top.

19063.e: Ice is solid and therefore hard. It cools everything it touches.

19064.q: What is glacier ice made from?
19064.e: Lots of snow is pressed together over many years. This turns it into solid glacier ice.
19064.m: Glacier ice is made from snow that has been pressed together.

19065.q: Why is a frozen lake dangerous?
19065.e: Thin ice cannot hold a person’s weight. You may only go onto ice that has been declared safe.
19065.m: Only go onto a frozen lake when the ice has been declared safe.

19066.q: Where do you put water to make ice cubes?
19066.e: In the freezer it is much colder than 0 degrees. The water turns to ice there.
19066.m: You make ice cubes in the freezer.

19067.q: What rises from a saucepan of boiling water?
19067.e: Boiling water turns into water vapour. The white clouds above it are tiny droplets of water.

19068.q: Why do you have to be careful with steam?
19068.e: Steam from boiling water is very hot. It can scald your skin.
19068.m: Hot steam can scald your skin.

19069.q: What happens to steam on a cold mirror in the bathroom?
19069.e: The steam cools down on the cold mirror. It turns back into little drops of water, and the mirror steams up.
19069.m: Steam turns back into water on cold surfaces.

19070.e: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They form when moist air cools down.
19070.m: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets.

19071.q: What do you see in winter when you breathe out outside?
19071.e: Our breath contains water vapour. In the cold air it turns into tiny droplets, which you see as a white cloud.
19071.m: In winter you can see your breath as a little cloud.

19072.q: Where does the steam go when you cook?
19072.e: Warm steam is lighter than the cool air. That is why it rises.

19073.q: What forms when steam collects on the saucepan lid?
19073.e: The lid is cooler than the steam. So the steam turns back into water there and drips down.
19073.m: On the lid, steam turns back into drops of water.

19074.q: Which of these is a solid?
19074.e: A stone has a fixed shape and stays the way it is. Milk, juice and air are not solid.

19075.q: What is typical of a solid?
19075.e: Solids have their own shape. A wooden block stays a block, whatever box it is in.

19076.q: Which of these objects is solid?
19076.e: Wood is a solid. Soup and syrup are liquid, and fog is made of air and droplets.

19077.e: Sand can trickle, but every single grain is solid. That is why sand counts as a solid.
19077.m: Every grain of sand is solid.

19078.q: Which solid is hard and see-through?
19078.e: Window panes are made of glass. Glass is solid and hard, and you can see through it.
19078.m: Glass is a solid that is see-through.

19079.q: Which of these is a solid?
19079.e: Cold chocolate is hard and keeps its shape. Tea and juice are liquid, and steam is a gas.

19080.q: Can you hold a solid in your hand?
19080.e: You can hold solids because they do not flow away. A cube stays a cube in your hand.
19080.m: You can hold solids in your hand.

19081.q: Which of these is a liquid?
19081.e: You can pour milk, and it flows. Wood, stone and glass are solid.

19082.q: What shape is water in a bottle?
19082.e: Liquids do not have their own shape. They take the shape of the container they are in.
19082.m: Liquids take the shape of their container.

19083.q: What can you do with a liquid?
19083.e: Liquids flow. That is why you can pour them from one glass into another.

19084.q: Which of these flows most slowly?
19084.e: Honey is thick. It flows much more slowly than water, juice or milk.
19084.m: Honey is thick and flows slowly.

19085.q: What is the surface of water like in a glass that is standing still?
19085.e: Still water forms a flat, level surface at the top. This is true of all liquids.
19085.m: Still water has a flat surface on top.

19086.q: What happens if you spill water on the table?
19086.e: Water has no fixed shape. On the table it flows apart and forms a puddle.

19087.q: Which oil do you often find in the kitchen?
19087.e: In the kitchen you use cooking oil for frying and for salad. It is a liquid.
19087.m: Cooking oil is a liquid from the kitchen.

19088.q: Which of these is a gas?
19088.e: Air is a gas. It is invisible and spreads out everywhere in a room.

19089.q: What does a gas do in a room?
19089.e: Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume. They spread out through the whole room.
19089.m: Gases spread out through the whole room.

19090.q: How can you tell that there is a gas in the room that you cannot see?
19090.e: Many gases are invisible. But some have a smell, for example the scent of freshly baked bread.

19091.q: Which gas makes a balloon so light that it floats upwards?
19091.e: Helium is lighter than air. That is why a helium balloon rises.
19091.m: A helium balloon rises because helium is lighter than air.

19092.q: What are the bubbles in sparkling mineral water?
19092.e: The bubbles in sparkling mineral water are a gas, usually carbon dioxide. It rises to the top and tingles in your mouth.
19092.m: The bubbles in sparkling water are a gas.

19093.q: Which gas do people breathe out much more of than they breathe in?
19093.e: The body makes carbon dioxide and gets rid of it when we breathe out. Plants take the carbon dioxide in again.
19093.m: People breathe out a lot of carbon dioxide.

19094.e: Gases are easy to squash. That is how you can pump a lot of air into a bicycle tyre.

19095.q: What happens to an ice cube in your warm hand?
19095.e: The warmth of your hand turns the ice back into water. This process is called melting.

a: Both melt at the same speed
19096.e: A small ice cube has less ice that needs to melt. That is why it is gone sooner.
19096.m: Small pieces of ice melt faster than big ones.

19097.q: What happens to butter in a hot frying pan?
19097.e: The heat of the pan makes the butter melt. Solid butter becomes liquid butter.
19097.m: Butter melts in a hot pan.

19098.q: When something melts, what does a solid become?
19098.e: When it melts, a solid becomes liquid. This needs warmth.
19098.m: When a solid melts, it becomes liquid.

19099.q: What happens to the snow in the mountains in spring?
19099.e: In spring it gets warmer, and the snow melts. The water then flows into streams and rivers.

19100.q: What happens to a candle when it burns?
19100.e: The flame is hot and makes the wax melt. Liquid wax collects around the wick.
19100.m: When a candle burns, the wax melts.

19101.q: At what temperature does water freeze?
19101.e: Pure water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. Below that, it stays solid.

19102.q: What happens to water when it freezes?
19102.e: When it freezes, liquid water becomes solid. It turns to ice.
19102.m: When water freezes, it becomes solid.

19103.q: Why should you not put a full glass bottle in the freezer?
19103.e: Water expands when it freezes and needs more space. The bottle can then crack.
19103.m: Water needs more space as ice.

19104.q: When does a pond freeze over?
a: When it is very cold for a long time
When it is calm and warm
19104.e: If it stays below 0 degrees for many days, the surface of the pond freezes. Underneath there is often still water.
19104.m: A pond freezes over when it is cold for a long time.

19105.q: What do you get if you put syrup in a mould in the freezer?
19105.e: In the freezer, syrup freezes into a solid stick. This makes a simple ice lolly.
19105.m: Frozen syrup becomes an ice lolly.

19106.q: When a lake freezes over, where does the water freeze first?
a: At the top, on the surface
19106.e: The cold air cools the lake from above. That is why ice forms first on the surface.
19106.m: A lake freezes from the top down.

19107.q: What are the fine ice crystals on the grass on cold mornings called?
19107.e: When it is freezing, water vapour from the air turns straight into fine ice crystals on grass and leaves. This is called frost.
19107.m: Frost is made of fine ice crystals.

19108.q: What happens to water when it boils for a long time?
19108.e: When water boils, it turns into steam and goes into the air. That is why there is less and less of it in the pan.

19109.q: Why does washing dry on the line?
a: The wind takes the fabric away
19109.e: The water in the washing slowly goes into the air as vapour. This is called evaporation.
19109.m: Wet washing dries because the water evaporates.

a: When it is warm and windy
When it is cold and foggy
19110.e: Warmth and wind help the water to evaporate. That is why washing dries quickly on warm, windy days.
19110.m: Warmth and wind make washing dry quickly.

19111.q: What is left when salt water in a bowl evaporates?
19111.e: Only the water evaporates. The salt stays behind as a white crust in the bowl.
19111.m: When salt water evaporates, the salt is left behind.

19112.q: When a liquid evaporates, what does it become?
19112.e: When it evaporates, a liquid becomes a gas. This needs warmth.
19112.m: When a liquid evaporates, it becomes a gas.

19113.q: Why does sweat cool the body?
19113.e: When sweat evaporates on the skin, it takes warmth with it. That is how the body cools down.

19114.q: Where does the water go when a puddle evaporates?
19114.e: The water turns into invisible water vapour and mixes with the air. Later it can come back as rain.
19114.m: Evaporated water goes into the air.

19115.q: What do you get if you pour sand and stones together?
19115.e: The sand and stones just lie jumbled together. You can separate them again, so it is a mixture.
19115.m: Sand and stones together make a mixture.

19116.q: What happens if you mix oil and water and wait?
a: The oil sinks to the bottom
19116.e: Oil and water do not mix well. The lighter oil collects on top.

19117.q: What do you use to separate pasta from the cooking water?
19117.e: The water runs through the holes in the sieve. The pasta stays inside.
19117.m: You use a sieve to separate pasta from water.

19118.q: What can you use to get iron nails out of sand?
19118.e: A magnet attracts iron, but not sand. So you can pull the nails out.

19119.e: In muesli, flakes, nuts and fruit are mixed together. You can still see the separate parts.
19119.m: Muesli is a mixture of many ingredients.

19120.q: What happens if you mix blue and yellow paint?
19120.e: When you paint with watercolours, blue and yellow together make green.
19120.m: Blue and yellow together make green.

19121.q: What is the easiest way to separate peas and rice?
19121.e: The peas are bigger than the grains of rice. A suitable sieve lets the rice through and keeps the peas back.
19121.m: A sieve separates big and small grains.

19122.q: What happens to sugar in warm tea when you stir it?
19122.e: The sugar spreads out in the tea in tiny particles. You can no longer see it, but you can taste it.

19123.q: Does sugar dissolve faster in warm or in cold water?
19123.e: In warm water the particles move faster. That is why the sugar dissolves faster.
19123.m: Sugar dissolves faster in warm water.

19124.q: Which substance does NOT dissolve in water?
19124.e: Sand stays in the water and sinks to the bottom. Salt, sugar and syrup dissolve.
19124.m: Sand does not dissolve in water.

19125.q: How can you tell that salt is dissolved in water, even though you cannot see it?
19125.e: Dissolved salt is invisible. But you can tell it is there by the taste.
19125.m: You can taste dissolved salt, even if you cannot see it.

19126.q: What helps sugar to dissolve faster?
19126.e: When you stir, the sugar keeps meeting fresh water. That makes it dissolve faster.

19127.q: What happens to a fizzy tablet in water?
19127.e: The tablet dissolves and makes gas bubbles as it does so. That is why the water fizzes.
19127.m: A fizzy tablet fizzes as it dissolves in water.

19128.q: Why does sea water taste salty?
19128.e: There is a lot of salt dissolved in sea water. That is why you cannot drink it.
19128.m: Salt is dissolved in sea water.

19129.q: What do you do in an experiment?
a: You try something out and watch
19129.e: In an experiment you test an idea. Then you look closely at what happens.
19129.m: In an experiment you try things out and watch closely.

19130.q: What should you do before an experiment?
19130.e: Before you start, you think about what will probably happen. Afterwards you compare your guess with the result.
19130.m: Before an experiment you write down a guess.

19131.q: What happens if you pour vinegar onto baking powder?
19131.e: Vinegar and baking powder react with each other. A gas forms, and it foams.
19131.m: Vinegar and baking powder foam up together.

19132.q: What does a raw egg do in very salty water?
19132.e: In tap water a raw egg sinks. If you dissolve a lot of salt in the water, the water becomes heavier and the egg floats.
19132.m: An egg floats in very salty water.

19133.q: What must you never do in an experiment without asking?
19133.e: Some substances are not meant to be eaten. That is why you never taste anything in experiments without permission.
19133.m: In experiments, never eat anything without permission.

19134.q: What happens to a jelly bear left in water overnight?
19134.e: The jelly bear soaks up water. That is why it is much bigger and softer in the morning.
19134.m: A jelly bear gets bigger in water.

19135.q: What happens to a paper clip that you place very carefully on water?
19135.e: The surface of the water acts like a thin skin. A light paper clip can stay lying on it.
19135.m: Water has a surface like a thin skin.

19136.q: What happens if you mix red cabbage juice with vinegar?
19136.e: Red cabbage juice changes colour. With vinegar it turns reddish, with soapy water more green or blue.
19136.m: Red cabbage juice turns red with vinegar.

19137.q: Which three kinds of particles is an atom made of?
19137.e: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. The electrons move around the nucleus in the electron shell.
19137.m: An atom is made of protons, neutrons and electrons.

19138.q: What electric charge does a proton have?
19138.e: Protons are positively charged and sit in the nucleus. Their charge is the same size as an electron’s, but with the opposite sign.

19139.q: Where are the electrons of an atom?
19139.e: The electrons move in the shell around the tiny nucleus. The shell is much bigger than the nucleus.
19139.m: Electrons move in the shell around the nucleus.

19140.q: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
a: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of neutrons in the nucleus
The number of atoms in the molecule
19140.e: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus. It decides which element it is.
19140.m: The atomic number counts the protons in the nucleus.

19141.q: What do we call an atom that has given away or taken in electrons?
19141.e: If an atom gives away or takes in electrons, it becomes electrically charged. A charged particle like this is called an ion.
19141.m: An electrically charged atom is called an ion.

19142.q: What does the Greek word “atomos”, from which “atom” comes, mean?
19142.e: The Greek thinker Democritus called the smallest particles “atomos”, meaning indivisible. Today we know that atoms are made of even smaller particles.
19142.m: The word atom originally means indivisible.

19143.q: Which atoms make up a water molecule (H2O)?
19143.e: In the formula H2O, the small 2 after the H stands for two hydrogen atoms. The O without a number stands for one oxygen atom.
19143.m: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

19144.q: How many atoms does a molecule of carbon dioxide (CO2) have?
19144.e: CO2 is made of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. Together that makes 1 + 2 = 3 atoms.
19144.m: The numbers in a formula show how many atoms of each kind are in the molecule.

19145.q: What is the formula of the oxygen molecule we breathe in?
19145.e: In the air, oxygen exists as a molecule made of two oxygen atoms. That is why we write O2.
19145.m: The oxygen in the air is made of molecules with two atoms.

19146.q: What is a molecule of ozone made of?
19146.e: Ozone has the formula O3. In the stratosphere the ozone layer protects us from UV radiation, while near the ground ozone irritates the airways in summer.
19146.m: Ozone is a molecule made of three oxygen atoms.

19147.q: How many atoms does a methane molecule (CH4) contain?
19147.e: Methane is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. That makes 1 + 4 = 5 atoms.
19147.m: Methane is the main part of natural gas.

a: A substance made of atoms with the same number of protons
A compound of two kinds of atom
A substance that is always a gas
19148.e: All the atoms of an element have the same number of protons in the nucleus. An element cannot be broken down chemically into other substances.
19148.m: An element is made of just one kind of atom.

19149.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
19149.e: The symbol Au comes from the Latin word “aurum” for gold. Ag is the symbol for silver.

19150.q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
19150.e: Fe comes from the Latin word “ferrum” for iron. Many symbols come from Latin or Greek.

19151.q: Which element has the symbol Na?
19151.e: Na stands for sodium, from the Latin “natrium”. Nitrogen has the symbol N, neon Ne and nickel Ni.

19152.q: Which element has the symbol K?
19152.e: K comes from the Latin name “kalium”. Calcium has the symbol Ca, krypton Kr and cobalt Co.

19153.q: Which element has the symbol Pb?
19153.e: Pb comes from the Latin “plumbum” for lead. Platinum is Pt, phosphorus P and palladium Pd.

19154.q: Which chemist published a periodic table of the elements in 1869?
19154.e: The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by their properties in 1869. He even predicted elements that were not yet known. At almost the same time, Lothar Meyer was working on a similar arrangement.
19154.m: Mendeleev is seen as one of the fathers of the periodic table.

19155.q: What are the horizontal rows in the periodic table called?
19155.e: The horizontal rows are called periods. The vertical columns are called groups.
19155.m: In the periodic table, the rows are periods and the columns are groups.

19156.q: What is the group containing helium, neon and argon called?
19156.e: The noble gases hardly ever react with other substances. They are in the last column of the periodic table.

19157.q: Which group do lithium, sodium and potassium belong to?
19157.e: The alkali metals are in the first main group. They are soft and react violently with water.
19157.m: Alkali metals are in the first main group.

19158.q: Which group do fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine belong to?
19158.e: Halogens are in the seventh main group. The name means “salt formers”, because they form salts with metals.

19159.q: Which element comes first in the periodic table?
19159.e: The elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number. Right at the front is the element with only one proton in its nucleus.
19159.m: The periodic table arranges the elements by atomic number.

19160.q: How many chemical elements are known and officially named (as of 2026)?
19160.e: So far, 118 elements have been detected and named by IUPAC. The heaviest ones were made artificially in laboratories.

19161.q: Roughly what percentage of dry air is oxygen?
19161.e: Dry air contains around 21 per cent oxygen by volume. Another gas makes up the largest part.
19161.m: About one fifth of the air is oxygen.

19162.q: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
19162.e: The symbol O comes from the scientific name “oxygenium”. S is the symbol for sulphur.

19163.q: In which process do green plants make oxygen?
19163.e: In photosynthesis, plants use sunlight to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water. Oxygen is released in the process.
19163.m: Plants give off oxygen during photosynthesis.

19164.q: What is the atomic number of oxygen?
19164.e: An oxygen atom has 8 protons in its nucleus. That is why its atomic number is 8.

19165.q: Which element is the most common in the Earth’s crust by mass?
19165.e: Almost half the mass of the Earth’s crust is oxygen. It is bound up in rocks and minerals, for example in quartz.
19165.m: A lot of oxygen is bound up in the rocks of the Earth’s crust.

19166.q: Which test is used to detect oxygen in the laboratory?
19166.e: A glowing wooden splint bursts back into bright flame in pure oxygen. This shows that oxygen helps things burn.
19166.m: A glowing splint relights in oxygen.

19167.q: What is the lightest chemical element?
19167.e: A hydrogen atom usually consists of just one proton and one electron. That makes it the lightest atom of all.

19168.q: Which element is the most common in the universe?
19168.e: About three quarters of the normal matter in the universe is hydrogen. Stars like the Sun are mostly made of it.
19168.m: The universe is mostly made of hydrogen.

19169.q: Which test is used to detect hydrogen in the laboratory?
19169.e: If you hold a test tube of hydrogen to a flame, there is a bang or a squeaky pop. Hydrogen and oxygen react violently.
19169.m: Hydrogen shows itself with a pop in the squeaky pop test.

19170.q: Which substance forms when hydrogen burns with oxygen?
19170.e: Hydrogen combines with oxygen to form H2O. Because no carbon dioxide is produced, hydrogen is seen as a clean source of energy.
19170.m: When hydrogen burns, only water is produced.

19171.q: What is the process called in which water is split into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity?
19171.e: In electrolysis, electric current drives a chemical reaction. In this way, water produces hydrogen and oxygen.
19171.m: Electricity can split water into its elements.

19172.q: What is the formula of a hydrogen molecule?
19172.e: Hydrogen gas is made of molecules with two hydrogen atoms. That is why we write H2.
19172.m: Hydrogen gas is made of H2 molecules.

19173.q: What is the chemical symbol for carbon?
19173.e: C comes from the Latin “carbo” for coal. K stands for potassium, Ca for calcium.

19174.q: Which gemstone is made of pure carbon, like graphite?
19174.e: Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms. They differ in how the atoms are arranged, which is why diamond is extremely hard.

19175.q: What is the lead of a pencil mainly made of?
19175.e: Despite its name, a pencil contains no lead. The core is a mixture of graphite and clay.
19175.m: Pencil leads contain graphite, not lead.

19176.q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
19176.e: Carbon atoms have 6 protons in their nucleus. The number 12 is the mass number of the most common carbon atom.

19177.q: Which gas is produced when carbon burns completely with enough oxygen?
19177.e: In complete combustion, each carbon atom joins with two oxygen atoms. This produces CO2.
19177.m: Complete combustion of carbon produces carbon dioxide.

19178.q: What is the branch of chemistry that studies carbon compounds called?
19178.e: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds such as sugars, fats and plastics. People used to believe that only living things could make such substances.
19178.m: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon.

19179.q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
19179.e: Mercury melts at about -39 °C. It is poisonous, so it is hardly used in thermometers any more.
19179.m: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

19180.q: Which property do all metals have in common?
a: They are solid at room temperature
19180.e: Metals contain electrons that can move freely. That is why all metals conduct electricity and heat.

19181.q: Which metals is bronze mainly made of?
19181.e: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. It gave the Bronze Age its name.
19181.m: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

19182.q: Which of these metals is attracted by a magnet?
19182.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic. Copper, aluminium and gold are not attracted by an ordinary magnet.

19183.q: Which metal is usually used for electric cables in the home because it conducts so well?
19183.e: Copper conducts electricity very well and is easy to shape into wires. Only silver conducts slightly better, but it is much more expensive.
19183.m: Electric cables are usually made of copper.

a: An alloy of iron and carbon
An alloy of copper and zinc
19184.e: Steel is iron with a little carbon and often other additives. This makes it stronger and easy to work with.
19184.m: Steel is an alloy of iron and a little carbon.

19185.q: Which light metal is used for drinks cans and kitchen foil?
19185.e: Aluminium is light, easy to shape and does not rust through. In Switzerland, used aluminium cans can be collected separately and recycled.
19185.m: Aluminium is a light metal that is easy to shape.

19186.q: Which non-metal is liquid at room temperature?
19186.e: Bromine is a red-brown, poisonous liquid. It is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

19187.q: Which yellow, solid non-metal is often found at volcanoes?
19187.e: Sulphur forms yellow crystals that are deposited from gases at volcanoes. When it burns, it has a sharp smell.

19188.q: Which property do most non-metals have?
19188.e: Most non-metals lack freely moving electrons. That is why they conduct electricity and heat poorly. Graphite is a well-known exception.
19188.m: Most non-metals are poor conductors of electricity.

19189.q: Which gas makes up about 78 % of the air?
19189.e: Nitrogen is the main part of the air. The gas is colourless and reacts only with difficulty with other substances.
19189.m: Most of the air is nitrogen.

19190.q: Which non-metal is often used to disinfect swimming pool water?
19190.e: Chlorine and its compounds kill bacteria in pool water. That is where the typical indoor pool smell comes from.
19190.m: Chlorine keeps pool water free of germs.

19191.q: Which element has been added to table salt in Switzerland since 1922 to prevent goitre?
19191.e: A lack of iodine can lead to an enlarged thyroid gland, called a goitre. That is why in 1922 Switzerland became the first country in the world to introduce iodised table salt.
19191.m: Iodised salt protects against a lack of iodine.

19192.q: How can you recognise a chemical reaction?
a: A substance is only broken into pieces
A substance only changes its state
19192.e: In a chemical reaction, substances with new properties are formed. Energy is often involved too, for example as heat or light.

19193.q: What are the starting substances of a chemical reaction called?
19193.e: The substances before the reaction are called reactants. The newly formed substances are called products.
19193.m: In a reaction, reactants turn into products.

a: A substance that speeds up a reaction and is not used up
A substance that stops every reaction immediately
The end product of a reaction
A substance that burns during the reaction
19194.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy needed, so a reaction runs faster. At the end it is left unchanged.
19194.m: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up.

19195.q: What do you call a reaction that releases heat?
19195.e: Exothermic reactions give off energy to their surroundings, for example a fire. Endothermic reactions take in energy.

19196.q: In a chemical reaction in a closed container, what happens to the total mass?
19196.e: According to the law of conservation of mass, no atoms are lost and none are added. They are only rearranged.
19196.m: Mass is conserved in chemical reactions.

19197.q: Which process is a chemical reaction?
19197.e: When baking, new substances are formed, for example the brown crust. Melting, grinding and evaporating only change a substance on the outside.
19197.m: Chemical reactions take place when baking.

19198.q: Which three things does a fire need?
19198.e: These three conditions form the fire triangle. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out.
19198.m: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat.

19199.q: Why can you smother a small fire with a fire blanket?
a: The blanket keeps the oxygen away
The blanket cools the fire a lot
The blanket takes away the fuel
The blanket makes the flames wet
19199.e: The fire blanket separates the fire from the air. Without oxygen, the burning cannot continue.
19199.m: Without oxygen, a fire goes out.

19200.q: Why must you never put out burning oil with water?
a: The water turns to steam suddenly and sprays burning oil
The water makes the oil poisonous
The water gives the fire oxygen
19200.e: Water sinks below the hot oil and turns to steam explosively. It carries burning droplets of oil with it, and a huge flame shoots up.
19200.m: Put out burning oil with a lid and never with water.

19201.q: Which poisonous gas is produced when something burns with too little oxygen?
19201.e: If there is not enough oxygen, burning substances that contain carbon produce carbon monoxide. The gas is colourless, odourless and very poisonous.
19201.m: Carbon monoxide is an invisible and dangerous gas.

19202.q: What do you call an extremely fast burning with a bang and a shock wave?
19202.e: In an explosion, the burning happens in fractions of a second. The hot gases expand suddenly.
19202.m: An explosion is a very fast burning.

19203.q: Why does wood wool burn more easily than a thick block of wood?
a: It has a much larger surface
It is made of a different wood
It is heavier than the block
19203.e: Finely divided materials have a lot of surface where oxygen can attack. That is why they catch fire more quickly.
19203.m: The more finely a fuel is divided, the more easily it burns.

19204.e: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. This produces iron oxides that contain water.
19204.m: Rust is an oxide of iron.

19205.q: What does iron need in order to rust?
19205.e: Iron only rusts when oxygen and moisture are present. Salt, for example road salt in winter, speeds up rusting.
19205.m: Iron rusts with air and moisture.

19206.q: What do you call a reaction in which a substance combines with oxygen?
19206.e: Originally, every reaction with oxygen was called oxidation. Today the term generally means the loss of electrons.
19206.m: When a substance combines with oxygen, it is called oxidation.

19207.q: What do you call the reaction in which oxygen is removed from an oxide?
19207.e: In reduction, oxygen is removed from a substance. This is how iron is extracted from iron ore in a blast furnace, for example.
19207.m: Reduction is the opposite of oxidation.

19208.q: Why do copper roofs turn green over time?
a: The colour of the copper fades
The copper melts in the sun
19208.e: Copper reacts with substances in the air and rain. A green layer forms, the patina, which protects the metal underneath.
19208.m: Green patina protects copper from further weathering.

19209.q: Why does a cut apple turn brown in the air?
a: Substances in the apple react with oxygen
The water in the apple evaporates
The sugar in the apple melts
19209.e: Enzymes in the apple help substances in it combine with oxygen from the air. This produces brown substances. Lemon juice slows this down.
19209.m: An apple turns brown because it reacts with oxygen.

19210.q: Which acid is found in stomach juice?
19210.e: The stomach makes dilute hydrochloric acid. It helps with digestion and kills many germs.
19210.m: In the stomach, hydrochloric acid helps with digestion.

19211.q: Which acid gives vinegar its sour taste?
19211.e: Vinegar contains acetic acid, which acetic acid bacteria make from alcohol. Kitchen vinegar usually contains about 5 % acid.

19213.q: Which acid do some ants spray to defend themselves?
19213.e: Formic acid was named after ants (Latin ‘formica’), because it used to be obtained from them. It is also found in stinging nettles.
19213.m: Formic acid is named after ants.

19214.q: Which particles do acids release when dissolved in water?
19214.e: Acids release hydrogen ions in water. The more of them there are in the solution, the more acidic it is.
19214.m: Acids release hydrogen ions in water.

19215.q: Which rule applies when diluting a concentrated acid?
a: First the water, then the acid
First the acid, then the water
Pour both in quickly at the same time
19215.e: If you pour water into concentrated acid, the strong heat can make it boil suddenly and spray acid. That is why you add the acid slowly to the water.
19215.m: When diluting, always add the acid to the water, never the other way round.

a: A solution of a base in water
19216.e: When a base dissolves in water, it forms an alkali solution. Alkalis are the chemical opposite of acids.
19216.m: An alkali solution is a base dissolved in water.

19217.q: Which household product often contains a strong alkali?
19217.e: Many drain cleaners contain sodium hydroxide. The strong alkali dissolves hair and grease and is corrosive, so you need gloves.
19217.m: Drain cleaners are often strongly corrosive alkalis.

19218.q: What colour does red litmus paper turn in an alkali?
19218.e: Litmus turns blue in basic solutions. This lets you tell alkalis apart from acids.

19219.q: What is the alkali called that forms when sodium hydroxide dissolves in water?
19219.e: Sodium hydroxide in water gives caustic soda solution. It is used, for example, to make soap and pretzels.
19219.m: Sodium hydroxide in water gives caustic soda solution.

19220.q: What is formed when an acid and an alkali come together in the right amounts?
19220.e: This reaction is called neutralisation. The acidic and basic particles cancel each other out.

19221.q: Which particles are typical of alkalis?
19221.e: Alkalis contain many hydroxide ions. They consist of one oxygen atom and one hydrogen atom and are negatively charged.
19221.m: Hydroxide ions make a solution basic.

19223.q: What does a pH value below 7 mean?
19223.e: The lower the pH value, the more acidic a solution is. Values above 7 mean basic.
19223.m: A pH value below 7 means acidic.

19224.q: What range does the usual pH scale cover?
19224.e: The common pH scale goes from 0 to 14. The neutral point is in the middle.
19224.m: The pH scale usually goes from 0 to 14.

19225.q: What colour does universal indicator show in a neutral solution (pH 7)?
19225.e: Universal indicator turns red to orange in acidic solutions and purple in strongly basic ones. At pH 7 it shows a green colour.
19225.m: Universal indicator turns green in neutral solutions.

19227.q: What can you use to find the pH value of a solution easily?
19227.e: Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes that shows a different colour depending on the pH value. You read the value off a colour chart.
19227.m: Universal indicator shows the pH value by its colour.

19228.q: How many times more acidic is a solution with pH 3 than a solution with pH 4?
19228.e: The pH scale is logarithmic. One step lower means ten times more acidic particles, so 10 times more acidic.
19228.m: Each pH step means a difference by a factor of ten.

19229.q: What is the easiest method to separate sand from water?
19229.e: When filtering, the sand stays in the filter paper. The water flows through as the filtrate.
19229.m: Solid particles are separated from liquids by filtering.

19230.q: How do the Swiss Saltworks get salt from brine?
19230.e: Brine is salty water from underground. When it is evaporated, the water turns to vapour and the salt is left behind.

19231.q: What is the easiest way to separate iron filings from sand?
19231.e: Iron is attracted by a magnet, sand is not. This makes it easy to separate the two.
19231.m: Magnetic substances are separated with a magnet.

19232.q: Which property of substances is used in distilling?
19232.e: When distilling, the substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first. The vapour is cooled and collected as a liquid again.
19232.m: Distilling separates liquids by their boiling points.

19233.q: Which method can separate the dyes in a felt-tip pen?
19233.e: In paper chromatography, the dyes travel through the paper with the solvent at different speeds. This separates them visibly.

19234.q: What do you call solid particles settling at the bottom of a liquid?
19234.e: Heavy particles sink because of gravity and settle. Afterwards you can carefully pour off the liquid.
19234.m: In sedimentation, solid particles settle at the bottom.

19235.q: Which separation method takes place when you brew tea?
19235.e: Hot water draws flavours and colours out of the tea leaves. Drawing substances out with a solvent is called extraction.
19235.m: When making tea, substances are extracted.

19236.q: Which experiment led Ernest Rutherford to propose a tiny, positively charged atomic nucleus?
a: Scattering alpha particles off gold foil
Deflecting cathode rays in a magnetic field
Diffracting electrons at a double slit
19236.e: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but a few were strongly deflected. It followed that almost all the mass and the positive charge are concentrated in a very small nucleus.
19236.m: Rutherford's scattering experiment showed that the atom is mostly empty.

19237.q: Which atomic model is often called the “plum pudding model”?
19237.e: Joseph John Thomson pictured the atom as an evenly positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it like raisins.
19237.m: In Thomson's model, the electrons sit like raisins in a positive mass.

19238.q: What did Niels Bohr propose for the hydrogen atom in 1913?
a: Electrons orbit without radiating on paths with fixed energies
Electrons are spread evenly through the whole atom
Electrons sit motionless in the nucleus
Electrons can have any energy at all
19238.e: Bohr introduced allowed orbits with particular energies on which the electron gives off no radiation. In doing so, he deliberately broke with classical physics.
19238.m: In Bohr's model, only certain electron orbits are allowed.

19239.q: In the orbital model, which quantum number determines the shape of an orbital?
19239.e: The azimuthal (angular momentum) quantum number distinguishes s, p, d and f orbitals. The principal quantum number, by contrast, gives the shell and so mainly the energy and size.
19239.m: The azimuthal quantum number sets the shape of an orbital.

19240.q: What does an orbital describe in the quantum mechanical model of the atom?
a: A region of space where an electron is very likely to be found
An exactly circular path of an electron
The path of an electron between two atoms
19240.e: According to quantum mechanics, the position of an electron cannot be stated exactly. An orbital describes where the electron is very likely to be found.
19240.m: An orbital is a region of space, not a fixed path.

19241.q: Who published an atomic theory from 1808 according to which the atoms of an element all have the same mass?
19241.e: In “A New System of Chemical Philosophy”, John Dalton described atoms as indivisible spheres whose mass differs from element to element.
19241.m: Dalton turned the idea of atoms into a scientific theory.

19242.q: What shape is an s orbital?
19242.e: The probability of finding an s electron depends only on the distance from the nucleus, not on the direction. That is why the s orbital is spherically symmetrical, whereas p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped.
19242.m: An s orbital is spread spherically around the nucleus.

19243.q: According to Bohr's model, how do the lines in the hydrogen spectrum arise?
a: Through electrons jumping between energy levels
Through protons decaying in the nucleus
19243.e: When an electron jumps to a lower level, a photon with exactly the energy difference is emitted. Because only certain levels exist, individual sharp lines appear.
19243.m: Each spectral line corresponds to a particular electron jump.

19244.q: Who showed in 1897 that the electron is a separate particle?
19244.e: Thomson studied cathode rays and determined the ratio of charge to mass. He concluded that they consist of very light, negatively charged particles.
19244.m: In 1897 the electron was discovered as the first elementary particle.

19245.q: According to the formula 2n², what is the maximum number of electrons that fit in the second shell?
19245.e: For n = 2: 2 · 2² = 2 · 4 = 8. The second shell consists of one 2s and three 2p orbitals with two electrons each.
19245.m: Shell n holds at most two times n squared electrons.

19246.q: What does the Pauli principle state?
a: No two electrons in an atom have the same four quantum numbers
Electrons fill the orbitals with the highest energy first
The position and momentum of an electron can both be measured exactly at the same time
An orbital can hold any number of electrons
19246.e: Wolfgang Pauli formulated this exclusion principle in 1925. It follows that an orbital contains at most two electrons with opposite spin.
19246.m: An orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spin.

19247.q: What is the electron configuration of a sodium atom (atomic number 11)?
19247.e: Sodium has 11 electrons: 2 in 1s, 2 in 2s, 6 in 2p and the last one in the lower-energy 3s orbital.
19247.m: Sodium has a single valence electron in the 3s orbital.

19248.q: How many valence electrons does a sulphur atom have?
19248.e: Sulphur is in group 16 (main group VI) and has the valence configuration 3s² 3p⁴, so six outer electrons.
19248.m: The elements of the oxygen group have six valence electrons.

a: Equivalent orbitals are first filled singly with the same spin
Each orbital is immediately filled with two electrons
The outermost shell is always filled first
19249.e: With orbitals of equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, each orbital first receives one electron with parallel spin. Only then are pairs formed.
19249.m: Electrons first spread out singly over equivalent orbitals.

19250.q: With which experiment did Robert Millikan determine the elementary electric charge?
19250.e: Millikan made charged oil droplets float in an electric field. The measured charges were always whole-number multiples of about 1.6 · 10⁻¹⁹ coulombs.
19250.m: Every electric charge is a multiple of the elementary charge.

19251.q: What does the number of protons in the nucleus determine?
a: How many isotopes the element has
How large the mass of the electron is
19251.e: The number of protons equals the atomic number. Each element is clearly identified by its number of protons.
19251.m: The number of protons is the identity card of a chemical element.

19252.q: Roughly how many times heavier than an electron is a proton?
19252.e: The proton has a mass of about 1.673 · 10⁻²⁷ kg, the electron about 9.109 · 10⁻³¹ kg. The ratio is about 1,836.
19252.m: Almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.

19253.q: Which quarks make up a proton?
a: Two up quarks and one down quark
One up quark and two down quarks
Two down quarks and one strange quark
19253.e: An up quark has a charge of +2/3, a down quark −1/3. Two times +2/3 plus −1/3 gives the proton charge of +1.
19253.m: The proton is made of three quarks.

19254.q: How many protons does the nucleus of an iron atom contain?
19254.e: Iron has the atomic number 26. The common mass number 56 also includes 30 neutrons.
19254.m: The atomic number gives the number of protons.

19255.q: How is an acid defined according to Brønsted's theory?
a: As a donor of hydroxide ions
19255.e: According to Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted, an acid gives off protons (H⁺) and a base takes up protons.
19255.m: A Brønsted acid gives protons to a partner.

19256.q: Who is regarded as the discoverer of the proton?
19256.e: Between about 1917 and 1919, Rutherford bombarded nitrogen with alpha particles and detected hydrogen nuclei. Around 1920 he suggested the name proton for them.
19256.m: The hydrogen nucleus is a single proton.

19257.q: In simplified terms, in what form is a hydrogen ion H⁺ found in aqueous solution?
19257.e: A free proton is extremely small and reactive. It immediately attaches to a water molecule and forms H₃O⁺.
19257.m: In water, the proton is bound to a water molecule.

19258.e: In 1932, James Chadwick detected an uncharged nuclear particle with about the mass of a proton. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1935.
19258.m: The neutron was only discovered in 1932 as an uncharged nuclear particle.

19259.q: How do the isotopes of an element differ?
a: In the number of valence electrons
In the number of electron shells
19259.e: Isotopes have the same number of protons and so practically the same chemical properties. They differ only in the number of neutrons and therefore in mass.
19259.m: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.

19260.q: How many neutrons does a carbon-14 nucleus contain?
19260.e: Carbon has 6 protons. The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the number of protons, so 14 − 6 = 8.
19260.m: The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number.

19261.q: How many neutrons does a uranium-235 nucleus (atomic number 92) have?
19261.e: The calculation is 235 − 92 = 143. The more common uranium-238, on the other hand, has 146 neutrons.
19261.m: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 differ by three neutrons.

19262.q: What happens in the nucleus during beta-minus decay?
a: A neutron changes into a proton
A proton changes into a neutron
The nucleus gives off an alpha particle
Two neutrons fuse to form a deuteron
19262.e: An electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted. The atomic number rises by 1 and the mass number stays the same.
19262.m: In beta-minus decay, a neutron becomes a proton.

19264.q: Which Swiss research institution operates the SINQ spallation neutron source?
19264.e: At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen, neutrons are produced by firing fast protons at a heavy target. The neutrons are used to study materials.
19264.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute produces neutrons for materials research.

19265.q: According to the Pauling scale, which element has the highest electronegativity?
19265.e: Fluorine has an electronegativity of about 4.0 and attracts bonding electrons most strongly. Oxygen follows with about 3.4.
19265.m: Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

19266.q: According to the usual rule of thumb, from what electronegativity difference is a bond called ionic?
19266.e: Below about 1.7 there is usually a polar covalent bond; above it the ionic character dominates. The boundary is not sharp.
19266.m: The larger the electronegativity difference, the more ionic the bond.

19267.q: What holds the atoms in a metal together?
a: Freely moving electrons between metal cations
Attraction between anions and cations of different elements
19267.e: In metallic bonding, the atoms give their valence electrons to a shared electron gas. This also explains the good electrical conductivity.
19267.m: The electron gas makes metals conductive and malleable.

19268.q: How many electrons are involved in the triple bond in the nitrogen molecule N₂?
19268.e: A triple bond consists of three shared electron pairs, so of 3 · 2 = 6 electrons.
19268.m: Each bond line stands for one shared electron pair.

19269.q: Why does water boil at a much higher temperature than hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)?
a: Because of hydrogen bonds between the water molecules
Because water molecules are heavier than H₂S molecules
Because water is an ionic compound
19269.e: Oxygen is strongly electronegative, so water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds. H₂S is actually heavier, but it already boils at about −60 °C.
19269.m: Hydrogen bonds explain the high boiling point of water.

19270.q: What does the octet rule state?
a: Atoms aim for eight valence electrons
Atoms always form exactly eight bonds
Every molecule consists of at most eight atoms
A nucleus contains at most eight neutrons
19270.e: Many main group elements reach a noble gas configuration with eight outer electrons by forming bonds. Hydrogen is stable with two electrons.
19270.m: Many atoms form bonds until they have a noble gas configuration.

19271.q: Which attractive forces mainly act between non-polar molecules such as methane?
19271.e: Short-lived fluctuations in the electron distribution create small dipoles that attract each other. These weak forces are called London or van der Waals forces.
19271.m: Even non-polar molecules attract each other weakly through van der Waals forces.

19272.q: What type of bond is found in the hydrogen chloride molecule HCl?
19272.e: Chlorine (about 3.2) is clearly more electronegative than hydrogen (about 2.2). The shared electron pair is shifted towards the chlorine, but the difference is below the limit for an ionic bond.
19272.m: Unevenly shared bonding electrons make a covalent bond polar.

19273.q: What is the energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous atom called?
19273.e: Ionisation turns the atom into a positively charged ion. The first ionisation energy is low for alkali metals and especially high for noble gases.
19273.m: The ionisation energy shows how tightly an atom holds on to its electrons.

19274.q: What is the formula of the sulphate ion?
19274.e: The sulphate ion is the acid residue ion of sulphuric acid H₂SO₄. SO₃²⁻, on the other hand, is the sulphite ion.
19274.m: Sulphate is the doubly negative acid residue ion of sulphuric acid.

19275.q: What is the formula of the ammonium ion?
19275.e: Ammonia NH₃ takes up a proton and so becomes the positively charged ammonium ion.
19275.m: Ammonium forms when ammonia takes up a proton.

19276.q: What charge does an aluminium ion typically have in its compounds?
19276.e: Aluminium is in group 13 and gives up its three valence electrons. In this way it reaches the electron configuration of neon.
19276.m: Metals form cations by giving up their valence electrons.

19277.q: What is the empirical formula of calcium chloride?
19277.e: Calcium forms Ca²⁺ ions and chlorine forms Cl⁻ ions. For electrical neutrality, two chloride ions are needed for each calcium ion.
19277.m: Ionic compounds are electrically neutral overall.

19278.q: Why does molten table salt conduct electricity, but solid table salt does not?
a: In the melt the ions can move freely
Free electrons form in the melt
Solid table salt contains no ions
Metal atoms form when it melts
19278.e: In the solid ionic lattice, the ions are bound to fixed positions. In the melt or in solution they can move and carry charge.
19278.m: Ionic compounds only conduct when their ions can move.

19279.q: With which noble gas is the sodium ion Na⁺ isoelectronic?
19279.e: After giving up one electron, Na⁺ still has 10 electrons. A neon atom has exactly the same number.
19279.m: Isoelectronic particles have the same number of electrons.

19280.q: What three-dimensional shape does a methane molecule CH₄ have?
19280.e: The four bonding electron pairs repel each other and, according to the VSEPR model, arrange themselves as far apart as possible. This gives bond angles of about 109.5°.
19280.m: Four electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves tetrahedrally.

19281.q: Roughly how large is the H-O-H bond angle in the water molecule?
19281.e: The two lone pairs on the oxygen take up more space than bonding pairs. They squeeze the bonds from the tetrahedral angle to about 104.5°.
19281.m: Lone pairs make bond angles smaller.

19282.q: What shape is the sulphur hexafluoride molecule SF₆?
19282.e: Around the sulphur atom there are six bonding electron pairs and no lone pair. They arrange themselves at angles of 90° at the corners of an octahedron.
19282.m: Six electron pairs around a central atom give an octahedron.

19283.q: What shape is an ammonia molecule NH₃?
19283.e: Nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The three hydrogen atoms form the base of a pyramid with the nitrogen at its tip.
19283.m: Ammonia is pyramidal because of its lone pair.

19284.q: Why is CO₂ non-polar, even though the C=O bonds are polar?
a: The bond dipoles cancel out because of the linear shape
Carbon and oxygen are equally electronegative
CO₂ has no electron pair bonds at all
19284.e: The two bond dipoles are equally strong and point in opposite directions. Added together, there is no dipole moment.
19284.m: Whether a molecule is polar also depends on its geometry.

19285.q: What hybridisation do the carbon atoms in ethene C₂H₄ have?
19285.e: Each carbon atom forms three σ bonds in a plane at about 120°. The remaining p orbital forms the π bond of the double bond.
19285.m: Double-bonded carbon is sp² hybridised and planar.

19286.q: What shape is the boron trifluoride molecule BF₃?
19286.e: Boron has three bonding electron pairs and no lone pair. The three fluorine atoms lie in one plane at angles of 120°.
19286.m: Three bonds without a lone pair give a flat triangular shape.

19287.q: Which coefficient x makes the equation C₃H₈ + x O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O correct?
19287.e: On the right there are 3 · 2 + 4 · 1 = 10 oxygen atoms. On the left, that needs 10 : 2 = 5 oxygen molecules.
19287.m: Both sides of a chemical equation have the same number of atoms of each kind.

19288.q: How many grams of water are produced when 4 g of hydrogen reacts completely with oxygen?
19288.e: According to 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, 4 g of H₂ (M = 2 g/mol) is exactly 2 mol. This produces 2 mol of water, so 2 · 18 g = 36 g.
19288.m: Stoichiometric calculations work via the amount of substance in moles.

19289.q: Roughly what is the molar mass of carbon dioxide CO₂?
19289.e: The calculation is 12 g/mol for carbon plus 2 · 16 g/mol for oxygen, so 44 g/mol.
19289.m: The molar mass is the sum of the atomic masses in a formula.

19290.q: What does the law of conservation of mass state?
a: In a reaction, the total mass of the substances stays the same
The mass of the products is always greater than that of the reactants
In every reaction some mass is lost as heat
Gases have no mass in a reaction
19290.e: In the 18th century, Antoine Lavoisier showed by precise weighing in closed vessels that no mass is lost in chemical reactions.
19290.m: In chemical reactions, atoms are only rearranged, not destroyed.

19291.q: How many particles does one mole of a substance contain?
19291.e: This number is called the Avogadro constant. Since 2019 it has been fixed at exactly 6.02214076 · 10²³ per mole.
19291.m: A mole is a fixed number of particles, a bit like a dozen.

19292.q: What amount of substance is 117 g of sodium chloride (M about 58.5 g/mol)?
19292.e: The amount of substance is mass divided by molar mass, so 117 g : 58.5 g/mol = 2 mol.
19292.m: The amount of substance is mass divided by molar mass.

19293.q: Which coefficient goes in front of Fe in the balanced equation … Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃?
19293.e: On the right there are 2 · 2 = 4 iron atoms and 2 · 3 = 6 oxygen atoms. So the left needs 4 Fe and 3 O₂.
19293.m: You balance an equation by changing the coefficients, never the formulas.

19294.q: In the wider sense, what is meant by oxidation?
19294.e: Originally, oxidation meant reacting with oxygen. Today any loss of electrons is called oxidation and any gain of electrons reduction.
19294.m: Oxidation is losing electrons, reduction is gaining electrons.

19295.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in potassium permanganate KMnO₄?
19295.e: Potassium is +1 and the four oxygen atoms together are −8. For the sum to be zero, manganese must be +7, because 1 + 7 − 8 = 0.
19295.m: The oxidation numbers of a neutral particle add up to zero.

19296.q: What is the oxidation number of sulphur in sulphuric acid H₂SO₄?
19296.e: Two hydrogen atoms give +2 and four oxygen atoms −8. So sulphur needs +6 for the sum to be zero.
19296.m: In oxygen compounds, oxygen usually has the oxidation number minus two.

19297.q: What is typical of an oxidising agent?
a: It takes up electrons and is reduced in the process
It gives up electrons and is oxidised in the process
It does not change its oxidation number
19297.e: An oxidising agent oxidises its reaction partner by taking electrons from it. In doing so, its own oxidation number goes down.
19297.m: The oxidising agent is itself reduced.

19298.q: Which substance is oxidised in the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu?
19298.e: Zinc gives up two electrons and becomes Zn²⁺. The copper ions take up these electrons and are reduced to metallic copper.
19298.m: The less noble metal gives its electrons to the ions of the more noble one.

19299.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂?
19299.e: The two hydrogen atoms are +1 each. For the sum to be zero, each of the two oxygen atoms is −1.
19299.m: In peroxides, oxygen has the oxidation number minus one.

19300.q: Which substance acts as the oxidising agent when iron rusts?
19300.e: When iron rusts, it gives up electrons. Oxygen takes them up in the presence of water and is reduced.
19300.m: Rusting is a redox reaction between iron and oxygen.

19301.q: Who managed to synthesise urea from an inorganic substance in 1828?
19301.e: Wöhler made urea from ammonium cyanate. This contradicted the idea that organic substances could only be made by living things.
19301.m: Organic substances can also be made in the laboratory.

19302.q: Which functional group is typical of alcohols?
19302.e: Alcohols have one or more OH groups on a saturated carbon atom. One example is ethanol.
19302.m: The OH group makes a molecule an alcohol.

19303.q: Which class of substances is identified by the carboxyl group -COOH?
19303.e: The carboxyl group can give off a proton, which is why these substances are acidic. Examples are formic acid and citric acid.
19303.m: Carboxylic acids have a carboxyl group.

a: A carboxylic acid and an alcohol
19304.e: In esterification, a carboxylic acid and an alcohol react and water is split off. Many esters smell fruity.
19304.m: An acid and an alcohol form an ester, splitting off water.

a: Compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structure
Atoms with different numbers of neutrons
Molecules with the same structure but a different mass
Different states of the same substance
19305.e: Butane and isobutane both have the formula C₄H₁₀ but are connected differently. That is why they have different boiling points.
19305.m: The same molecular formula does not mean the same substance.

19306.q: What is the systematic name of the acid in table vinegar?
19306.e: Acetic acid has the formula CH₃COOH and so two carbon atoms. In IUPAC nomenclature it is called ethanoic acid.
19306.m: Acetic acid is the carboxylic acid with two carbon atoms.

19307.q: Which functional group do aldehydes have?
19307.e: In aldehydes, a carbonyl group at the end of the chain is bonded to a hydrogen atom. One example is methanal (formaldehyde).
19307.m: Aldehydes have a carbonyl group at the end of the chain.

19308.q: What is the general molecular formula of the alkanes?
19308.e: Alkanes are saturated and chain-shaped. Each carbon atom carries two hydrogen atoms, and there is one extra at each end of the chain.

19309.q: What is the unbranched alkane with eight carbon atoms called?
19309.e: The series is methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane, hexane, heptane, octane. Octane is an important component of petrol.
19309.m: From five carbon atoms on, alkane names mostly come from Greek number words.

19310.q: Which bond is typical of the alkenes?
19310.e: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons with at least one double bond. The simplest alkene is ethene.
19310.m: Alkenes contain at least one double bond.

19311.q: Which reaction takes place when ethene decolourises bromine water?
19311.e: The bromine adds on to the double bond, forming 1,2-dibromoethane. This loss of colour is used as a test for double bonds.
19311.m: Bromine water detects double bonds by losing its colour.

19312.q: What is the molecular formula of benzene?
19312.e: Benzene is a ring-shaped aromatic hydrocarbon. The six π electrons are spread over the whole ring.
19312.m: Benzene is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon.

19313.q: Which substance is the main component of natural gas?
19313.e: Depending on the deposit, natural gas usually consists of about 75 to 99 per cent methane CH₄. When it burns, carbon dioxide and water are formed.
19313.m: Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and the main part of natural gas.

19314.q: How do alkanes react with chlorine in the presence of light?
19314.e: Light splits chlorine molecules into radicals. In a chain reaction, these replace hydrogen atoms of the alkane with chlorine atoms.
19314.m: Alkanes react with halogens in light by substitution.

a: A small molecule that can join up into long chains
A single atom of a metal
19315.e: Monomers are the building blocks of polymers. Linking many monomers together creates macromolecules.
19315.m: Many monomers join to form a polymer.

19316.q: Through which reaction is polyethylene made from ethene?
19316.e: In polymerisation, the double bonds of the ethene molecules open up. The molecules join into long chains without splitting off a by-product.
19316.m: Monomers with a double bond form long chains by polymerisation.

19317.q: Which small molecule is split off when polyesters are made by polycondensation?
19317.e: Acid and alcohol groups of the monomers join to form ester bonds. Each time they link, a water molecule is released.
19317.m: In polycondensation, a small molecule is split off.

a: They are closely cross-linked and cannot be melted
They consist of non-cross-linked thread-like molecules
They are loosely cross-linked and rubbery
They become soft and mouldable when heated
19318.e: After curing, the chains are tightly linked to each other. When heated, thermosets decompose instead of melting.
19318.m: Once cured, thermosets cannot be reshaped.

19319.q: Which bond links the building blocks in polyamides such as nylon?
19319.e: An amino group and a carboxyl group react, splitting off water, to form the amide bond -CO-NH-. The same bond also links the amino acids in proteins.
19319.m: Polyamides and proteins are linked by amide bonds.

19320.q: What does the abbreviation PET on drinks bottles stand for?
19320.e: PET is a polyester made from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol. In Switzerland, PET drinks bottles are collected separately and recycled.
19320.m: PET is a polyester that is easy to recycle.

19321.q: From which monomer is the natural substance cellulose built up?
19321.e: Cellulose consists of many β-glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds. It is the main component of plant cell walls.
19321.m: Cellulose is a natural polymer made of glucose.

19322.q: At which electrode does oxidation take place in a galvanic cell?
19322.e: By definition, the anode is the electrode at which electrons are given off. Reduction takes place at the cathode.
19322.m: Oxidation happens at the anode, reduction at the cathode.

19323.q: What voltage does a Daniell cell provide under standard conditions?
19323.e: The standard potential of Cu/Cu²⁺ is +0.34 V, that of Zn/Zn²⁺ is −0.76 V. The difference is 0.34 V − (−0.76 V) = 1.10 V.
19323.m: The cell voltage is the difference between the two electrode potentials.

19324.q: What is the standard potential of the standard hydrogen electrode?
19324.e: The standard hydrogen electrode is the reference point of the electrochemical series. Its potential is therefore set to zero by definition.
19324.m: All standard potentials are measured relative to the hydrogen electrode.

19325.q: Which gas is produced at the negative pole during the electrolysis of water?
19325.e: At the negative pole, the cathode, hydrogen ions or water molecules take up electrons. Twice as much hydrogen is produced as oxygen at the positive pole.
19325.m: In the electrolysis of water, hydrogen forms at the cathode.

19326.q: Roughly what is the value of the Faraday constant?
19326.e: The Faraday constant is the charge of one mole of electrons. It is the Avogadro constant multiplied by the elementary charge.
19326.m: One mole of electrons carries a charge of about 96,500 coulombs.

19327.q: Which metal was produced by molten salt electrolysis in Neuhausen am Rheinfall from 1888?
19327.e: One of the first aluminium smelters using Paul Héroult's process was built in Neuhausen. The hydropower of the Rhine supplied the electricity needed.
19327.m: Aluminium is obtained from its oxide using a lot of electrical energy.

19328.q: How much copper is deposited when 1 mol of electrons flows through a copper sulphate solution (M(Cu) about 63.5 g/mol)?
19328.e: For Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, 2 mol of electrons are needed per mole of copper. So 1 mol of electrons produces 0.5 mol, which is 0.5 · 63.5 g = 31.75 g.
19328.m: The amount deposited depends on the charge of the ions.

19329.q: What does Le Chatelier's principle state?
a: An equilibrium shifts to counteract an outside constraint
The reaction rate is always constant
19329.e: If an equilibrium is disturbed by pressure, temperature or concentration, it shifts so that the disturbance is reduced.
19329.m: A disturbed equilibrium shifts so that the constraint becomes smaller.

19330.q: What effect does raising the pressure have on the equilibrium N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃?
a: It shifts towards more nitrogen and hydrogen
The reaction comes to a standstill
19330.e: There are 4 gas particles on the left and only 2 on the right. At higher pressure the side with fewer particles is favoured, which is why the Haber-Bosch process works at high pressure.
19330.m: High pressure favours the side with fewer gas particles.

19331.q: What does an equilibrium constant K much greater than 1 mean?
a: The equilibrium lies on the side of the products
The equilibrium lies on the side of the reactants
19331.e: According to the law of mass action, the product concentrations are in the numerator. A large K means that there is a lot of product at equilibrium.
19331.m: A large K value shows an equilibrium on the product side.

19332.q: What effect does a catalyst have on a chemical equilibrium?
a: It is reached faster, but its position stays the same
19332.e: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the forward and reverse reactions equally. That is why it only speeds up reaching equilibrium.
19332.m: A catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium but does not change its position.

19333.q: What is true of the forward and reverse reactions at chemical equilibrium?
a: They take place at the same rate
Only the forward reaction is still taking place
The reverse reaction is twice as fast
19333.e: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic. Particles are reacting all the time, but the concentrations stay constant because the forward and reverse reactions balance each other.
19333.m: At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations no longer change.

19335.q: What effect does raising the temperature have on the equilibrium of an exothermic reaction?
19335.e: The reverse reaction of an exothermic reaction is endothermic and takes in heat. So heating favours the reverse reaction.
19335.m: Adding heat favours the endothermic direction of a reaction.

19336.e: 91 has 9 tens, which is more than all the other numbers.
19336.m: With two-digit numbers, compare the tens first.

19337.m: The next number is always one bigger.

19338.m: The number before is always one smaller.

19339.q: How many tens does the number 47 have?
19339.e: 47 is made up of 4 tens and 7 ones.
19339.m: In a two-digit number, the tens digit comes first.

19340.q: How do you write “fifty-eight” as a number?
19340.e: Fifty is 5 tens and eight is 8 ones, which makes 58.
19340.m: You write the tens first and then the ones.

19341.q: Which number is exactly halfway between 10 and 20?
19341.e: From 10 to 15 is 5 steps, and from 15 to 20 is also 5 steps.
19341.m: The middle is the same distance from both sides.

19342.e: 19 has only 1 ten, 25 has 2 tens, so 19 is smaller.
19342.m: Fewer tens means a smaller number.

19343.q: How many fingers do you have on both hands together?
19343.e: Each hand has 5 fingers, and 5 + 5 makes 10.
19343.m: Our ten fingers help us count.

19344.q: How many days are there in a week?
19344.e: The week has the days Monday to Sunday, which is 7 days.

19345.q: How many months are there in a year?
19345.e: From January to December you count 12 months.

19346.q: How many legs do 3 hens have altogether?
19346.e: Each hen has 2 legs, so 2 + 2 + 2 makes 6.

19347.q: Lena is counting backwards: 10, 9, 8, 7. Which number does she say next?
19347.e: When counting backwards, each number is 1 smaller, so after 7 comes 6.
19347.m: Counting backwards means always saying one less.

19348.q: How many wheels do 2 bikes have altogether?
19348.e: A bike has 2 wheels, and 2 + 2 makes 4.

19349.q: How many letters are there in the word “school”?
19349.e: You count s, c, h, o, o, l, which is 6 letters.
19349.m: When counting letters, point to each one separately.

19350.m: When adding past ten, first make up to ten.

19351.m: First up to ten, then add the rest.

19352.e: 2 tens and 3 tens are 5 tens, which is 50.
19352.m: Add tens like small numbers with a zero on the end.

19353.e: You only add the ones together, 4 + 5 makes 9, so 39.
19353.m: Ones are added to the ones.

19354.e: You add the tens together, 40 + 20 makes 60, then add the 5 ones, so 65.
19354.m: Tens are added to the tens.

19355.m: A number plus itself makes double.

19356.q: Tim has 12 marbles and gets 7 more. How many marbles does he have now?
19356.m: When something is added, you do a plus sum.

19357.m: You can add the tens first and then the ones.

19358.m: When taking away, first go back to ten.

19359.m: You can split the number you take away into two parts.

19360.e: 6 tens minus 2 tens are 4 tens, which is 40.
19360.m: Take away tens like small numbers.

19361.e: For the ones you work out 6 − 4, which makes 2, so 32.
19361.m: Ones are taken away from the ones.

19362.m: Take away the tens first and then the ones.

19363.q: A bus has 20 passengers. At the bus stop, 6 get off. How many passengers are left on the bus?
19363.m: When something goes away, you do a minus sum.

19364.m: Minus one always gives the number before.

19365.m: Take away bigger numbers in steps.

19366.m: Multiplying is adding the same number several times.

19367.m: Five times five is part of the times tables.

19369.e: 10 times 7 makes 70; you add a zero to the 7.
19369.m: When you multiply by ten, you add a zero.

19370.q: A box holds 6 eggs. How many eggs are in 3 boxes?
19370.e: 3 boxes with 6 eggs each is 3 times 6, which is 18.
19370.m: You count equal groups together by multiplying.

19371.e: 4 times 9 makes 36, because 2 times 9 is 18 and double that is 36.
19371.m: Times four is double the double.

19372.e: If you take something 0 times, you have nothing, so 0.
19372.m: Any number times zero makes zero.

19373.e: 10 divided into 2 equal parts makes 5, because 2 times 5 makes 10.

19374.e: 3 times 7 makes 21, so 21 divided by 3 is 7.
19374.m: The times tables help with dividing.

19375.e: 4 times 5 makes 20, so 20 divided by 4 makes exactly 5.
19375.m: Dividing is the opposite of multiplying.

19376.q: 24 apples are shared fairly between 6 children. How many apples does each child get?
19376.e: 24 divided by 6 makes 4, because 6 times 4 makes 24.

19377.e: 10 times 3 makes 30, so 30 divided by 10 makes exactly 3.
19377.m: When dividing by ten, the zero at the end disappears.

19378.m: You find half of a number by dividing by two.

19379.q: 16 children make groups of four. How many groups are there?
19379.e: 16 divided by 4 makes 4, because 4 times 4 makes 16.
19379.m: When splitting into groups, you divide.

19380.q: What comes next in the sequence: 5, 10, 15, 20, ...?
19380.e: Each number is 5 bigger than the one before, 20 + 5 makes 25.
19380.m: In a number sequence, first look for the rule.

19381.q: What comes next in the sequence: 3, 6, 9, 12, ...?
19381.e: The numbers always get 3 bigger, 12 + 3 makes 15.
19381.m: The three times table always jumps on by three.

19382.q: What comes next in the sequence: 20, 18, 16, 14, ...?
19382.e: The numbers always get 2 smaller, 14 − 2 makes 12.
19382.m: A sequence can also get smaller.

19383.q: What comes next in the sequence: 1, 3, 5, 7, ...?
19383.e: The numbers always jump on by 2, 7 + 2 makes 9.
19383.m: Equal jumps make a sequence regular.

19384.q: What comes next in the sequence: 10, 20, 30, 40, ...?
19384.m: In steps of ten, only the tens digit changes.

19385.q: What comes next in the sequence: 1, 2, 4, 8, ...?
19385.e: Each number is doubled, and double 8 is 16.

19386.q: What comes next in the sequence: 100, 90, 80, 70, ...?
19386.e: The numbers always get 10 smaller, 70 − 10 makes 60.
19386.m: Counting back in tens makes the tens digit smaller.

19387.q: Which of these numbers is even?
19387.e: 14 can be divided by 2 with no remainder, because 7 + 7 makes 14.

19388.q: Which of these numbers is odd?
19388.e: 21 ends in 1 and leaves a remainder when divided by 2.

19389.q: How can you recognise an even number?
a: It divides by 2 with no remainder
19389.e: An even number can be split into two equal parts with nothing left over.
19389.m: Even numbers can be halved with no remainder.

19390.q: What is the smallest even number that is bigger than 10?
19390.e: 11 is odd, the next even number after 10 is 12.
19390.m: Even numbers follow each other in steps of two.

19391.q: How many even numbers are there from 1 to 10?
19391.e: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, which is 5 numbers.
19391.m: Even and odd numbers always take turns.

19392.q: Which odd number comes straight after 15?
19392.e: 16 is even, then comes the odd number 17.
19392.m: Between two odd numbers there is always an even number.

19393.e: 33 ends in 3, and 3 is an odd digit.
19393.m: The last digit tells you whether a number is even.

19394.q: How many corners does a triangle have?
19394.e: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners; that is where its name comes from.
19394.m: The name triangle tells you the number of corners.

19395.q: How many sides does a rectangle have?
19395.e: A rectangle has one side each at the top and bottom and one side each on the left and right, which is 4 sides.
19395.m: In a rectangle, opposite sides are the same length.

19396.e: A circle is completely round and so has not a single corner.
19396.m: A circle is round and has no corners.

19397.q: Which shape has 4 sides of equal length and 4 right angles?
19397.e: In a square, all 4 sides are the same length and all corners are right angles.
19397.m: A square is a rectangle with sides of equal length.

19398.q: How many sides does a hexagon have?
19398.e: A hexagon has 6 corners and so also 6 sides.
19398.m: Polygons have as many sides as corners.

19399.q: What shape are the faces of a cube?
19399.e: A cube has 6 faces, and each of them is a square.
19399.m: A cube is made of six squares.

19400.q: What shape is the stop sign on the road?
19400.e: The red stop sign has 8 corners and is an octagon.
19400.m: You can recognise the stop sign by its eight corners.

19401.q: How many seconds are there in a minute?
19401.e: A minute lasts 60 seconds; that is how long the second hand takes to go round once.

19402.q: How many hours are there in a day?
19402.e: A whole day including the night lasts 24 hours.

19403.q: The big hand is on the 12 and the little hand is on the 3. What time is it?
