19753.e: When electricity flows through a coil, it becomes a magnet itself. The attraction and repulsion between coil and magnets makes the motor turn.
19753.m: An electric motor turns because of magnetic forces.

19754.q: What powers almost all SBB trains today?
19754.e: The Swiss rail network is almost completely electrified. The locomotives get their electricity from the overhead line.
19754.m: Almost all Swiss trains run on electricity.

19755.q: Who built the first usable battery around 1800?
19755.e: The Italian Alessandro Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with cardboard soaked in salt water. This “voltaic pile” supplied electricity continuously for the first time.
19755.m: The first battery was the voltaic pile.

19756.q: What voltage does a normal household socket in Switzerland supply?
19756.e: In Switzerland and throughout Europe the mains voltage is 230 volts alternating current. For large appliances such as cookers there are 400-volt connections.

19757.q: Who invented the lightning conductor in the 18th century?
19757.e: Around 1752 Benjamin Franklin showed that lightning is an electrical discharge. His lightning conductor carries lightning safely into the ground.
19757.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning into the ground.

19758.q: A device with a resistance of 46 ohms is connected to 230 volts. What is the current?
19758.e: According to Ohm's law, current equals voltage divided by resistance. 230 V divided by 46 ohms gives 5 A.
19758.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

19759.q: Which of these materials conducts electricity very well?
19759.e: Metals like copper have lots of free-moving electrons. That is why electric cables are usually made of copper inside.
19759.m: Copper is a very good electrical conductor.

19760.q: Which inventor championed alternating current in the so-called War of the Currents in the 1880s?
19760.e: Nikola Tesla developed alternating current systems together with George Westinghouse. Edison, on the other hand, backed direct current, but alternating current won out for power grids.
19760.m: Power grids today work with alternating current.

19762.q: How were sounds transmitted in the early telephone?
a: As electrical signals along a wire
19762.e: A microphone turned the sound waves into electrical signals. These travelled along a wire and became sounds again at the other end.
19762.m: The telephone transmits sounds as electrical signals.

19763.q: Who developed the alphabet of dots and dashes for the telegraph that is named after him?
19763.e: Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail developed a code of short and long signals. It meant messages could be sent over telegraph lines.
19763.m: Morse code is made up of short and long signs.

19764.q: What is the mobile phone traditionally called in Switzerland?
19764.e: “Natel” was originally short for “Nationales Autotelefon” (national car telephone). The name is still used for mobile phones in Switzerland today.
19764.m: In Switzerland people often call a mobile phone a Natel.

19765.q: In which year did Martin Cooper make the first public call with a handheld mobile phone?
19765.e: In 1973 Martin Cooper made a call in New York with a handheld mobile phone that weighed about one kilogram. It was many more years before there were small mobiles for everyone.
19765.m: The first mobile phone call took place in 1973.

19766.q: What does the abbreviation SMS stand for?
19766.e: SMS stands for “Short Message Service”. A single SMS can be no more than 160 characters long.
19766.m: An SMS is a short text message.

19767.q: Roughly how long did it take to make the oldest surviving photograph around 1826?
19767.e: The early processes were not very sensitive to light. That is why the plate had to be exposed for many hours before a picture appeared.
19767.m: The first photos needed hours of exposure.

19768.q: What were the first photographs captured on?
19768.e: In the daguerreotype, the picture was formed on a silver-plated copper plate. Paper prints and film came later.
19768.m: The first photos were made on metal plates.

19769.q: What is a dark room with a small hole, through which an image of the outside world falls on the wall, called?
19769.e: Camera obscura is Latin for “dark room”. It is the basic principle of every camera.
19769.m: Every camera is based on the camera obscura.

19770.q: How does the picture appear in a simple pinhole camera?
19770.e: The light rays cross in the small hole. That is why top ends up at the bottom and left ends up on the right.
19770.m: In a pinhole camera the picture is upside down.

19771.q: What replaces the old-fashioned film in a digital camera?
19771.e: The image sensor is made of millions of light-sensitive cells. It turns light into electrical signals, which are stored.
19771.m: In a digital camera the image sensor captures the light.

19772.q: What does the aperture of a camera control?
a: How much light comes through the lens
How big the image file is
19772.e: The aperture is an adjustable opening in the lens. A large opening lets in a lot of light, a small one only a little.
19772.m: The aperture decides the amount of light.

19773.q: How many pixels does a photo of 4,000 by 3,000 pixels have?
19773.e: You work out 4,000 times 3,000 and get 12,000,000 pixels. That is 12 megapixels.
19773.m: The number of pixels is width times height.

19774.q: Which brothers held one of the first public film screenings with paid admission in Paris in 1895?
19774.e: Auguste and Louis Lumière presented their Cinématographe on 28 December 1895. This day is often seen as the birthday of cinema.
19774.m: The Lumière brothers are seen as the fathers of cinema.

19775.q: Why do we see smooth movement when single pictures are shown quickly one after another?
a: The eye and brain join the pictures together
The pictures move on the screen
19775.e: Our visual system can't see very quickly changing pictures one by one. The brain joins them into a flowing movement.
19775.m: A film is made of lots of single pictures shown quickly.

19776.q: How many frames per second does a classic cinema film show?
19776.e: Since the days of sound films, cinema has used a standard of 24 frames per second. This looks smooth to the eye.
19776.m: A cinema film usually shows 24 frames per second.

19777.q: How many single frames does a 2-minute film at 24 frames per second have?
19777.e: 2 minutes are 120 seconds. 120 times 24 makes 2,880 frames.
19777.m: The number of frames is the length in seconds times the frame rate.

19778.q: What was new in cinemas from the end of the 1920s?
19778.e: Before that there were only silent films, often with a pianist playing along. From 1927 sound films with speech and singing took over.

19779.q: What is the animation technique called in which figures are moved slightly and photographed frame by frame?
19779.e: In stop motion a figure is moved a little after each photo. When played back, it looks as if it is moving by itself.
19779.m: Stop motion is made from lots of individually photographed scenes.

19780.q: In front of which wall are actors often filmed so the background can be changed on the computer later?
19780.e: The computer recognises the even green colour and replaces it with a different background. Green hardly appears in skin tones.
19780.m: With a green screen you can change the background.

19783.q: What is the force called that lifts an aeroplane upwards through its wings?
19783.e: The curved wings deflect the air downwards. This creates an upward force that carries the aeroplane.

19784.q: Which engine sucks in air, compresses it, burns kerosene and pushes hot gases out of the back?
19784.e: A jet engine creates thrust by pushing gases out of the back at high speed. Almost all large airliners use it.
19784.m: Large airliners fly with jet engines.

19785.q: Which Swiss solar aeroplane flew around the Earth without fuel from 2015 to 2016?
19785.e: Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying Solar Impulse 2 around the world. The electricity came only from solar cells on the wings.
19785.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone.

19786.q: Who was the first to fly alone and non-stop across the Atlantic in 1927?
19786.e: Charles Lindbergh flew the “Spirit of St. Louis” from New York to Paris. The flight took about 33 hours.
19786.m: Charles Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic alone in 1927.

19787.q: What colour is the flight data recorder that is often called the “black box”?
19787.e: Flight recorders are usually bright orange so that they are easier to find after an accident. They record flight data and conversations in the cockpit.
19787.m: The black box is actually orange.

19788.q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth in 1957?
19788.e: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 into space on 4 October 1957. The metal ball sent radio signals back to Earth.

19789.q: Who was the first person to fly into space in 1961?
19789.e: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth once in Vostok 1. The flight lasted about 108 minutes.
19789.m: Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space.

19790.q: Who was the first Swiss person to fly into space in 1992?
19790.e: Claude Nicollier from the canton of Vaud flew on the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 1992. Altogether he went into space four times.
19790.m: Claude Nicollier was the first Swiss astronaut in space.

19791.q: On which principle can a rocket fly even in the vacuum of space?
19791.e: The rocket pushes hot gases out of the back with great force. As a reaction it is pushed forwards, so it doesn't need air.
19791.m: A rocket flies on the recoil principle.

19792.q: Which Swiss university built the solar wind sail that was set up on the Moon during Apollo 11 in 1969?
19792.e: The University of Bern's solar wind sail caught particles from the solar wind. It was the only non-American experiment on the Apollo 11 mission.
19792.m: An experiment from Bern was already on the Moon in 1969.

19793.q: Who built the first working program-controlled computer, the Z3, in 1941?
19793.e: The German engineer Konrad Zuse built the Z3 from relays. It already calculated using the binary system.
19793.m: Konrad Zuse built the Z3 in 1941.

19794.q: Who is seen as the first computer programmer in history?
19794.e: Around 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote a program for Charles Babbage's planned calculating machine. The programming language Ada is named after her.
19794.m: Ada Lovelace wrote one of the first computer programs.

19795.q: Which two digits does the binary system of computers use?
19795.e: Computers work with two states, for example power on or off. These are shown as 0 and 1.
19795.m: Computers calculate with the digits 0 and 1.

19796.q: How many bits are there in a byte?
19796.e: A bit is the smallest unit of information. Eight bits together make a byte.
19796.m: A byte is made of eight bits.

19797.q: Which decimal number is the same as the binary number 1011?
19797.e: From the right, the places have the values 1, 2, 4 and 8. You work out 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 and get 11.
19797.m: In the binary system, the place value doubles to the left.

19798.q: Which programming language did Niklaus Wirth develop at ETH Zurich around 1970?
19798.e: Niklaus Wirth created Pascal mainly for teaching. He received the Turing Award in 1984 for his work.
19798.m: The programming language Pascal comes from Zurich.

19799.q: Which component, the “brain” of the computer, carries out the instructions of programs?
19799.e: The processor, also called the CPU, calculates and controls the processes in the computer. Modern processors manage billions of steps per second.
19799.m: The processor is the computer's calculating centre.

19800.q: Who invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989?
19800.e: The Briton Tim Berners-Lee wanted to make it easier for researchers to share documents. For this he developed linked web pages and the language HTML.
19800.m: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web.

19801.q: In which area is the CERN research centre, where the web was born?
19801.e: CERN is in Meyrin near Geneva, on the border with France. It is one of the largest research centres for particle physics.
19801.m: The World Wide Web was born in Switzerland.

19802.q: Since when have there been the first computer networks from which the internet grew?
19802.e: From 1969 the first university computers in the USA were connected to each other. This later developed into the internet.
19802.m: The forerunners of the internet appeared in the late 1960s.

19803.q: What is a program called that you use to open and view websites?
19803.e: A browser loads websites from the internet and displays them on the screen. Well-known browsers include Firefox, Chrome and Safari.
19803.m: You view websites with a browser.

a: A number that identifies a device on the network
19804.e: Every device on the internet needs an IP address. That way data packets know where they have to be sent.
19804.m: Every device on the internet has an IP address.

19805.q: What does the “s” in “https” stand for?
19805.e: With https, data is sent encrypted. That way others can't simply read it along the way.

19806.q: Which country ending do Swiss internet addresses have?
19806.e: The ending .ch comes from “Confoederatio Helvetica”, the Latin name of Switzerland. The ending .cz belongs to the Czech Republic.

19807.q: Which language does the word “robot” come from?
19807.e: The word comes from the play “R.U.R.” by Karel Čapek from 1920. In Czech, “robota” means forced labour.
19807.m: The word robot comes from Czech.

19808.q: Which writer came up with the famous Three Laws of Robotics?
19808.e: Isaac Asimov described the laws in a short story in 1942. The first law says that a robot may not injure a human being.
19808.m: The Laws of Robotics come from Isaac Asimov.

19809.q: Which parts of a robot sense its surroundings, such as distance or light?
19809.e: Sensors measure things like distance, brightness, pressure or temperature. With this data the robot can react to its surroundings.
19809.m: Sensors are a robot's sense organs.

19810.q: In which industry do particularly large numbers of industrial robots work worldwide?
19810.e: In car factories, robots have been welding, painting and assembling for decades. They work quickly, precisely and without breaks.
19810.m: Lots of robots work in car factories.

19811.q: What is the name of the NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2021 and brought a small helicopter with it?
19811.e: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater in February 2021. The helicopter Ingenuity made the first powered flights on another planet there.
19811.m: Perseverance has been exploring Mars since 2021.

19812.q: How does the robot ANYmal, developed at ETH Zurich, get around?
19812.e: ANYmal is a four-legged walking robot. It can climb stairs and inspect industrial plants.
19812.m: ANYmal is a walking robot from Zurich.

19813.q: What does it mean when a robot works “autonomously”?
a: It acts on its own without constant control
It is always steered with a joystick
It can only do one single movement
19813.e: An autonomous robot decides for itself using its program and its measurements. One example is a robot lawnmower.
19813.m: Autonomous robots work on their own.

19814.q: How does a 3D printer build an object?
a: By cutting it out of a block
By pouring it into a mould
19814.e: The printer puts down one thin layer after another. Many layers make a three-dimensional object.
19814.m: A 3D printer builds objects layer by layer.

19815.q: What raw material is the popular 3D printing plastic PLA usually made from?
19815.e: PLA, polylactide, is made from plant starch or sugar. It prints well at a low temperature.
19815.m: PLA is a plastic made from plants.

19816.q: In what form is the plastic fed into an ordinary home 3D printer?
a: As a wire on a reel
19816.e: This plastic wire is called filament. It is melted in a hot nozzle and applied layer by layer.
19816.m: Home 3D printers usually work with filament.

19817.q: In stereolithography, what is used to harden liquid plastic layer by layer?
19817.e: In stereolithography, UV light hardens liquid plastic layer by layer. It is one of the first 3D printing processes, from the 1980s.
19817.m: Stereolithography hardens plastic with UV light.

19818.q: Why is 3D printing also called “additive manufacturing”?
19818.e: “Additive” means adding. With milling or drilling, on the other hand, material is removed from a block.
19818.m: In 3D printing material is added instead of taken away.

19819.q: Which file format is very often used for 3D printing models?
19819.e: An STL file describes the surface of an object with lots of small triangles. Software then slices the model into layers.
19819.m: 3D models are often saved as STL files.

19820.q: A 3D printer prints layers 0.2 mm thick. How many layers does a 3 cm high object need?
19820.e: 3 cm is 30 mm. 30 mm divided by 0.2 mm makes 150 layers.
19820.m: The number of layers is the height divided by the layer thickness.

19821.q: Which energy source provides most of Switzerland’s electricity?
19821.e: More than half of Swiss electricity comes from hydroelectric power stations (as of 2024). The Alps, with their rivers and reservoirs, offer good conditions for this.
19821.m: Switzerland gets most of its electricity from hydropower.

19822.q: What does a solar cell turn directly into electricity?
19822.e: Solar cells are usually made of silicon. When light falls on them, electrons are set in motion and a current flows; this is called photovoltaics.
19822.m: Solar cells turn light into electricity.

19823.q: What is the use of heat from inside the Earth called?
19823.e: Geo means earth and thermal means heat. In Switzerland, many houses are heated with ground probes and a heat pump.
19823.m: Geothermal energy uses the Earth’s heat.

19824.q: Which dam in Valais, at 285 metres, is the tallest gravity dam in the world?
19824.e: The Grande Dixence holds back the Lac des Dix in the Val d’Hérémence. It was completed in 1961.
19824.m: The Grande Dixence in Valais is a record-breaking dam.

19825.q: Why does wind energy count as a renewable energy?
a: Because wind keeps forming again and again
Because wind is stored in barrels
Because wind is made from coal
19825.e: Wind forms because the Sun heats the Earth unevenly. On a human timescale, this source never runs out.
19825.m: Renewable energies do not run out.

19826.q: What does a pumped-storage power station do with surplus electricity?
a: It pumps water up into a higher lake
It charges big batteries in cars
It sends it into the ground
19826.e: When electricity is needed, the pumped-up water flows back down and drives turbines. So the power station works like a giant store.
19826.m: Pumped-storage power stations store energy with water.

19827.q: Which of these energy sources is NOT renewable?
19827.e: Natural gas formed over millions of years and is used up much faster than it forms again. That is why it counts as a fossil fuel.
19827.m: Fossil fuels like natural gas are not renewable.

19853.q: Which DeepMind program defeated the Go professional Lee Sedol in 2016?
19853.e: AlphaGo won the match in March 2016 by 4 to 1. The program combined neural networks with a Monte Carlo tree search.
19853.m: In 2016 AlphaGo proved that AI can beat top players even at the complex game of Go.

19854.q: What is the name of the early chat program that Joseph Weizenbaum wrote in the mid-1960s?
19854.e: ELIZA used simple patterns to imitate a therapy conversation. Weizenbaum was shocked at how seriously some people took the program.
19854.m: As early as the 1960s, ELIZA showed how easily people treat machines as if they were human.

19855.q: Which network architecture, introduced in 2017 in the paper “Attention Is All You Need”, are today's large language models based on?
19855.e: The transformer processes text with the attention mechanism, which weighs the relationships between all words at the same time. It can be trained well in parallel.
19855.m: Large language models are based on the transformer architecture.

19856.q: By which basic principle does the EU's 2024 AI regulation classify AI systems?
a: By the size of the manufacturer
19856.e: Among other things, the AI Act distinguishes between banned applications, high-risk systems and low-risk systems. The higher the risk, the stricter the obligations.
19856.m: The EU regulates AI systems according to their risk.

a: The model learns from examples with known correct answers.
The model learns only from rewards and punishments.
The model finds groups in data by itself without guidance.
The model is controlled live by a human.
19857.e: In supervised learning, the training data are given target values (labels). The model learns to map inputs onto these target values.
19857.m: Supervised learning needs labelled training data.

19858.q: What is it called when a model memorises the training data but performs poorly on new data?
19858.e: With overfitting, the model also adapts to random quirks in the training data. As a result it generalises poorly.
19858.m: An overfitted model memorises instead of generalising.

19859.q: What is the perceptron, introduced in 1958?
a: An early model of an artificial neuron
A device for measuring brain waves
19859.e: Frank Rosenblatt developed the perceptron as a classifier that can learn. It weights its inputs and decides using a threshold. Today's neural networks consist of many such units.
19859.m: The perceptron is an ancestor of today's neural networks.

19860.q: What is adjusted step by step when training a neural network so that it makes fewer mistakes?
a: The weights of the connections between the neurons
The clock speed of the computer
The order of the letters in the program
19860.e: The network compares its output with the correct answer. Using backpropagation, the error is passed backwards and the weights are changed so that the error gets smaller.
19860.m: A neural network learns by adjusting its weights.

19861.q: In which type of learning does an agent learn through rewards for its actions in an environment?
19861.e: In reinforcement learning, an agent tries out actions and receives rewards for them. It learns a strategy that maximises the total reward.
19861.m: Reinforcement learning works through trial and reward.

19862.q: What is the k-means algorithm used for?
19862.e: k-means is a method of unsupervised learning. It assigns each data point to the nearest of k centres and moves these centres repeatedly.
19862.m: k-means divides data without labels into groups.

19863.q: Why is a test data set held back in machine learning?
a: To check how well the model works on unseen data
To save storage space on the computer
To fix the number of weights
19863.e: The test data are not used during training. So the performance on them shows whether the model generalises or has only memorised.
19863.m: A model is tested with data it never saw during training.

19864.q: A spam filter marks 50 emails as spam, and 40 of them really are spam. What is its precision?
19864.e: Precision is the share of correct hits among all positive results. 40 / 50 = 0.8, so 80 per cent.
19864.m: Precision tells you how many of the reported hits are actually correct.

19865.q: What is the name of the control device widely used in industry whose sequence is set by a program (PLC in English)?
19865.e: A programmable logic controller (PLC) reads sensor signals and switches actuators according to its program. From the 1970s it replaced many hard-wired relay circuits.
19865.m: A PLC controls machines according to a stored program.

19866.q: What distinguishes closed-loop control from open-loop control?
a: Closed-loop control measures the output and corrects it continuously.
Closed-loop control always works without electricity.
Closed-loop control has no target values.
19866.e: In closed-loop control the actual value is measured and compared with the target value, creating a closed control loop. Open-loop control, on the other hand, works without feedback.
19866.m: Closed-loop control works with feedback, open-loop control does not.

19867.q: Which invention by Joseph-Marie Jacquard controlled weaving patterns with punched cards from 1804?
19867.e: The punched cards determined which warp threads were lifted. The principle later inspired Charles Babbage and data processing with punched cards.
19867.m: The Jacquard loom was an early program-controlled machine.

19868.q: Which businessman introduced the moving assembly line in car production in 1913?
19868.e: In 1913 Ford introduced the moving assembly line for the Model T in Highland Park. As a result, the time needed to assemble a car fell dramatically.
19868.m: Henry Ford turned the car into a mass product through assembly line work.

19869.q: What does the “I” stand for in the term PID controller?
19869.e: A PID controller combines a proportional, an integral and a derivative part. The I part adds up the control error over time and removes lasting deviations.
19869.m: The integral part of a controller removes lasting control errors.

19870.q: With which device did James Watt automatically regulate the speed of his steam engine?
19870.e: In the centrifugal governor, rotating balls rise as the speed increases and reduce the steam supply through a linkage. It is an early example of mechanical control.
19870.m: The centrifugal governor kept the steam engine running at a steady speed.

19871.q: What does the term “Industry 4.0” stand for?
a: Mechanisation of factories by steam power
The first introduction of computers in factories
19871.e: The term became known in Germany in 2011. Machines, workpieces and software exchange data on their own and optimise production.
19871.m: Industry 4.0 means the digitally networked factory.

19872.q: Which SAE level of automated driving means full automation without a driver?
19872.e: The SAE J3016 standard has levels 0 to 5. Only at level 5 does the vehicle drive in all conditions without any human intervention.
19872.m: Level 5 means a car drives completely without a driver.

19873.q: Which effect is a thermocouple for measuring temperature based on?
19873.e: Two different metals produce a small voltage at their junction when there is a temperature difference. The temperature can be worked out from this thermoelectric voltage.
19873.m: A thermocouple turns temperature differences into electrical voltage.

19874.q: What does a Hall sensor measure?
19874.e: When current flows through a conductor in a magnetic field, the Hall voltage appears at right angles to it. Hall sensors can thus detect rotation speeds or the position of magnets, for example.
19874.m: A Hall sensor reacts to magnetic fields.

19875.q: Which physical effect are the image sensors in digital cameras based on?
19875.e: In CCD and CMOS sensors, incoming photons release electrons in the semiconductor. The charge collected in each pixel corresponds to the brightness.
19875.m: Camera sensors turn light into electrical charge in a semiconductor.

19876.q: Which effect describes certain crystals producing an electrical voltage when under pressure?
19876.e: In quartz and other crystals, the centres of charge shift when the crystal is deformed. Piezo sensors use this to measure forces, pressure and acceleration.
19876.m: Piezo crystals produce a voltage when they are deformed.

19877.q: A LiDAR pulse returns after 200 nanoseconds. How far away is the object?
19877.e: The light travels there and back. Distance = c · t / 2 = 3 · 10⁸ m/s · 200 · 10⁻⁹ s / 2 = 30 m.
19877.m: With time-of-flight measurements you have to halve the measured time.

19878.q: An ultrasonic sensor receives the echo after 0.02 s. How far away is the obstacle if the speed of sound is 343 m/s?
19878.e: The sound travels there and back. Distance = 343 m/s · 0.02 s / 2 = 3.43 m.
19878.m: An echo covers the distance to the obstacle twice.

19879.q: Which sensor in a smartphone detects whether the device is held upright or sideways?
19879.e: The accelerometer also measures the direction of gravity. From this the device works out its position in space.
19879.m: The accelerometer uses gravity to detect the smartphone's position.

19880.q: Which 1920 play does the word “robot” come from?
a: “The Sandman” by E. T. A. Hoffmann
19880.e: The play “R.U.R.” (Rossum's Universal Robots) features artificial workers. The word comes from the Czech “robota”, meaning forced labour.
19880.m: The word robot comes from Czech and originally meant forced labour.

19881.q: What kind of work did the first industrial robot do in 1961 in a General Motors car factory?
a: Taking hot die-cast parts out of the machine
19881.e: The robot Unimate removed hot metal parts from a die-casting machine. It thus took over dangerous and strenuous work.
19881.m: In 1961 the first industrial robot did dangerous work with hot cast parts.

19882.q: How many laws of robotics did Isaac Asimov originally write in 1942?
19882.e: Asimov presented the three laws in the short story “Runaround”. A higher “zeroth law” was only added later.
19882.m: Isaac Asimov wrote three laws of robotics.

19883.q: What is the minimum number of degrees of freedom a robot arm needs to hold a tool in any position and orientation in space?
19883.e: Three degrees of freedom determine the position, three more the orientation. That is why many industrial robots have six axes.
19883.m: Free position and orientation in space need six degrees of freedom.

19884.q: What does the inverse kinematics of a robot arm calculate?
a: The joint angles for a desired gripper position
The gripper position from known joint angles
The power consumption of the individual motors
The top speed of the robot arm
19884.e: Forward kinematics determines the position of the gripper from the joint settings. Inverse kinematics solves the reverse task, which often has more than one answer.
19884.m: Inverse kinematics works back from the goal to the joint angles.

a: It works directly with people without a safety fence.
It is programmed only by voice commands.
It is made entirely of soft materials.
19885.e: Cobots (collaborative robots) have sensors and limited forces. They stop when touched and may therefore work next to people.
19885.m: A cobot safely shares the workplace with people.

19886.q: What is the name of the four-legged walking robot developed at ETH Zurich and sold by the spin-off ANYbotics?
19886.e: ANYmal was created at the Robotic Systems Lab of ETH Zurich. It is used, for example, for inspections in industrial plants.
19886.m: ANYmal is a well-known walking robot from Switzerland.

19887.q: What does SLAM stand for in mobile robotics?
19887.e: SLAM means Simultaneous Localization and Mapping. The robot builds a map of an unknown environment and at the same time works out its own position in it.
19887.m: With SLAM a robot creates a map and finds its way around in it at the same time.

19888.q: How many metres is a nanometre?
19888.e: The prefix “nano” stands for one billionth. A nanometre is therefore a thousand times smaller than a micrometre.
19888.m: A nanometre is one billionth of a metre.

19889.q: Who gave the famous 1959 talk “There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom”, regarded as the vision of nanotechnology?
19889.e: Feynman described the possibility of working with matter atom by atom. Among other things, he spoke of writing a whole encyclopaedia on the head of a pin.
19889.m: Richard Feynman is seen as the intellectual father of nanotechnology.

19890.q: Where did Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer develop the scanning tunnelling microscope in 1981?
a: At the IBM research lab in Rüschlikon
19890.e: The scanning tunnelling microscope made individual atoms on surfaces visible for the first time. Binnig and Rohrer received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1986.
19890.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope was invented in Switzerland.

19891.q: What does the lotus effect describe?
a: The self-cleaning of surfaces through nanostructures
19891.e: Micro- and nanostructures on the lotus leaf make water roll off. The drops take dirt particles with them.
19891.m: The lotus effect uses tiny structures for water-repellent, self-cleaning surfaces.

a: A single layer of carbon atoms
An alloy of iron and carbon
A plastic made from crude oil
A crystal of silicon and oxygen
19892.e: Graphene consists of carbon atoms in a honeycomb lattice and is only one atom thick. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 2010.
19892.m: Graphene is a carbon lattice only one atom thick.

19893.q: How many carbon atoms make up the best-known fullerene, which looks like a football?
19893.e: Buckminsterfullerene C60 was discovered in 1985. Its atoms form 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, like a football.
19893.m: The football molecule C60 consists of 60 carbon atoms.

19894.q: A cube with 1 cm sides is cut into cubes with 1 mm sides. By what factor does the total surface area increase?
19894.e: Before: 6 · 100 mm² = 600 mm². After: 1000 cubes · 6 mm² = 6000 mm², so ten times as much.
19894.m: The smaller the particles, the larger their surface area compared with their volume.

19895.q: Who received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors?
19895.e: In 2012 Charpentier and Doudna showed that CRISPR/Cas9 can be programmed to cut DNA precisely. The method has made genetic engineering much simpler.
19895.m: The CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors cut DNA at precisely chosen places.

19896.q: Which medicine was approved in 1982 as the first genetically engineered drug for humans?
19896.e: Genetically modified bacteria produced human insulin. Before that, insulin was obtained from the pancreases of pigs and cattle.
19896.m: Insulin was the first genetically engineered medicine.

19897.q: Which method copies specific sections of DNA many times and was developed by Kary Mullis in 1983?
19897.e: PCR doubles the amount of the desired DNA section in every temperature cycle. After 30 cycles, this produces around a billion copies.
19897.m: PCR copies DNA over many temperature cycles.

19898.q: Which animal was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell, in 1996?
19898.e: Dolly was created at the Roslin Institute in Scotland by nuclear transfer. She showed that specialised body cells can be reprogrammed.
19898.m: Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from a body cell.

19899.q: For discovering which enzymes did the Swiss scientist Werner Arber receive the Nobel Prize in 1978?
19899.e: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at particular base sequences. They became a basic tool of genetic engineering.
19899.m: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at fixed recognition sites.

a: Biotechnology in plant breeding and farming
Biotechnology in the sea and in waters
19900.e: The colours stand for fields of use, such as red for medicine, white for industry and blue for marine organisms. Green stands for plants and farming.
19900.m: Green biotechnology deals with plants and farming.

19901.q: What did Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman receive the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for?
a: For modified nucleosides that made mRNA vaccines possible
For decoding the DNA double helix
For inventing the polymerase chain reaction
19901.e: They showed that altered building blocks make mRNA more tolerable for the immune system. This was one of the foundations of the mRNA vaccines against Covid-19.
19901.m: Modified mRNA made fast vaccine development possible.

19902.q: What is the name of the container in which microorganisms or cells make products under controlled conditions?
19902.e: In a bioreactor, temperature, pH, oxygen and nutrients are precisely controlled. In this way cells produce antibodies or enzymes, for example.
19902.m: In a bioreactor, cells work like tiny factories.

19903.q: What distinguishes a qubit from a classical bit?
a: It can be in a superposition of 0 and 1.
It can only have the value 1.
It always stores three values at once.
It works entirely without an energy supply.
19903.e: A qubit can take on a superposition of the states 0 and 1. Only when it is measured is there a definite result.
19903.m: A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 at the same time.

19904.q: How many basis states does the state space of a register of 10 qubits contain?
19904.e: Each extra qubit doubles the number of basis states. With 10 qubits there are 2¹⁰ = 1024.
19904.m: The state space of qubits grows exponentially with their number.

19905.q: Which problem does Shor's algorithm solve efficiently, thereby threatening today's encryption such as RSA?
a: Breaking large numbers down into prime factors
Finding the shortest routes on maps
19905.e: The security of RSA rests on the fact that factorising large numbers is very hard for classical computers. In 1994 Peter Shor showed that a quantum computer could do this efficiently.
19905.m: Shor's algorithm threatens encryption that relies on factorisation being hard.

19906.q: For which task could a quantum computer using Grover's algorithm be faster than a classical computer?
a: Searching large unsorted amounts of data
19906.e: A classical computer has to check unsorted entries one by one. Grover's algorithm needs far fewer steps: with a million entries only about 1,000 instead of 500,000 on average.
19906.m: Grover's algorithm speeds up searching in unsorted data.

19907.q: What is the loss of a qubit's quantum properties through interaction with its surroundings called?
19907.e: Heat, radiation or vibrations disturb the delicate quantum state. Decoherence limits how long a quantum computer can calculate.
19907.m: Decoherence destroys the delicate states of qubits.

19908.q: Which quantum phenomenon did Albert Einstein call “spooky action at a distance”?
19908.e: Entangled particles show correlated measurement results even when they are far apart. Quantum computers use entanglement as an important resource.
19908.m: The measurement results of entangled particles are linked over any distance.

19909.q: At what temperatures are superconducting qubits typically operated?
19909.e: Superconducting qubits are cooled in dilution refrigerators to a few thousandths of a kelvin above absolute zero. This keeps thermal disturbances to a minimum.
19909.m: Superconducting quantum computers need temperatures close to absolute zero.

19910.q: Which company was the first to announce, in 2019, that it had achieved “quantum supremacy” with a quantum computer?
19910.e: Google's Sycamore processor solved a special random task in about 200 seconds. Google estimated it would take a supercomputer thousands of years, which IBM disputed.
19910.m: Quantum supremacy means a quantum computer solves a task faster than any classical computer.

19911.q: What is the Carnot efficiency of a heat engine working between 600 K and 300 K?
19911.e: η = 1 − T_cold / T_hot = 1 − 300 / 600 = 0.5. No real engine working between these temperatures can do better.
19911.m: The Carnot efficiency is the upper limit for any heat engine.

19912.q: Roughly what efficiency do standard silicon solar panels reach today (as of 2025)?
19912.e: Common silicon panels turn about a fifth of the sunlight into electricity. Laboratory cells and multi-junction cells reach much higher values.
19912.m: Solar panels turn about a fifth of sunlight into electricity.

19913.q: What kind of power station is Nant de Drance in Valais?
19913.e: When there is surplus electricity, Nant de Drance pumps water into the upper reservoir and generates electricity again when needed. The plant has an output of 900 MW and has been fully in operation since 2022.
19913.m: Pumped storage power stations store energy by pumping water uphill.

19914.q: Why is electrical energy transmitted over long distances at high voltage?
a: For the same power, less current flows, so there are smaller line losses.
High voltage makes the electrons flow faster than light.
High voltage makes the lines lighter and cheaper.
High voltage creates extra energy in the line.
19914.e: Power is P = U · I, and the losses in the line are P_L = I² · R. A higher voltage lowers the current and so reduces the losses greatly.
19914.m: High voltage means low current and therefore small losses.

19915.q: A device with a power of 2 kW runs for 3 hours. How much does that cost at a price of 30 centimes per kWh?
19915.e: Energy = 2 kW · 3 h = 6 kWh. Cost = 6 · 0.30 francs = 1.80 francs.
19915.m: Energy is power multiplied by time.

19916.q: A heat pump has a coefficient of performance of 4. How much heat does it deliver with 1 kWh of electricity?
19916.e: The coefficient of performance is the ratio of heat delivered to electrical energy used. 1 kWh · 4 = 4 kWh; the rest comes from the heat of the surroundings.
19916.m: A heat pump delivers more heat than it uses in electricity.

19918.q: Which energy source supplied about 60 per cent of Switzerland's domestic electricity production in 2024?
19918.e: According to the Swiss Federal Office of Energy, around 48 of just over 80 terawatt hours came from run-of-river and storage power stations in 2024. Nuclear energy supplied just under a third.
19918.m: Hydropower is Switzerland's most important source of electricity.

19919.q: Which invention mainly drove the first industrial revolution in Great Britain in the late 18th century?
19919.e: James Watt made decisive improvements to the steam engine from 1769. It powered spinning machines, mine pumps and later locomotives.
19919.m: The steam engine was the engine of the first industrial revolution.

19920.q: Which technology particularly shaped the second industrial revolution from around 1870?
19920.e: Electricity, chemistry and the combustion engine changed factories and everyday life. Electric drives made mass production on the assembly line possible.
19920.m: The second industrial revolution was based on electricity and mass production.

19921.q: What characterises the third industrial revolution from the 1970s?
a: Automation through electronics and information technology
Mechanisation through water and steam power
The first use of electric motors
19921.e: Microprocessors and computers increasingly controlled machines and processes. It is also called the digital revolution.
19921.m: The third industrial revolution brought computers into production.

19922.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450 sparked a media revolution?
19922.e: With movable metal type, books could be copied quickly and cheaply for the first time. As a result, knowledge spread much faster.
19922.m: Gutenberg's printing press made knowledge available to many people.

19923.q: Where did Tim Berners-Lee develop the World Wide Web in 1989?
19923.e: Berners-Lee proposed a hypertext system so that researchers could share information. In 1993 CERN made the technology freely available.
19923.m: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in Switzerland.

19924.q: Between which places did the first railway running entirely on Swiss soil operate in 1847?
19924.e: The Swiss Northern Railway opened the line on 9 August 1847. It is popularly known as the “Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn” (Spanish bun railway).
19924.m: The first Swiss railway ran from Zurich to Baden in 1847.

19925.q: Which event in 1832 in the Zurich Oberland is a well-known example of machine breaking in Switzerland?
19925.e: Home weavers who feared for their income set fire to a mechanical weaving mill in Uster. The incident shows the social consequences of industrialisation.
19925.m: In the Uster fire, home workers fought back against the machines.

19926.q: What do you need money for?
19926.e: With money you pay for things you want to buy. The seller gets the money and you get the goods.

19927.q: What did people swap before there was money?
19927.e: In the past, people swapped grain for tools, for example. This is called bartering.

19928.q: What do you call money in coins and banknotes that you can hold in your hand?
19928.e: You can touch coins and banknotes. Together they are called cash.

19929.q: What can you use to pay without cash?
19929.e: With a bank card or credit card you pay without handing over coins or notes. The money is taken from your account.
19929.m: You can also pay with a card.

19930.q: What is the money called that you get back if you have given too much?
19930.e: If you pay with a big note, you get the rest back. This money is called change.
19930.m: You get your change back at the till.

19931.q: What do you call the money of a country?
19931.e: Every country has its own money, its currency. In Switzerland it is the franc.
19931.m: The money of a country is called its currency.

19932.q: What is the money called that many countries in Europe use?
19932.e: In Germany, Austria, France and Italy you pay with the euro. But Switzerland has the franc.
19932.m: Many of Switzerland’s neighbouring countries pay with the euro.

19933.q: Which money is used in the USA?
19933.e: In the United States of America you pay with the US dollar.
19933.m: In the USA you pay with dollars.

19934.q: What material are coins made of?
19934.e: Coins are small round discs made of metal. That is why they are hard and heavy.

19935.e: All Swiss coins are round discs. That way they roll well and fit into machines.

19936.q: What is the smallest coin you can pay with in Switzerland today?
19936.e: The smallest Swiss coin is the 5-centime piece. The 1-centime coin has not been valid since 2007.
19936.m: The smallest coin is the 5-centime piece.

19937.q: What is the largest coin in Switzerland?
19937.e: The 5-franc piece is the largest and most valuable Swiss coin. It is bigger than all the other coins.
19937.m: The 5-franc piece is the largest Swiss coin.

19938.q: What nickname do people in Switzerland give the 5-franc piece?
19938.e: This is what the 5-franc piece is called in everyday life in Switzerland. Almost every child knows the name.
19938.m: The 5-franc piece is called a Fünfliber.

19939.q: How many different coins are there in Switzerland today?
19939.e: There are 5, 10 and 20 centimes as well as 1/2, 1, 2 and 5 francs. That makes 7 coins.

19940.e: The Swiss mint is called Swissmint. It is in Bern.

19941.q: Which woman can be seen on the 1-franc piece?
19941.e: The 1-franc piece shows Helvetia with a spear and shield. She is a symbol of Switzerland.
19941.m: Helvetia is on the franc piece.

19942.q: What material are banknotes made of?
19942.e: Banknotes are made of special paper. The new Swiss notes also have a layer of plastic in the middle.
19942.m: Banknotes are made of special paper.

19943.q: What colour is the Swiss 10-franc note?
19943.e: The 10-franc note is yellow. Every Swiss banknote has its own colour.

19944.q: What colour is the Swiss 20-franc note?
19944.e: The 20-franc note is red. This makes it easy to tell apart from the other notes.

19945.q: What colour is the Swiss 50-franc note?
19945.e: The 50-franc note is green. It shows a hand with dandelion seeds.

19946.q: What colour is the Swiss 100-franc note?
19946.e: The 100-franc note is blue. It shows water, for example hands scooping up water.

19947.q: Which Swiss banknote has the highest value?
19947.e: The biggest Swiss note is worth 1,000 francs. It is violet.
19947.m: The biggest Swiss note is the 1,000-franc note.

19948.q: Which Swiss banknote has the lowest value?
19948.e: The smallest Swiss banknote is the 10-franc note. Smaller amounts come as coins.
19948.m: The smallest Swiss note is the 10-franc note.

19949.q: Who issues the banknotes in Switzerland?
19949.e: Only the Swiss National Bank is allowed to issue banknotes. It makes sure there is enough money.
19949.m: The National Bank issues the banknotes.

19950.q: What is the money of Switzerland called?
19950.e: In Switzerland you pay with the Swiss franc. It comes as coins and as banknotes.
19950.m: The money of Switzerland is called the franc.

19951.e: One franc has 100 centimes. So two francs are 200 centimes.
19951.m: One franc has a hundred centimes.

19952.q: How is the Swiss franc shortened internationally?
19952.e: The short form CHF stands for the franc of the “Confoederatio Helvetica”. That is the name of Switzerland in Latin.
19952.m: The Swiss franc is shortened to CHF.

19953.q: How many centimes make half a franc?
19953.e: A whole franc has 100 centimes. Half of that is 50 centimes.
19953.m: Half a franc is fifty centimes.

19954.e: One franc has 100 centimes. 2 times 100 centimes is 200 centimes.
19954.m: Two francs are two hundred centimes.

19955.q: In which other country do people also pay with the Swiss franc?
19955.e: Liechtenstein is a small neighbouring country of Switzerland. It also uses the Swiss franc.
19955.m: In Liechtenstein, too, people pay with francs.

19956.q: Since which year has the Swiss franc existed?
19956.e: The franc was introduced in 1850 as the money for the whole of Switzerland. Before that, the cantons had their own money.
19956.m: The Swiss franc has existed since 1850.

19957.q: How many 10-centime coins do you need for 1 franc?
19957.e: 1 franc is 100 centimes. 100 divided by 10 makes 10 coins.

19958.q: Where do you pay in a shop?
19958.e: If you want to buy something, you put the goods down at the till. That is where you pay.
19958.m: In a shop you pay at the till.

19959.q: What do you get at the till as proof of your shopping?
19959.e: The receipt shows what you bought and how much you paid. It is also called a till receipt.
19959.m: The receipt shows what you bought.

19960.q: What do you write down so that you do not forget anything when shopping?
19960.e: A shopping list has all the things you need on it. That way you do not forget anything and do not buy too much.
19960.m: A shopping list helps when you go shopping.

19961.q: Where can you buy vegetables straight from the farmer?
19961.e: At the weekly market, farmers sell fresh vegetables and fruit. You can often buy straight from the farm too.
19961.m: There are fresh vegetables at the market.

19962.q: Where do you buy fresh bread?
19962.e: At the bakery, bakers bake fresh bread every day. You can buy it there.
19962.m: You buy fresh bread at the bakery.

19963.q: Where do you buy meat and sausages?
19963.e: The butcher’s sells meat and sausages. Many supermarkets also have a meat counter.
19963.m: You buy meat at the butcher’s.

19964.q: What do you take with you to carry your shopping home?
19964.e: In a shopping bag you can carry the goods easily. If you bring your own bag, you do not need a new one.
19964.m: Your own bag is good for your shopping.

19965.q: What is a large shop called where you can buy food, drinks and much more?
19965.e: A supermarket has many different goods under one roof. You take them off the shelf yourself.
19965.m: You find lots of goods in a supermarket.

19966.q: What does the price tag on an item show?
19966.e: The price tag shows how much you have to pay for the item.
19966.m: The price tag shows the price.

19967.q: An apple costs 1 franc. How much do 3 apples cost?
19967.e: One apple costs 1 franc. 3 times 1 franc is 3 francs.
19967.m: Three apples cost three times as much as one.

19968.q: An ice cream costs 3 francs. You pay with 5 francs. How much do you get back?
19968.e: You work out 5 francs minus 3 francs. That makes 2 francs change.
19968.m: The change is the money you paid minus the price.

19969.q: An exercise book costs 2 francs and a pencil 1 franc. How much do they cost together?
19969.e: You work out 2 francs plus 1 franc. Together they cost 3 francs.
19969.m: For the total price you add the prices together.

19970.q: What do you call it when an item costs less for a short time?
19970.e: With a special offer, the price is lowered for a short time. You then save a bit of money when shopping.
19970.m: With a special offer the price is lower.

19971.q: A loaf of bread costs 4 francs. How much do 2 loaves cost?
19971.e: You work out 2 times 4 francs. Two loaves cost 8 francs.
19971.m: Two loaves cost twice as much as one.

19972.q: You have 10 francs. A book costs 7 francs. How much money do you have left?
19972.e: You work out 10 francs minus 7 francs. There are 3 francs left over.
19972.m: You find out what is left over by taking away.

a: Keeping money instead of spending it
Spending all your money straight away
19973.e: If you save, you do not spend your money straight away. You put it aside to buy something bigger later.
19973.m: Saving means keeping money for later.

19974.q: Which animal is often a money box?
19974.e: The piggy bank is a well-known money box. It has a slot on top for the coins.
19974.m: The piggy bank is a popular money box.

19975.q: Where can you keep your savings safely?
19975.e: In a savings account at the bank, the money is safe. It cannot get lost or be stolen.
19975.m: Your savings are safe at the bank.

19976.q: You save 2 francs every week. How much do you have after 4 weeks?
19976.e: You work out 4 times 2 francs. After 4 weeks you have saved 8 francs.
19976.m: If you save regularly, you soon have more money.

a: For something big they wish for
So that the bank keeps it
So that they never need it again
19977.e: Some things are too expensive to buy in one go. If you save, you can buy them later.
19977.m: Saving helps you get bigger things you wish for.

19978.q: What is an account where you save money called?
19978.e: In a savings account at the bank, you put money aside for later. Many children already have one.
19978.m: You save money in a savings account.

19979.q: What does the bank sometimes give you if you leave money in your savings account?
19979.e: For money in a savings account, the bank sometimes pays a small amount. This is called interest.
19979.m: You sometimes get interest on your savings.

19980.q: How can you save money when shopping?
19980.e: If you compare prices, you often find a cheaper item. That way more money is left over.

19982.q: Who usually gives children pocket money?
19982.e: Children usually get their pocket money from their parents. Often there is an amount every week or every month.
19982.m: Usually parents give the pocket money.

19983.q: Who is allowed to decide what the pocket money is spent on?
19983.e: With pocket money, children learn to handle money themselves. That is why they decide for themselves what to use it for.
19983.m: The child decides about their own pocket money.

19984.q: What do you learn with pocket money?
a: How to read without a book
19984.e: If you get pocket money, you have to plan and sometimes save. That is how you learn to handle money well.
19984.m: Pocket money teaches you how to handle money.

19985.q: You get 3 francs of pocket money a week. How much do you have after 2 weeks?
19985.e: You work out 2 times 3 francs. After 2 weeks you have 6 francs.
19985.m: Pocket money grows if you do not spend it.

19986.q: What happens when all your pocket money has already been spent?
19986.e: When your pocket money is gone, you have to wait until next time. That is why it is worth planning well.
19986.m: When the pocket money is gone, you have to wait.

19987.q: How often do many children get their pocket money?
19987.e: Younger children usually get their pocket money every week. Older children often get it every month.
19987.m: Younger children often get their pocket money weekly.

19988.q: What does every person need to live?
19988.e: People cannot live without food and drink. These are basic needs.
19988.m: Every person needs food and drink.

19989.q: Which is a wish and not a basic need?
19989.e: A toy is fun, but you do not need it to survive. That is why it is a wish.
19989.m: A toy is a wish, not a basic need.

19990.q: Why do people need a flat or a house?
19990.e: A home protects you from cold, rain and wind. A roof over your head is a basic need.

19991.q: What do you need in winter so that you do not freeze?
19991.e: Warm clothes protect the body from the cold. Clothing is a basic need.
19991.m: In winter you need warm clothes.

19992.q: What should you buy first when money is short?
19992.e: What you really need comes first, and that is food. Wishes only come after that.
19992.m: First you buy what you really need.

a: I would like a new bike
19993.e: You need drinking, sleeping and breathing to live. A new bike is something you would like to have, so it is a wish.
19993.m: A wish is something you would like to have.

19994.q: Can money make all wishes come true?
19994.e: You cannot buy friendship, health or time with your family. And usually there is not enough money for everything anyway.
19994.m: Not everything can be bought with money.

19995.q: What does the body need every night?
19995.e: The body recovers while you sleep. Sleeping is a basic need of every person.
19995.m: The body needs sleep every night.

19996.e: Bakers get up very early. They bake bread, croissants and cakes.

19997.e: A vet examines and treats sick animals. She works in a vet’s practice or on the farm.

19998.e: The postman delivers letters and parcels every day. He brings them to the letterbox or to the front door.

19999.e: Firefighters put out fires and rescue people and animals. In Switzerland you call them on the number 118.
19999.m: The fire brigade puts out fires.

20000.e: You go to the hairdresser to have your hair cut. In Switzerland the job is often called coiffeur or coiffeuse.

20001.q: Who makes furniture out of wood?
20001.e: Carpenters work with wood. They make tables, cupboards and doors.
20001.m: The carpenter makes furniture out of wood.

20002.e: Pilots fly aeroplanes. They have done a long training for it.

20003.q: What is the training called that many young people in Switzerland do after school?
20003.e: In Switzerland many young people do an apprenticeship. They learn at a company and at vocational school.
20003.m: Many young people do an apprenticeship after school.

20004.q: What, among other things, do adults work for?
20004.e: Adults get money for their work. With it they pay, for example, for food and a home.

20005.q: What is the money called that you get for your work?
20005.e: If you work, you get wages for it. They are usually paid into your account every month.

20006.q: Which work is often done at home without pay?
20006.e: Cooking, cleaning and washing are housework. It is important, but it is usually not paid.

20007.q: What is the place where you work called?
20007.e: The place where you work is called your workplace. It can be an office, a workshop or a field.
20007.m: Where you work is your workplace.

20008.q: What do you call a person who works for a company?
20008.e: Someone who works for a company and is paid wages for it is an employee. The company is then the employer.
20008.m: Someone who works for a company is an employee.

20009.q: Which is a small job that children can help with at home?
20009.e: Children can help at home, for example by laying the table. That way the whole family helps.

20010.q: What do you have at the end of the working day?
20010.e: When the work is finished for the day, the working day is over. Then you have free time.
20010.m: After work you have free time.

20011.q: What can you do at a bank before the holidays?
20011.e: At a bank you can change money. For holidays abroad you might swap francs for euros, for example.
20011.m: You can change money at the bank.

20012.q: What is the thing at the bank where your money is recorded called?
20012.e: At the bank you have an account. It shows how much money you have.
20012.m: Your account shows how much money you have.

20013.q: What is the sheet from the bank called that shows what has happened in your account?
20013.e: On the bank statement you can see how much money came into the account and how much was taken out. You get it on paper or online.
20013.m: The bank statement shows what has happened in the account.

20014.q: What is it called when you put money into your account?
20014.e: If you put money into your account, you pay it in. Then there is more money in the account.
20014.m: When you pay in, money goes into the account.

20015.q: What is it called when you take money out of your account?
20015.e: If you take money out of your account, you withdraw it. Afterwards there is less money in the account.
20015.m: When you withdraw, you take money out of the account.

20016.q: Which banks in Switzerland belong to a canton?
20016.e: Almost every canton has its own cantonal bank. For example, there is the Zürcher Kantonalbank.
20016.m: Many cantons have their own cantonal bank.

20017.q: What is the money you borrow from the bank called?
20017.e: If you borrow money from the bank, you get a loan. You have to pay the money back later.
20017.m: You have to pay back a loan.

20018.q: Where does a bank clerk work?
20018.e: Bank clerks give customers advice about money. They work in a bank.
20018.m: Bank clerks work in the bank.

20019.q: What do people in Switzerland often call a cash machine?
20019.e: In Switzerland a cash machine is usually called a Bancomat. That is where you get cash.
20019.m: In Switzerland the cash machine is called a Bancomat.

20020.q: What comes out of a cash machine?
20020.e: At a cash machine you can withdraw banknotes from your account. You need a bank card for it.
20020.m: You get cash from a cash machine.

20021.q: What do you need to get money from a cash machine?
20021.e: You put the bank card into the machine. Then you type in your PIN.
20021.m: You need a bank card at a cash machine.

20022.q: What should you do at a cash machine when you type in your PIN?
a: Cover the keypad with your hand
Write the PIN on the card
20022.e: Your PIN is secret. If you cover it while typing, you stop other people or hidden cameras from seeing it.
20022.m: Always cover the keypad when you type in your PIN.

20023.q: Who can you tell the PIN of your card to?
20023.e: The PIN protects the money in your account. That is why you tell it to nobody.
20023.m: You tell your PIN to nobody.

20024.q: What should you do when typing in your PIN?
20024.e: You cover the keys with your hand. That way nobody can see your PIN.
20024.m: When typing, you cover the keys.

20025.q: Where does the money you withdraw from a cash machine come from?
20025.e: The money is taken from your own bank account. If there is no money in the account, you do not get any either.
20025.m: The money from the machine comes from your own account.

20026.q: Lea gets 40 francs of pocket money a month and wants to save 25 per cent of it. How much money does she have left to spend?
20026.e: 25 per cent of 40 francs is 10 francs. 40 minus 10 makes 30 francs to spend.
20026.m: If you save a fixed part first, you can spend the rest without feeling guilty.

20027.q: What does a balanced budget mean?
a: Income and spending are the same
There is no spending at all
20027.e: With a balanced budget, exactly as much is spent as comes in. There are neither debts nor savings.
20027.m: A balanced budget does not spend more than it takes in.

20028.q: Which expense in a household budget is one of the fixed costs?
20028.e: Fixed costs come up regularly at the same amount, for example the rent every month. The cinema or presents, on the other hand, are irregular.
20028.m: You must always plan for fixed costs every month.

20029.q: Why do you plan a reserve in a budget?
a: So that the bank charges fees
20029.e: Something unexpected can always happen, for example broken glasses. A reserve means you do not have to get into debt then.
20029.m: A reserve in the budget protects you from nasty surprises.

20030.q: Tim has a monthly budget of 120 francs. He spends 45 francs on his mobile phone, 30 francs on going out and 20 francs on clothes. How much is left?
20030.e: The spending comes to 45 + 30 + 20, which is 95 francs. 120 minus 95 makes 25 francs.
20030.m: If you add up all your spending, you can see how much is left.

20031.q: What do you call it when spending in a budget is higher than income?
20031.e: A deficit is a shortfall: more is spent than comes in. The missing money has to be borrowed or taken from savings.
20031.m: A deficit happens when you spend more than you have.

20032.q: Which of these counts as income for a young person?
20032.e: Income is money you receive. A mobile phone contract, a bus ticket and a cinema ticket, on the other hand, cost money and are expenses.
20032.m: Income is all the money that comes in to me.

a: Money you receive for your work
A fee for your bank account
20033.e: If you work, you get wages from your employer. For many adults, wages are their most important income.
20033.m: Wages are the payment for work done.

20034.q: What do you call wages before deductions such as AHV (old-age insurance) contributions are taken off?
20034.e: Gross wages are the full wages before deductions for social insurance. What arrives in your account afterwards is less.

20035.q: Mia helps in her neighbour’s garden for 6 hours and gets 12 francs an hour. How much does she earn?
20035.e: You work out hours times hourly pay: 6 times 12 makes 72 francs.
20035.m: You work out earnings as hours worked times hourly pay.

20036.q: What is the 13th month’s salary that many employees in Switzerland receive?
a: An extra month’s salary each year
20036.e: With a 13th month’s salary, the yearly salary is divided into 13 parts instead of 12, and the extra part is often paid in December. It applies if it is agreed in the employment contract.
20036.m: With a 13th month’s salary, you get one extra month’s pay in the year.

20037.q: What is the money called that parents in Switzerland receive for each child on top of their wages?
20037.e: The child allowance is one of the family allowances and is usually paid through the employer. It helps to cover the cost of children.
20037.m: In Switzerland, families receive a child allowance for each child.

a: Expenses that change from month to month
Expenses that are always the same
Income you receive from the state
Interest you get on a savings account
20038.e: Variable expenses go up and down, for example for leisure, clothes or eating out. They are easier to influence than fixed costs.
20038.m: Variable expenses are the easiest place to save.

20039.q: Which insurance premium has to be paid for every person in Switzerland?
20039.e: Basic health insurance is compulsory for all residents in Switzerland. A premium has to be paid for children too.
20039.m: Health insurance is compulsory for everyone in Switzerland.

20040.q: A jumper costs 60 francs and is reduced by 20 per cent. How much does it cost now?
20040.e: 20 per cent of 60 francs is 12 francs. 60 minus 12 makes 48 francs.
20040.m: With a discount, you take the percentage off the old price.

20041.q: Which expense covers a basic need?
20041.e: Basic needs are essential for life, for example food, housing and clothing. Games consoles or designer clothes are wishes you can afford on top.
20041.m: First you cover your basic needs, then you fulfil your wishes.

20042.q: A music subscription costs 15 francs a month. How much does it cost in a year?
20042.e: A year has 12 months: 12 times 15 makes 180 francs.
20042.m: Small monthly amounts add up to a large sum over a year.

a: The PIN of your bank card
The interest rate of an account
20043.e: IBAN stands for International Bank Account Number. With it you can transfer money to the right account at home and abroad.
20043.m: For a transfer you need the recipient’s IBAN.

20044.q: With which two letters does a Swiss IBAN begin?
20044.e: Every IBAN begins with the country code. For Switzerland this is CH, followed by check digits and the account number.
20044.m: You can recognise a Swiss IBAN by the letters CH at the start.

20045.q: What is a savings account for?
a: Putting money aside for the longer term
20045.e: In a savings account you put aside money you do not need straight away. You usually get some interest for it, but you can often only withdraw limited amounts.
20045.m: A savings account is for money you want to use later.

20046.q: What is the PIN code of a bank card used for?
a: To confirm payments and cash withdrawals
20046.e: The PIN is a secret number that proves you are the owner of the card. You must never tell anyone and never write it on the card.
20046.m: Always keep your PIN code to yourself.

20047.q: Sina has 250 francs in her account. She pays in 80 francs and then withdraws 120 francs. What is her balance now?
20047.e: First, 250 + 80 makes 330 francs. Then 330 minus 120 makes 210 francs.
20047.m: Deposits increase the balance and withdrawals reduce it.

20048.q: What does it mean if an account is “overdrawn”?
a: More money was taken out than was in the account
The bank has blocked the account
The account has just been opened
20048.e: If an account is overdrawn, the balance is negative. Banks usually charge high interest for this.
20048.m: An overdrawn account means you owe the bank money.

20049.q: Where can you see a list of all the deposits and withdrawals on an account?
20049.e: The bank statement shows all the movements on the account and the current balance. You get it on paper or through online banking.
20049.m: You should check your bank statement regularly.

a: A fee for shopping in a shop
20050.e: Anyone who takes out a loan from a bank pays interest on top of the amount borrowed. Interest is usually given as a percentage per year.
20050.m: Interest is the payment for borrowing money.

20051.q: Jan puts 500 francs into a savings account with 2 per cent interest per year. How much interest does he get after one year?
20051.e: You work out 2 per cent of 500 francs like this: 500 times 2 divided by 100 makes 10 francs.
20051.m: Yearly interest is calculated as a percentage of the savings.

20052.q: Who pays the interest when you put money into a savings account?
a: The bank pays it to the account holder
The account holder pays it to the bank
The state pays it to the bank
The employer pays it to the bank
20052.e: The bank may work with the saved money and, for example, lend it out to others. In return it pays the saver interest.
20052.m: If you save, the bank pays you interest.

a: Interest that is also calculated on interest received earlier
Interest that you have to pay twice
Interest that is paid out only once in your life
Interest that is set by the state
20053.e: If the interest stays in the account, it earns interest itself the next year. That way the savings grow faster and faster over time.
20053.m: With compound interest, the interest earns interest too.

20054.q: 1000 francs are invested for 2 years at 5 per cent interest, and the interest stays in the account. How much is in the account afterwards?
20054.e: After the 1st year it is 1000 times 1.05, so 1050 francs. After the 2nd year it is 1050 times 1.05, so 1102.50 francs.
20054.m: With compound interest, the new balance earns interest each year.

20055.q: Which institution sets the key interest rate in Switzerland?
20055.e: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) sets the key interest rate for the franc. It affects how high interest rates are at the banks.
20055.m: The National Bank uses the key interest rate to steer interest rates in Switzerland.

20056.q: A loan of 1200 francs is paid back without interest in 12 equal monthly instalments. How much is one instalment?
20056.e: You divide the amount by the number of instalments: 1200 divided by 12 makes 100 francs.
20056.m: With equal instalments, you divide the amount by the number of instalments.

20057.q: Someone borrows 2000 francs at 10 per cent interest per year. How much must be paid back in total after one year?
20057.e: 10 per cent of 2000 francs is 200 francs interest. 2000 + 200 makes 2200 francs.
20057.m: A loan costs more than the amount you originally borrowed.

20058.q: In Switzerland, what is the official procedure called that someone can use to collect unpaid debts?
20058.e: If bills are not paid, the creditor can start debt enforcement at the debt enforcement office. An entry in the debt enforcement register can later make it harder to find a flat, for example.
20058.m: Unpaid bills can lead to debt enforcement.

20059.q: From what age are you generally allowed to take out a consumer loan in Switzerland?
20059.e: Only someone who is of age, so at least 18 years old, can sign a loan agreement. The bank must also check whether you can afford the loan.
20059.m: In Switzerland you can only get a loan once you are of age.

20060.q: What is leasing, for example with a car?
a: You use the car for monthly payments but do not own it
You buy the car with cash straight away
The state gives you the car as a present
You sell your own car to the bank
20060.e: With leasing you pay monthly instalments over several years to use a car. The car still belongs to the leasing company.
20060.m: With leasing you pay to use something, not to own it.

20061.q: What does the state use taxes for?
a: For schools, roads and the police
For the profits of private companies
20061.e: With taxes the state pays for tasks that serve everyone, for example education, transport and safety.
20061.m: Taxes pay for services that benefit everyone.

a: The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities
20062.e: In Switzerland all three levels of the state collect taxes. That is why the tax burden differs depending on where you live.
20062.m: In Switzerland the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities collect taxes.

20063.q: Which document do adults in Switzerland fill in every year to state their income and wealth?
20063.e: In the tax return you state your income, wealth and deductions. The tax office uses it to work out the tax.
20063.m: With the tax return you report your income to the tax office.

20064.q: Why do people with a high income in Switzerland pay a bigger share of it in tax?
a: Because income tax rises as income rises
Because you can choose the amount of tax yourself
Because the tax is based on age
Because people with a high income may not make deductions
20064.e: Income tax is progressive: the higher the income, the higher the tax rate. That way those who are better off contribute more.
20064.m: If you earn more, you pay a higher percentage in tax.

20065.q: What is a public limited company (AG)?
a: A company whose capital is divided into shares
A company owned by only one person
20065.e: An AG belongs to its shareholders. Each share is a part of the company.
20065.m: If you own shares, you are a part-owner of the company.

a: A young company with a new business idea
A shop that has to close
20066.e: Start-ups are newly founded companies that often want to grow fast with an innovative idea. Many of them work with new technology.
20066.m: A start-up is a young company with a new idea.

20067.q: What is the public register called in which companies in Switzerland are entered?
20067.e: The commercial register lists, for example, the name, registered office, purpose and responsible people of a company. Anyone can look at it.
20067.m: In the commercial register you can look up who is behind a company.

a: A business owned by a single person
A business with exactly one product
A business with only one customer
A business that exists for only one day
20068.e: In a sole proprietorship one person runs the business on their own account. They are liable with all their private wealth.
20068.m: A sole proprietorship belongs to exactly one person.

20069.q: What share of all companies in Switzerland has fewer than 250 employees (as of 2021)?
20069.e: According to the Federal Statistical Office, about 99.7 per cent of companies in Switzerland are small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). They employ about two thirds of all employees.
20069.m: Almost all companies in Switzerland are small or medium-sized businesses.

20070.q: What is the money called that the owners themselves put into their company?
20070.e: Equity comes from the owners of the company. Money borrowed from banks, on the other hand, is called borrowed capital.
20070.m: Equity is the company owners’ own money.

a: Selling goods in your own village
20071.e: Exporting means selling goods or services to customers in other countries. Exports are very important for Switzerland.
20071.m: When exporting, goods leave your own country.

20072.e: When importing, a country buys goods from other countries, for example bananas or crude oil that it does not have itself.
20072.m: When importing, goods come into your own country.

20073.q: Which group of goods does Switzerland export most of by value (as of 2025)?
20073.e: According to the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security, medicines and other chemical and pharmaceutical products made up a good half of Swiss exports in 2025. Watches come far behind.
20073.m: The pharmaceutical industry is Switzerland’s biggest export sector.

20074.q: Which economic area is Switzerland’s most important trading partner overall (as of 2025)?
20074.e: Switzerland trades by far the most with the EU countries taken together. A large share of imports in particular comes from there, for example from Germany.
20074.m: The neighbours in the EU are the most important for Swiss trade.

a: A charge on goods brought across the national border
20075.e: Customs duties are charged when goods are brought into a country. They make foreign goods more expensive and bring the state income.
20075.m: A customs duty is due when goods cross the border.

a: Goods are swapped directly for other goods
Goods are paid for only with cash
Goods are sold on the internet
20076.e: Before there was money, people swapped goods directly, for example grain for tools. Money later made trade much easier.
20076.m: When bartering, you do not need money.

20077.q: What is the trade called that sells goods directly to end customers?
20077.e: Consumers shop in the retail trade, for example in a grocery shop. Wholesale trade, on the other hand, supplies other companies.
20077.m: In the retail trade, people shop for their own use.

20078.q: What usually happens to the price when demand for a product rises but supply stays the same?
a: The price always stays the same
20078.e: When more people want to buy something than is available, they are willing to pay more. That is why the price rises.
20078.m: If something is scarce and in demand, it becomes more expensive.

20079.q: In summer there are lots of local strawberries at the market. What usually happens to their price?
a: It is set by the state
20079.e: With a large supply, many sellers compete for customers. That is why strawberries are cheaper in season.
20079.m: A large supply usually leads to lower prices.

20080.q: In economics, what does the term “demand” mean?
a: The amount buyers want to buy at a certain price
The amount of money in the bank
20080.e: Demand shows how much of a product people would like to buy. It usually falls when the price rises.
20080.m: Demand is customers’ wish to buy something.

a: There is only one single supplier of a product
There are very many suppliers of a product
There are no buyers for a product
A product is free for everyone
20081.e: In a monopoly a supplier has no competition. It can therefore largely set the prices itself.
20081.m: Without competition, a monopolist can set the prices itself.

20082.q: What effect does strong competition between suppliers usually have for customers?
20082.e: When many companies compete for the same customers, they have to win them over with good prices and better quality.

20083.q: What is the price called at which the amount supplied and the amount demanded are equal?
20083.e: At the equilibrium price exactly as much is sold as people want to buy. No goods are left over and nobody goes without.
20083.m: Supply and demand meet at the equilibrium price.

20084.q: How do you calculate a company’s profit?
20084.e: You subtract all the costs from the money taken in. What is left is the profit.
